definition: He originated it;
sourceDefinition: He originated it; invented it; devised it; excogitated it; innovated it; made it, did it, produced it, caused it to be or exist, or brought it into existence, newly, for the first time, it not having been or existed before, and not after the similitude of anything pre-existing; syn. AixotaraEahu laA EalaY mivaAlK , (S,) and Asotaxorajahu , and A^aHodavahu , (Msb,) and A^abodaA^ahu ; (K, TA; but in both without the pronoun;) as also ↓ AbtdEh ; (Msb;) syn. AibotadaA^ahu , and A^aHodavahu , (Mgh,) and A^ano$aA^ahu , (K,) and badaA^ahu ; (TA;) and so ↓ badaEahu , aor. , (K, TA,) inf. n. badoEN ; (TA;) but A^abodaEa is more commonly used than badaEa . (TA.) You say, AbdE A@ll~`hu Alxaloqa God created the creation, not after any similitude. (Msb.) And in the Kur [lvii. 27], we find, ↓ wa rahobaAniy~apF A@botadaEuwhaA And monkery which they originated, or innovated. (TA.) And you say, ↓ badaEa Alr~akiy~apa , (IDrd, K,) inf. n. badoEN , (IDrd,) He produced, or fetched out, by his labour in digging, the water of the well; (IDrd, K;) and originated it; or made it to be for the first time, it not having been before. (IDrd.) And AbdE Alr~ajulu The man introduced an innovation, or what is termed a bidoEap ; [the object being understood;] as also ↓ AbtdE . (TA.) And AbdE Al$~aAEiru The poet produced a new saying, or new poetry, not after the similitude of anything preceding. (S, * K, * TA.) ― -b2- AbdEt Alr~aAHilapu , (S, K,) or Alr~ikaAbu , (Ks, Mgh,) The ridden camel, or travelling camel, became fatigued, or jaded, and broke down, or perished; (Ks, S, Mgh, K;) as though doing a new thing: (Ks, Mgh:) or the former phrase, (K,) followed by bihi , (TA,) she limped [with him], halted, or was slightly lame: (K, TA:) or she lay down upon her breast in the road, by reason of emaciation or disease: or she ceased from going on, by reason of fatigue, or of limping, or halting, or slight lameness; as though she did a new and unaccustomed thing: (TA:) or AbdAE is not without limping, or halting, or slight lameness, (K, TA,) accord. to certain of the Arabs of the desert; but, says AO, this is not at variance with the explanations given. (TA.) And A^ubodiEa biAlr~ajuli The man's camel which he rode became fatigued, or jaded: (S:) or A^ubodiEa bifulaAnK (Mgh, K) such a one's camel which he rode ceased from going on, by reason of fatigue or lameness: (Mgh:) or broke down, or perished, (K, TA,) or became fatigued, or jaded, (TA,) and he became unable to prosecute his journey; (K, TA;) and his beast became so fatigued that it was left to remain where it was; or stood still with him. (TA.) [See also A^uEobida bihi .] It is said in a proverb, A_i*aA Talabota AlbaATila A^ubodiEa bika [ When thou seekest what is vain, or false, thou wilt be prevented from attaining thine object ]. (TA.) ― -b3- A^abodaEa fulaAnN bifulaAnK (tropical:) Such a one prevented such a one from attaining his wish, ( qaTaEa bihi ,) and abstained from aiding, or assisting, him, and did not undertake the accomplishment of his want, (Lh, K, TA,) and was not [at hand] when he thought he would be. (TA.) ― -b4- A^abodaEato Huj~atuhu (tropical:) His argument, or plea, or the like, was, or became, vain, or false, or ineffectual: (Aboo-Sa'eed, K:) or was, or became, weak. (A, TA.) And A^ubodiEato Huj~atuhu (tropical:) His argument, or plea, &c., was rendered vain, or ineffectual. (Aboo-Sa'eed, K, * TA.) A^abodaEa bir~uhu bi$ukoriY wafaDoluhu wa A_yjaAbuhu biwaSofiY (assumed tropical:) [ His kindness has crippled my power of thanking, and his bounty, and the obligation which he has imposed, my power of description ]: so in the L; but in the O and K, qaSoduhu [ his intention ] is put in the place of fDlh ; and in the K, wAyjAbh is omitted: (TA:) said when one thanks another for his beneficence, acknowledging that his thanks are inadequate to his beneficence. definition: An innovation; a novelty; anything originated, invented, or innovated; anything made, done, produced, caused to be or exist, or brought into existence, newly, for the first time, it not having been...
sourceDefinition: An innovation; a novelty; anything originated, invented, or innovated; anything made, done, produced, caused to be or exist, or brought into existence, newly, for the first time, it not having been or existed before, and not after the similitude of anything pre-existing: (ISK:) a dissentient state or condition: (Msb:) a subst. from AibotidaAEN , like rifoEapN from AirotifaAEN , (Mgh, Msb,) and xilofapN from AixotilaAfN : (Mgh:) subsequently and generally applied to an addition, or an impairment, in religion: (Mgh, Msb:) or a novelty, or an innovation, in religion, after the completion [thereof ]: (S, K:) or an opinion declining, or swerving, from the right way, and an action, innovated after [the time of] the Prophet: (Lth, K:) or an action at variance with the Sunneh: (KT:) [generally a heretical innovation; or a new heresy: but] there is a bdEp not disapproved, termed bidoEapN mubaAHapN [ an allowed, or allowable, innovation ]; which is that whereof the goodness is attested by some principle in the law, or which is required to prevent some cause of evil; such as the Khaleefeh's seclusion of himself from the promiscuous classes of the people: (Msb:) there are two kinds of bdEp ; namely bidoEapN hudFY [ an innovation of a right kind ], and bidoEapN DalaAlK [ an innovation of an erroneous kind ]. (IAth.)

sourceDefinition: i. q. bidoEN , which see in three places, (S, Msb,) and ↓ mubotadaEN ; [i. e. Originated; invented; innovated; made, done, produced, caused to be or exist, or brought into existence, newly, for the first time, not having been or existed before, and not after the similitude of anything pre-existing; ] (S, Msb, K;) new; wonderful; unknown before. (TA.) You say, jiy^ota biA^amorK badiyEK Thou hast done a new thing; a wonderful thing; a thing unknown before: and ↓ A^amorN baAdiEN signifies the same as A^amorN badiyEN . (TA.) And jaA='a biA lbadiyEi , (S,) or A^ataY biAlbadayEi , (K,) said of a poet, (S, K,) He produced a new saying, or new poetry, not after the similitude of anything preceding. (TA.) And HabolN bad$yEN A new rope: (AHn:) or a rope begun to be twisted, not being yet a rope, but undone, then spun, then twisted again. (K.) And zimaAmN badiyEN A new nose-rein of a camel. (TA.) And rakiy~apN badiyEN A newly-dug well. (TA.) [See also badiYo'N .] And badiyEN alone, A skin for wine &c.: (S:) or a new skin for wine &c.: (K:) and a new skin for water or milk: an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant. (TA.) Hence the trad., A_in~a tihaAmapa kabadiyEi AlEasali HulowN A^aw~aluhu HulowN A=xiruhu [ Verily Tihámeh is like the skin, or new skin, of honey: the first part thereof is sweet: the last part thereof is sweet ]: (S, K *:) because honey does not change in flavour, whereas milk does change. (S.) ― -b2- Fat; as an epithet: (As, K:) pl. budoEN . (K.) -A2- Also i. q. ↓ mubotadiEN [ An originator, inventor, or innovator; one who makes, does, produces, causes to be or exist, or brings into existence, newly, for the first time, and not after the similitude of anything pre-existing ]: (S, K:) of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure faAEilN , like qadiyrN in the sense of qaAdirN ; from badaEa . (TA.) [See also bidoEN .] You say, Aall~`hu badiyEN Als~am`waAti waAlA^aroDi God is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, not after the similitude of anything pre-existing. (Aboo-Is-hák, S. *) And hence AlbadiyEu is a name of God, meaning The Originator of the creation, according to his own will, not after the similitude of anything pre-existing. (TA.)

definition: A long stone: pl.
sourceDefinition: A long stone: pl. baraATiylN : (S:) or a broad stone: (TA in art. brm :) or a stone (Seer, A, K) of an oblong form (A, TA) a cubit in length, (Seer, TA,) or an iron, long, broad, and hard by nature, (K,) not such as is made long, or sharpened or made sharp-pointed, by men, (TA,) with which the millstone is pecked ( tunoqaru [i. e., wrought into shape, and roughened in its surface, by pecking ]): so says Lth: (TA:) to this is sometimes likened the muzzle, or fore part of the nose and mouth, of a she-camel of high breed: (Lth, TA:) [and hence,] it signifies also (assumed tropical:) the muzzle, or fore part of the nose and mouth, of an old bear: (TA:) some say that the dual signifies two elongated stones, of the hardest kind, slender, and sharp-pointed, with which the millstone is pecked ( tunoqaru [explained above]). (TA.) Also, (K,) accord. to Sh, (TA,) A pickaxe, or stonecutter's pick; syn. miEowalN : (Sh, Msb, K:) pl. as above: accord. to IAar, what is called in Persian Asknh [app. a mistranscription, or a dial. var., of A_isokank ]. (TA.) -A2- A bribe; syn. ri$owapN : (Msb, K:) app. mentioned in the K as an Arabic word; and if so, the pronunciation with fet-h to the b is a vulgarism, since there is no such measure as faEoliylN : Abu-l-'Alà El-Ma'arree says that it is not known in this sense in the [classical] language of the Arabs; and it seems as though it were taken from the same word signifying “an oblong stone;” as though the bribe were likened to a stone that is thrown: (TA:) or it seems as though it were taken from the same word signifying a miEowal ; because therewith a thing is got out; (Msb;) and so El-Munáwee asserts it to be: (TA:) pl. as above. (Msb, K.) Hence the phrase, A^aloqamahu AlbiroTiyla [ He tipt him the bribe; conveyed it to him in like manner as one puts a morsel into another's mouth; somewhat like our phrase he greased his fist ]. (TA.) And the saying, AlbaraATiylu tanoSuru AlA^abaATiyli [ Bribes render victorious false allegations ]: (Msb, TA:) a prov. (Msb.)

definition: He kept, or applied himself, constantly, or perseveringly, to it;
sourceDefinition: He kept, or applied himself, constantly, or perseveringly, to it; (Lh, K;) namely, an affair, (TA in art. HfZ ,) or commerce, or traffic, &c. (Lh, TA.) -A2- bArk A@ll~`hu fiyka , (Fr, S, Msb, K,) and laka , and Ealayoka , (S, K,) and baArakaka , (Fr, S, K,) inf. n. mubaArakapN , (TK,) [ God bless, beatify, felicitate, or prosper, thee; ] God put in thee, (TA,) give thee, make thee to possess, (T, K,) barakap [i. e. a blessing, good of any kind, prosperity or good fortune, increase, &c.]. (TA, TK.) baAriko EalaY muHam~idK wa EalaY A=li muHam~adK (in a trad., TA,) means Continue Thou, or perpetuate Thou, (O God,) to Mohammad and to the family of Mohammad the eminence and honour which Thou hast given them: (K, TA:) [or still bless or beatify, or continue to bless or beatify, Mohammad &c.: though it may well be rendered simply bless or beatify &c.:] Az says that it is from baraka said of a camel, meaning “he lay down upon his breast in a place and clave thereto.” (TA.) And Aall~`huma baAriko lanaA fiY Almawoti , in another trad., means [ O God, bless us ] in the state to which death will bring us. (TA.) The Arabs say to the beggar, buwrika fiyka [ Mayest thou be blest; and, in the present day, Aall~`h yubaArik fiyk God bless thee ]; meaning thereby to repel him; not to pray for him: and by reason of frequency of usage of this phrase, they have made ↓ buwrik a noun: a poet [in Har $ry$ AlEdwY (app. Sherees, not Shereesh, El-'Adawee), in the TA Aboo-Fir'own,] says, taZun~u A^an~a buwrikFA yakofiyniY A_i*aA xarajotu baAsiTFA yamiyniY [ She imagines that the saying “Mayest thou be blest” will suffice me when I go forth stretching out my right hand for an alms]. (Har p. 378. [This verse is differently cited in the TA; for there, instead of tZn~ and xrjt , we find tuHib~u and gadawotu .]) ― -b2- [You also say of a man, bArk fiyhi , and lahu , &c., meaning He blessed him; i. e. he prayed God to bless him. ] ― -b3- See also 6.

definition: Many camels: (S, K:) or a herd of camels lying down upon their breasts: (K:) or any camels, males and females, lying down upon their breasts by the water or in the desert by reason of the heat of the...
sourceDefinition: Many camels: (S, K:) or a herd of camels lying down upon their breasts: (K:) or any camels, males and females, lying down upon their breasts by the water or in the desert by reason of the heat of the sun or by reason of satiety: (TA:) or all the camels of the people of an encampment, that return to them from pasture in the evening, or afternoon, to whatever number they may amount, even if they be thousands: (K:) one thereof is termed ↓ baArikN ; (K;) the two words being like tajorN and taAjirN ; (TA;) fem. ↓ baArikapN : (K:) pl. buruwkN , (S, K,) i. e., pl. of barokN . (S.) -A2- Also, (S, Msb, K,) and ↓ birokapN , which is with kesr, (S, K,) The breast (S, Msb, K) of a camel: (Msb, TA:) this is the primary signification: (TA:) as some say, the former signifies the breast of the camel with which he crushes a thing beneath it: (TA:) and (K) accord. to Lth, (TA,) the latter is the part next to the ground of the skin of the breast of the camel; (or, as in the 'Eyn, of the skin of the belly of the camel and of the portion of the breast next to it; TA;) as also the former: (K:) or, as some say, the former is the middle of the breast, where [ the two prominences of flesh called ] the fahodataAni conjoin at their upper parts: (Ham p. 66:) or the latter is pl. of the former, like as HiloyapN is of HaloYN : or the former is of man; and the latter, of others: or the former is the interior of the breast; (or, as Yaakoob says, the middle of the breast; TA;) and the latter, the exterior thereof: (K:) or the former is the breast, primarily of the camel, because camels lie down ( taboruku ) upon the breast; and metaphorically of others. (Ham p. 145.) ― -b2- Hence, barok Al$~itaA='i (tropical:) The first part of winter; (L, TA; *) and the main part thereof. (L.) ― -b3- And hence, (TA,) Alburuwku is an appellation applied to (tropical:) The stars composing the constellation of the Scorpion, of which are Alz~ubaAnaY and AlA_ikoliylu and Alqalobu and Al$~awolapu [the 16th and 17th and 18th and 19th of the Mansions of the Moon], which rise [aurorally] in the time of intense cold; as is also Aljuvuwmu : (L, TA: *) or, accord. to IF, to a nawo' of the A^anowaA=' of AljawozaA=' ; because the AnwA' thereof do not set [aurorally] without there being during their period a day and a night in which the camels lie upon their breasts ( taboruku ) by reason of the vehemence of the cold and rain. (TA.)

definition: A mode, or manner, of buruwk [i.
sourceDefinition: A mode, or manner, of buruwk [i. e. of a camel's kneeling and lying down upon the breast ]; (S, * O, * K;) a noun like rikobapN and jilosapN . (S, O.) One says, maA A^aHosana birokapa h`*ihi Aln~aAqapi [ How good is this she-camel's manner of lying down on the breast! ]. (S.) -A2- See also barokN . -A3- A HawoD [i. e. watering-trough or tank ]: (K:) or the like thereof, (S, TA,) dug in the ground, not having raised sides constructed for it above the surface of the ground; (TA;) and ↓ birokN signifies the same: (Lth, K:) said to be so called because of the continuance of the water therein: (S:) pl. birakN , (S, Msb, K,) which Az found to be applied by the Arabs to the tanks, or cisterns, that are constructed with baked bricks, and plastered with lime, in the road to Mekkeh, and at its wateringplaces; sing. birokapN ; and sometimes a brkp is a thousand cubits [in length], and less, and more: but the watering-troughs, or tanks, that are made for the rain-water, and not cased with baked bricks, are called A^aSonaAEN , sing. SinoEN : (TA:) [ birokapN often signifies a basin; a pool; a pond; and a lake: and in the present day, also a bay of the sea: and a reach of a river: ] also a place where water remains and collects, or collects and stagnates, or remains long and becomes altered. (ISd, K.)

definition: (T, S, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and bugaAvN and bigaAvN ;
sourceDefinition: (T, S, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and bugaAvN and bigaAvN ; (A, Mgh, K;) only the second of these three mentioned by Sb; (TA;) but the second and third asserted to be correct by Yoo; (AZ, TA;) and the last heard by Az; (TA;) or neither of these two is allowable; (Msb;) A bird that does not prey, and such as one does not desire to make an object of prey because it is not eaten: (T, Msb:) or small birds that do not prey, such as sparrows and the like; [a coll. gen. n.;] n. un. with p : (Mgh:) or [accord. to Lth,] a certain dust-coloured bird, (T, A, K,) of the birds of the water, ash-coloured, and long-necked; as also ↓ A^abogavu ; pl. [of the latter] bugovN and A^abaAgivu : (T:) [but this appears to be wrong; for AM says, in the T,] Lth makes the bgAv and the Abgv to be one, asserting them to be of aquatic birds; but in my opinion, the former is different from the latter: as to the latter, it is a well-known kind of aquatic bird, so called because it is of the colour termed bugovap , i. e. white inclining to xuDorap [explained above, voce bugovapN ]: but as to the bgAv , it is any bird that is not one of prey: and the word is said to be a coll. gen. n., signifying the class of birds that are objects of prey: (TA:) ISk says that the bagaAv is a bird of a colour inclining to that of dust, (S, Msb, *) a little less than the raxamap [or vultur percnopterus ], (S,) or less than the rxmp , (Msb,) slow in flight: (S, Msb:) but IB says that this is a mistake in two points of view; first, because bgAv is a [coll.] gen. n., of which the n. un. is with p , like as is that of HamaAmN ; and secondly, because it applies to the class of birds that do not prey; but the ↓ A^abogav is a bird of the colour of dust, and this may be a bird of prey, and it may be not a bird of prey: (TA:) AZ says that bgAv signifies the [ species of vulture called ] raxam ; and the n. un. is with p others, the young ones of the rxm and birds of the crowkind: or [ birds ] like the [ hawks called ] sawaAdiq [pl. of sawodaqN ], not predaceous: in the T, it is said to be [ a kind of bird ] like the [ hawk called ] baA$aq , that does not prey upon any other bird: (TA:) or bigaAvN and bugaAvN (ISd, K) and bagaAvN (K) signify the worst [or most ignoble ] of birds, (ISd, K, [the latter giving this as a second and distinct signification,]) and such as do not prey: (ISd, TA:) Fr says, bagaAvu AlT~ayori signifies the worst of birds, and such as do not prey; and bugaAvN and bigaAvN are dial. vars.: (S:) the pl. is bigovaAnN , (Sb, T, S, Msb, K,) accord. to those who make bgAv a sing., (Yoo, S, Msb, TA,) or accord. to those who make the sing. to be with p ; (T, TA;) or those who apply bagaAvapN [as a n. un.] to the male and the female make bagaAvN to be pl. [or rather a coll. gen. n.]; (Yoo, S, Msb;) as is done in the case of naEaAmapN and naEaAmN : (Yoo, S:) ISd says that bagaAvapN , with fet-h, is the n. un., applied alike to the male and the female: (TA:) [and Fei says,] it is not allowable to pronounce this with damm or with kesr to the first letter: (Msb:) but Yoo asserts both of these forms to be used: (AZ, TA:) and bgAvp is said to signify a weak bird. (TA.) It is said in a prov., A_in~a AlbagaAva biA^aroDinaA yasotanosiru (S, A, Msb, K *) Verily the bgAv in our land becomes [ like ] a vulture, or become [ like ] vultures: (Msb:) applied to the low person who becomes of high rank: (A:) meaning (tropical:) the weak in our land becomes strong: (Msb:) or he who makes himself our neighbour becomes mighty, strong, or of high rank, by our means, (S, K, TA,) acquiring the might, or strength, of the vulture, after having been low, or mean, in condition. (TA.)

definition: Of a white colour inclining to xuDorap [which here app.
sourceDefinition: Of a white colour inclining to xuDorap [which here app. means a dark, or ashy, dustcolour ]: (T:) [or of a colour resembling that of ashes: (see 1:)] or dust-coloured: (A:) or of a colour near to that of dust: (S:) an epithet, like A^aHomaru : [fem. bagovaA='u : and] pl. bugovN : and sometimes, when used as a subst., it has for pl. A^abaAgivu . (IB, TA.) You say TaAy^irN A^abogavu A bird of the colour above described: (T, S:) whether it be a bird of prey or not: see bagaAvN in two places: (IB, TA:) and SaqorN A^abogavu [ a hawk of that colour. ]; (ISh, A;) as well as A^aHowaY and A^aboyaDu ; i. e., that wherewith men take game. (ISh, TA.) bagovaA='u applied to sheep or goats, (S, K,) or, as in some lexicons, to sheep, (TA,) is like raqoTaA='u ; (S, K;) [ Black speckled with white; or the reverse; ] or in which are blackness and whiteness, with predominance of the latter colour: (TA:) or $aApN bagovaA='u and ganamN bugovN signify a sheep or goat, and sheep or goats, in which are blackness and whiteness. (A.) ― -b2- Also, [as a subst.,] A certain bird, (K, TA,) dustcoloured, in truth different from the bagaAv , as shown above: see the latter word: (TA:) pl. bugovN and A^abaAgivu . (T, TA.) You say, huwa mino A^abaAgivi AlT~ayori [ He is of the birds thus called ]. (A.) ― -b3- And AlA^abogavu signifies The lion; (TS, K;) because he is of the colour termed bugovapN . (TA.) ― -b4- And AlbagovaA='u (tropical:) The medley, or mixed or promiscuous multitude or collection, of men or people; or of the lowest or basest or meanest sort, or refuse, or riffraff, thereof; (S, A, K;) the commonalty, or vulgar, and collective body, of the people. (S.) One says, xaraja falaAnN fiY AlbagovaA='i and AlgavoraA='i (tropical:) Such a one went forth among the medley, &c., of the people. (A.) And daxalonaA fiY AlbagovaA='i (tropical:) We entered among the commonalty, or vulgar, and the collective body, of the people. (S.)

definition: , inf. n. tabokiytN , He reprehended, reproved, blamed, chid, or reproached, him, for an affair, or for a crime or the like; (S, A, Msb, K;) accord. to some, with justice; (TA;) or he did so...
sourceDefinition: , inf. n. tabokiytN , He reprehended, reproved, blamed, chid, or reproached, him, for an affair, or for a crime or the like; (S, A, Msb, K;) accord. to some, with justice; (TA;) or he did so severely; (S, * TA;) and threatened him; (TA;) and declared his deed to be evil; (Msb;) as when one says, “ O wicked man! wast thou not ashamed? didst thou not fear God? ” (TA:) and sometimes this is done by using an enunciative phrase, such as the saying of Abraham, [mentioned in the Kur xxi. 64,] “ Nay, the chief of them, this, did it; ” for thus he said to reprove their worship of idols; (Msb;) and it may be by means of the hand, and a staff or stick, and the like. (Hr, TA.) ― -b2- He accused him, to his face, ( Aisotaqobalahu , q. v.,) of that which he disliked, or hated; (As, A, K;) as also ↓ bakatahu , (As, K,) aor. , inf. n. bakotN . (TA.) ― -b3- He overcame him, biAlHuj~api [ with the argument, allegation, or plea ]; (S, A, K;) as also ↓ bakatahu ; (A, TA;) and both, he obliged him to be silent by reason of his inability to reply. (A, * TA.) You say, bk~thu Hat~aY A^asokatahu , and ↓ bakatahu , He overcame him [by an argument, &c.,] so that he silenced him. definition: [The balsam-tree;
sourceDefinition: [The balsam-tree; or the species that produces the balsam of Mekkeh; i. e., the amyris opobalsamum; ] a certain kind of tree, (M,) or shrub, resembling the Hin~aA=' , (K,) having many leaves, inclining to white, in odour resembling the sa*aAb [or rue ], (TA,) the berry of which has an unguent, (Lth, M, TA,) which is hot, (Lth, TA,) and its unguent is in great request: (Lth, K, TA:) its unguent [ opobalsamum ] is more potent than its berry [ carpobalsamum ], and its berry is more so than its wood [ xylobalsamum ] : the best of its wood is the smooth, tawny-coloured, pungent and sweet in odour: it is hot and dry in the second degree; and its berry is a little hotter than it: its wood opens stoppages of the nose, and is good for the sciatica and vertigo and headache, and clears cloudiness of the eye, and is good for asthma and oppression of the breath, and for flaccidity of the womb, used by fumigation; it is also beneficial in cases of barrenness, and counteracts poisons and the bite of vipers: (the Minháj, TA:) it is said in the K and in the Minháj, and by most of the physicians and those who treat of drugs, that it grows only at 'Eyn-Shems, in the neighbourhood of El-Káhireh, the place called ElMatareeyeh; but MF observes that this is strange, as it is well known that it is mostly found in the district of El-Hijáz, between the Harameyn and El-Yembo' , whence it is conveyed to all countries: the truth, however, is, that it ceased to grow at ' Eyn-Shems in the latter part of the eighth century [of the Flight], and it was endeavoured [successfully] to be made to grow in El-Hijáz. (TA.) [See also De Sacy's “ Abd-allatif, ” p. 89.]

definition: [The hazel-nut; or hazel-nuts; so in the present day;] a certain thing that is eaten; (Msb;) i. q. jil~awoz : (IDrd, K:) or, as some say, like jl~wz ; brought from an island; the best whereof is the...
sourceDefinition: [The hazel-nut; or hazel-nuts; so in the present day;] a certain thing that is eaten; (Msb;) i. q. jil~awoz : (IDrd, K:) or, as some say, like jl~wz ; brought from an island; the best whereof is the fresh, heavy, white, and sweet in taste; the old being bad: it is beneficial as a remedy for palpitation, parched with anise-seed; and for poisons, and wasting of the kidneys, and burning of the urine; and with pepper, it excites the venereal faculty; with sugar, it removes cough; and the shell thereof, burnt, and applied as a collyrium, sharpens the sight: (TA:) they assert that the suspending it upon the upper arm preserves from scorpions, (K,) i. e., from their stinging: (TA:) the moistening of the top of the head of a child with the powder of it when burnt, together with oil, removes the blueness of its eyes and the redness of its hair: and the Indian kind thereof is an antidote very beneficial to the eyes: (K, TA:) but in some copies of the K, [and so in the CK,] instead of liloEayonayoni , we here find liloEin~iyni [ for the impotent in respect of the venereal faculty ]: (TA:) [it is said in the Msb that most hold the n to be augmentative: but this is not the case; for] the word is Persian [arabicized, from funoduqo ]: (K:) [it is a coll. gen. n.:] n. un. with p : pl. banaAdiqu . (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence, Bullets, i. e.] certain things that one shoots, (S, Msb, K,) made of clay: (Msb:) n. un. with p : (S, Msb, K:) the latter signifies a piece of clay, made round, which one shoots, or casts; or i. q. julaAhiqN : (Mgh:) it is said in the Shifá el-Ghaleel to be an arabicized word: (TA:) pl. as above. (S, Msb.) [See a prov. voce HidaA^apN . Hence qawosu Albunoduqi The crossbow. In modern Arabic, bunoduq is also applied to Balls of any kind of the size of hazel-nuts: n. un. with p .]

definition: , (S, A, Msb,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Msb,) aor. , (Msb,) inf. n. bahorN , (S, Msb, K,) He overcame him: (S, A, Msb, K:) he overpowered him; subdued him: (TA:) he surpassed him; excelled him. (Msb.) See also 3. You say, baharato fulaAnapu Aln~isaA='a Such a woman surpassed the [other] women in beauty. (S.) And bahara [alone] He excelled in knowledge &c.; or he was, or became, accomplished, or perfect, in every excellence, and in goodliness. (S, K.) And bahara Alqamaru , (S, K,) or bahara Alqamaru Aln~ujuwma , (TA,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. buhuwrN , (TA,) (tropical:) The moon overcame with its light the light of the stars. (S, K, TA.) And baharati Al$~amosu AlA^aroDa (assumed tropical:) The light of the sun overspread the earth. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] bahara , aor. , (TA,) inf. n. bahorN and buhuwrN , (K,) (tropical:) It shone, or shone brightly: (K, TA:) and Als~aHaAbapu ↓ tabah~arati (tropical:) The cloud shone, or shone brightly. (K.) -A2- baharahu , (S, A,) aor. , inf. n. buhorN , (S,) also signifies (tropical:) It (a load, or burden, S, A, and running, A) [ caused him to be out of breath; interrupted his breathing; (see buhorN ;)] caused to pant, or breathe [ shortly or] uninterruptedly. (S, A.) ― -b2- Also, (ISh, JK, TA,) inf. n. bahorN , (K, TA,) (assumed tropical:) He stopped his breath by beating, or by squeezing his throat, or throttling him, or by any other means: (ISh, TA:) (assumed tropical:) he plied him, or worked him, ( EaAlajahu ,) until he became out of breath, or until he panted: (JK, TA:) (assumed tropical:) he imposed upon him a thing that was above his power, or ability. (K, TA.) A poet says, A_in~a Albaxiyla A_i*aA saA^alota baharotahu Verily the niggardly, when thou askest of him, thou stoppest his breath. (ISh, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence,] buhira , i. q. Anbhr , as explained below. (K.) -A3- baharahaA , (JK,) or baharahaA bibuhotaAnK , (TA,) inf. n. bahorN , (K,) He reproached her, or accused her, falsely; (JK;) he aspersed her; calumniated her; or brought a false accusation against her. (K, * TA.) You say, baharahaA bika*aA He reproached her falsely with, or accused her falsely of, such a thing. (JK.) [See also 8.]

definition: inf. n. of 1 [q. v.]. (S, Msb, K.) You say, bahorFA lahu , an imprecation, meaning May he be overcome! (A:) or i. q. taEosFA lahu [ may he fall, having stumbled! or stumble and fall! &c.]: (AA, S,...
sourceDefinition: inf. n. of 1 [q. v.]. (S, Msb, K.) You say, bahorFA lahu , an imprecation, meaning May he be overcome! (A:) or i. q. taEosFA lahu [ may he fall, having stumbled! or stumble and fall! &c.]: (AA, S, K:) and thus used [app. in the latter sense] as an imprecation, accord. to Sb, it has no verb, but is put in the accus. case on the supposition of a verb. (TA.) One says also, ↓ quhorFA wabuhorFA , with damm to each. (TA in art. qhr .) And bahorFA maA A^asoxaAhu [ May he fall, having stumbled! &c.: how bountiful is he! ], like as one says taEosFA lahu [when not meaning it to be understood as an imprecation]. (A.) ― -b2- It also signifies Distance, or remoteness: (K:) and remoteness from good or prosperity. (TA.) ― -b3- Disappointment. (IAar, TA.) ― -b4- Wonder; syn. EajabN . (K.) One says, bahorA meaning EajabFA [for A^aEojabu EajabFA I do wonder: or wonderful! ]. (S.) So [sometimes] in the phrase bahorFA lahu [ I do wonder at him, or it ]. (IAar, TA.) ― -b5- Love. (K.) Accord. to some, bahorFA lakumo means Love to you. (JK.) ― -b6- AlA^azowaAju valAavapN zawoju bahorK wazawoju dahorK wazawoju mahorK is a saying of the Arabs, meaning Husbands are three: a husband who overcomes the eyes by his goodliness, (S,) or a husband of noble race, though he may be of little wealth; (TA;) and a husband prepared for the accidents, or calamities, of fortune; and a husband from whom a dowry is got, (S,) or a husband who has not nobility of race, and who therefore doubles the dowry to make himself desired. definition: A certain thing with which one weighs;
sourceDefinition: A certain thing with which one weighs; (S, Msb, K;) the weight of three hundred pounds: (Fr, IAar, A'Obeyd, S, K:) thought by A'Obeyd to be not Arabic, but Coptic; (S;) having this signification in Coptic; (JK;) but thought by Az to be pure Arabic: (TA:) or four hundred pounds: or six hundred: or a thousand: (K:) and, (K,) or as some say, (TA,) one half of a load (K, TA) borne by a camel, (TA,) containing four hundred pounds, (K, TA,) in the dial. of Syria: (TA:) or a load borne by a camel: (Kt:) or a camel-load of household-goods or furniture and utensils: (As:) and commodities, or utensils, or the like, of the sea; expl. by mataAEa AlbaHori [perhaps a mistranscription for mataAEa Alt~ajori or Alt~ujuri , commodities, or goods, of the merchants: the poet Bureyk El-Hudhalee speaks of camels bearing buhaAr ]. (JK, K.) It is said that Talhah the son of 'Obeyd-Allah left a hundred buhaAr , in each bhAr of which was three hundred-weight of gold (S, TA) and silver; (TA;) bhAr being thus made to signify a receptacle: (S, TA:) accord. to As and Kt, the meaning is, a hundred camel-loads. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: [The aorta; so in the present day;] a certain vein [or artery ], (S, A, K,) in the back, (K,) lying within, or at the inner side of, the back-bone (A'Obeyd, A, TA) and the heart, (A'Obeyd, TA,) the severing of which causes death: (A'Obeyd, S, A:) it is name given to each of two veins [or arteries, or the two portions of the aorta which are called the aorta ascendens and aorta descendens, ] which issue from the heart, and from which then branch off all the other arteries: (S:) and, (K,) or as some say, (TA,) the wariyd [i. e. either the carotid artery or the external jugular vein ] of the neck: (K:) and, (K,) or as some say, (TA,) [the vein in the arm called ] the A^akoHal : (K:) or, accord. to the more full description of IAth, a certain vein [or artery ] arising from the head, and extending to the foot, and having arteries which communicate with most of the extremities and the body: what is in the head is called the naAm~ap ; and hence the saying, A^asokata A@ll~`hu naAm~atahu , meaning “God killed him,” or “may God kill him!” and it extends to the throat, and is there called the wariyd ; and to the chest, and is there called [ especially ] the A^abohar [meaning the aorta ascendens ]; and to the back, and is there called the watiyn [meaning the aorta descendens ]; and the heart is suspended to it; and it extends to the thigh, and is there called the nasaA ; and to the shank, and is there called the SaAfin : the ' in it is augmentative. (TA.) You say, qaTaEa A^aboharahu [ It severed his aorta ]; meaning (tropical:) it (pain) destroyed him. (A.) ― -b2- Also The back: (K:) or the place of the vein [or artery ] so called. (As, in art. xdE of the S.) One says, fulaAnN $adiydN AlA^abohari Such a one is strong in the back: (TA:) or strong in the place of the vein [or artery ] called the Abhr . (As, ubi suprà.) ― -b3- And The back of the curved part of the extremity of a bow: (K:) or the part between the TAy^if and the kuloyap : (S, K:) in the bow is its kabid , which is the part between the two extremities of its string or the like; then, next to this, the kuloyap ; then, next to this, the A^abohar ; then, the TaAy^if ; then, the siy^ap , which is the curved part of the extremity. (As.) ― -b4- And A tent-pole. (JK.) ― -b5- And The shorter side of a feather: (K:) [or] so A^abaAhiru [which is the pl.]: (JK:) [or] the latter signifies the feathers (Lh, S) of the wing (Lh) of a bird (Lh, S) next after those called AlxawaAfiY , (Lh,) [ and ] next [ before ] those called AlkulaY : (S:) the first of them are those called AlqawaAdimu , (S,) four in number, in the fore part of the wing; (Lh;) the next, AlmanaAkibu , (Lh, S,) also four; (Lh;) the next, AlxawaAfiY , (Lh, S,) also four; (Lh;) the next, AlA^abaAhiru , (Lh, S,) also four; (Lh;) and the next, AlkulaY [which are also four]. (S.)

(KL.) -A2- tabina , (T, S, M, K,) aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. tabanN , (T, S,) or tabonN , (M, K,) and tabaAnapN (T, S, * M, K) and tabaAniyapN , (M,) He was, or became, intelligent, sagacious, skilful, or knowing; syn. faTina , (K,) or SaAra faTinFA ; (S;) and nice, or minute, in inspection (S, K) into affairs: (S:) or tabaAnapN signifies the being very intelligent or sagacious or skilful or knowing, and nice, or minute, in inspection; as also TabaAnahN ; accord. to AO and AA: (T:) these two words signify the same (T, S, M *) accord. to [most of] the leading authorities: (T:) and Yaakoob asserts that the t is a substitute for T : (M:) [or the reverse seems to be the case in the opinion of Az, who here remarks that there are many instances of the change of t into T :] or the former is in evil; and the latter, in good: (M:) or, accord. to Lth, Tabina means in evil; and tabina , in good; so that he makes TbAnp to be in deceiving, or beguiling, and suddenly, or unexpectedly, attacking or destroying: but En-Nadr says the contr.; and accord. to him, TabanN signifies the having knowledge of affairs, and intelligence, or sagacity, and science: (T:) and ↓ tb~n , inf. n. tatobiynN signifies the same as tabina : (K:) or he inspected nicely, or minutely: as in a trad. in which it is said, respecting a woman whose husband has died leaving her pregnant, yunofaqu EalayohaA mino jamiyEi AlmaAli Hat~aY tab~anotumo maA tab~anotumo , meaning [ She shall be expended upon from the whole of the property ] until ye make a nice, or minute, inspection [into the circumstances of the case], and say otherwise, (T, S,) i. e., that she shall be expended upon from her own share: (T:) and so in another trad., in which it is said, A_in~a Alr~ajula layatakal~amu biAlkalimapi yutab~inu fiyhaA yahowiY bihaA fiY Aln~aAri , (A 'Obeyd, T, M,) i. e. [ Verily a man will say a saying ] in which he will be nice, or minute [in expression, whereby he will fall into the fire of Hell]: (TA:) here A 'Obeyd thinks the meaning to be the making language obscure, or abstruse, and disputing in a matter of religion. (T.) You say also, tabina lahu (T, M, TA) He understood it; or knew it; or had knowledge, or was cognizant, of it; (TA;) i. q. Tabina . (M.)

(KL.) -A2- tabina , (T, S, M, K,) aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. tabanN , (T, S,) or tabonN , (M, K,) and tabaAnapN (T, S, * M, K) and tabaAniyapN , (M,) He was, or became, intelligent, sagacious, skilful, or knowing; syn. faTina , (K,) or SaAra faTinFA ; (S;) and nice, or minute, in inspection (S, K) into affairs: (S:) or tabaAnapN signifies the being very intelligent or sagacious or skilful or knowing, and nice, or minute, in inspection; as also TabaAnahN ; accord. to AO and AA: (T:) these two words signify the same (T, S, M *) accord. to [most of] the leading authorities: (T:) and Yaakoob asserts that the t is a substitute for T : (M:) [or the reverse seems to be the case in the opinion of Az, who here remarks that there are many instances of the change of t into T :] or the former is in evil; and the latter, in good: (M:) or, accord. to Lth, Tabina means in evil; and tabina , in good; so that he makes TbAnp to be in deceiving, or beguiling, and suddenly, or unexpectedly, attacking or destroying: but En-Nadr says the contr.; and accord. to him, TabanN signifies the having knowledge of affairs, and intelligence, or sagacity, and science: (T:) and ↓ tb~n , inf. n. tatobiynN signifies the same as tabina : (K:) or he inspected nicely, or minutely: as in a trad. in which it is said, respecting a woman whose husband has died leaving her pregnant, yunofaqu EalayohaA mino jamiyEi AlmaAli Hat~aY tab~anotumo maA tab~anotumo , meaning [ She shall be expended upon from the whole of the property ] until ye make a nice, or minute, inspection [into the circumstances of the case], and say otherwise, (T, S,) i. e., that she shall be expended upon from her own share: (T:) and so in another trad., in which it is said, A_in~a Alr~ajula layatakal~amu biAlkalimapi yutab~inu fiyhaA yahowiY bihaA fiY Aln~aAri , (A 'Obeyd, T, M,) i. e. [ Verily a man will say a saying ] in which he will be nice, or minute [in expression, whereby he will fall into the fire of Hell]: (TA:) here A 'Obeyd thinks the meaning to be the making language obscure, or abstruse, and disputing in a matter of religion. (T.) You say also, tabina lahu (T, M, TA) He understood it; or knew it; or had knowledge, or was cognizant, of it; (TA;) i. q. Tabina . (M.)

definition: A small road branching off from a main road: (As, S, K:) a Persian word, arabicized: (As, S:) pl.
sourceDefinition: A small road branching off from a main road: (As, S, K:) a Persian word, arabicized: (As, S:) pl. tur~ahaAtN (As, S, K) and tur~uhaAtN . (TA.) ― -b2- A [ desert, such as is termed qaforN , (see 1,) or] mafaAzapN , and SaHoraA='u . (JK.) ― -b3- The first in this paragraph is the primary signification: (TA:) and hence, metaphorically, (As, S,) (tropical:) A false, or vain, saying or action or affair; (As, JK, S K;) as also ↓ tur~ahN : (S, K:) pl. of the former, tur~ahaAtN (JK, S, K *) [and tur~uhaAtN , as above]; and of the latter, taraAriyahu : (S, K: *) or the primary signification of tur~ahaAtN is qifaArN : [see 1:] and it is metaphorically applied to (tropical:) false, or vain, sayings or actions or affairs; (K;) and unprofitable sayings: (Z, K, TA:) or, accord. to Az, false, or vain, affairs: and the sing. is ↓ tur~ahN : or, accord. to IB, this last is pl. of tur~ahapN : [or rather a coll. gen. n.:] or, as some say, it is a sing.: (TA:) and accord. to Lth it signifies the act of lying, and confusing [ truth and falsehood ]. (Har p. 165.) [Sometimes it is followed by a syn., to give greater force to the signification:] one says Altur~ahaAtu AlbasaAbisu and Altur~ahaAtu AlS~aHaASiHu : and sometimes the former word is used as a prefixed noun governing the gen. case [so that one says tur~ahaAtu AlbasaAbisu and tr~hAtu AlS~aHaASiHi : AlS~aHoSaHu is mentioned in the K, in this art., as a syn. of Alt~ur~ahapu ]. (S.) ― -b4- Also A calamity; a misfortune; an evil accident: (JK, * K:) pl. [ tur~ahaAtN and] taraAriyahu . (JK.) ― -b5- Wind. (JK, K.) ― -b6- Clouds, or a collection of clouds. (JK, * K.) -A2- A certain small creeping thing ( duwayob~ap ) [ found ] in the sand. (JK, K.)

definition: The tree of the balas [or common fig;
sourceDefinition: The tree of the balas [or common fig; ficus carica ]: or the bls itself: (M:) [or both; i. e.] a certain well-known kind of tree; and the fruit thereof: (TA:) [or the latter only;] a certain thing that is eaten, (S, Msb,) well known: (Msb, K:) fresh and ripe, it is the most approved of fruits, and the most nutritious, and the least flatulent; drawing, dissolvent, having the property of opening obstructions of the liver and spleen, and laxative; and the eating much thereof engenders lice: (K: [the last word in this explanation in the K is muqomilN , which I render agreeably with the TK, having found no authoritative explanation of it: but in my own opinion, the meaning of this word is fattening, for qamila signifies “ he became fat after being lean; ” and my opinion is confirmed by what here follows:]) it is a pleasant fruit, having nothing redundant, and a nice food, quick of digestion, and a very useful medicine, for it has a laxative property, dissolves phlegm, purifies the kidneys, removes sand of the bladder, opens obstructions of the liver and spleen, and fattens the body: it is also said, in a trad., that it stops hemorrhoids, and is good for the gout: (Bd xcv. 1:) AHn says, there are many kinds thereof; that of the desert, that of the cultivated land, that of the plains, and that of the mountains; and it is abundant in the land of the Arabs: and he adds, on the authority of an Arab of the desert, of the Saráh, that it is, in the Saráh, very abundant, and allowed to be commonly taken; and is eaten by the people there in its fresh state, and also dried and stored: (M:) the word is Arabic: (Msb:) [a coll. gen. n.:] n. un. with p . (S, M, Msb.) This is what is meant in the Kur [xcv. 1], where it is said, waAlt~iyni waAlz~ayotuwni , (T, S, M, Msb,) accord. to I'Ab, (T, S, Bd, Jel,) and the generality of the interpreters: (Msb:) or these two words mean two mountains (S, M, Bd, Jel) of Syria, (S, Jel,) or of the Holy Land, (Bd,) that produce the two fruits thus named: (Jel:) or, accord. to a Syrian interpreter, certain mountains extending from Hulwán, to Hemdán, and the mountains of Syria: (Fr, T:) or Damascus and Jerusalem: (M, Bd:) or the mosque of Damascus and that of Jerusalem: (Bd:) or two mosques in Syria: accord. to AHn, the former is the name of a mountain in the country of Ghatafán; but there is no mountain thus called in Syria. (M.) ― -b2- Among the kinds of tiyn is that called tiynu Aljum~ayozi [ The sycamore-fig; ficus sycomorus; also called the Egyptian fig ]; describe voce jum~ayozN , q. v. (AHn.) ― -b3- [ Alt~iynu AlA_iforanojiY~u and Alt~iynu Al$~awokiY~u are appellations applied in the present day to The Indian fig, or prickly pear; cactus opuntia: Forskål (Flora Aegypt. Arab. p. lxvii) applies the former name to the cochineal Indian fig; cactus cochinillifer. ] ― -b4- Alt~iynapu also signifies (assumed tropical:) The anus: (AHn, M, K:) [opposed to Aljum~ayozapu as meaning “ the pudendum muliebre. ”.]

(Aboo-Turáb, TA.) taAha baSarahu [in the CK, erroneously, qaSoruhu ] signifies also taAfa , (K, TA, [in the CK nAfa ,] i. e., accord. to 'Arrám, He looked at a thing continually, or continuously ( fiY dawaAmK [app. as one confounded, or perplexed, and unable to see aright ]). (Aboo-Turáb, TA.) ― -b2- Also, taAha , (S, K,) aor. yatiyhu , (S,) inf. n. tiyhN , (S, K,) and tiyahN is said to be a dial. var. of this, but is doubtful; (MF;) [like taAha having for its aor. yatuwhu ;] He magnified himself; or behaved proudly, haughtily, or insolently: (S, K:) and he affected to be commended for, or praised for, or he gloried in, that which he did not possess; [i. e. he was, or became, conceited, or vain-glorious; or he overpassed the due bounds in elegance of mind or manners or address or speech or person or attire and the like, and arrogated to himself superiority therein, through pride: (K:) [or rather, he was, or became, vain; or he behaved vainly: for] Er-Rághib makes a distinction between muEojabN and taAy^ihN ; saying that the mEjb believes himself with respect to the opinion or judgment that he forms of himself indecisively, from evidence outweighed in probability; whereas the tAy^h believes himself decisively. (MF and TA in art. Ejb .) One says, huwa yatiyhu EalaY qawomihi [ He behaves proudly, or conceitedly, or vainly, towards his people ]. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (T, S, M, Msb, K,) inf. n. valomN , (S, M, Msb,) He broke its edge; (S, * M, Msb, K;) namely, that of a vessel, (M, Msb, K,) and of a sword, and the like; (M, K;) as also valimahu , aor. ; (K, TA; [but I suspect that this latter form of the verb has been taken from a copy of the S in which the intrans. verb valima has been erroneously made trans,;]) and ↓ vl~mhu ; (M, K;) or this last signifies he did so much, or in many places: (S:) and the first signifies also he made a gap, or breach, in it; namely, a wall. (T, * S.) ― -b2- [Hence,] vulima fiY maAlihi , (TA,) or vulima fiY maAlihi valomapF , (M,) (tropical:) He suffered the loss of somewhat of his property. (M, TA.) And h`*aA mim~aA yakolimu Ald~iyna wayavolimu Alyaqiyna (assumed tropical:) [ This of the things that wound religion and impair sure faith ]. (TA.) -A2- valima , aor. , inf. n. valamN ; (S;) and ↓ Anvlm , and ↓ tvl~m ; (S, M, Msb, K;) said of a thing, (S,) a vessel, (M, Msb, K,) a sword, and the like, (M, K,) It was, or became, broken in its edge: (S, * M, Msb, K:) [or ↓ the last, being quasi-pass. of 2, it was, or became, broken much, or in several places, in its edge: ] and ↓ Anvlm and ↓ tvl~m are said of a wall [as signifying it had a gap or breach, or gaps or breaches, made in it ]. (T.) valamN , [the inf. n. of valima ,] when relating to a valley, signifies The having its Harof , (T, M, K, and so in a copy of the S, [meaning brink, or edge, ]) or its juruf , (so in other copies of the S, [meaning its abrupt, water-worn, bank, ]) broken; (T, S, M, K, TA;) i. e., broken down: (TA:) and in like manner, in relation to a trench dug round a tent to prevent the rain-water from entering it, and in relation to a watering-trough, or tank. (M, TA.) [Golius and Freytag have explained it as signifying the part so broken; but I do not think that this can be meant by the explanation given above.]

definition: A bull: (S, M, Msb, K:) and ↓ vaworapN a cow: (S, M, Msb:) pl.
sourceDefinition: A bull: (S, M, Msb, K:) and ↓ vaworapN a cow: (S, M, Msb:) pl. [of pauc] A^avowaArN (M, Msb, K) and viyorapN (S, M, K) and [of mult.] viyraAnN and viyarapN (T, S, M, Msb, K) and viwarapN (S, M, K) and viyaArN (M, K) and viyaArapN ; (M, TA:) Sb says of the pl. viyarapN that w in it is changed into Y because of the kesreh before it, though this is not accordant to general rule: (S:) accord. to Mbr, they said viyarapN to distinguish it from the viwarap of A^aqT , and that it was originally of the measure fiEolapN : (S, M: * *) accord. to Aboo-'Alee, it is a contraction of viyaArapN . (M.) [Hence,] Alv~aworu (tropical:) [ The constellation Taurus; ] one of the signs of the Zodiac. (S, M, K.) ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) A lord, master, or chief, (M, A, K,) of a people. (A.) 'Othmán is called, in a trad., Alv~aworu AlA^aboyaDu ; the epithet AlAbyD being added because he was hoary; or it may denote celebrity. (M.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) Stupid; foolish; of little sense: (T, K:) a stupid, dull man, of little understanding. (T.) ― -b4- (assumed tropical:) Possessed by a devil, or insane, or mad; syn. majonuwnN ; so in copies of the K; but in some copies, [and in the CK,] junuwn [ diabolical possession, or insanity, or madness ]. (TA; and thus in Har p. 415.) -A2- A piece, (T, S, Mgh, Msb,) or large piece, (M, K,) of A^aqiT , (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K,) i. e. milk which [ has been churned and cooked and then left until it ] has become congealed and hard like stone: (TA:) pl. [of mult.] viwarapN (T, S, M, K) and A^avowaArN . (M, K.) -A3- The green substance that overspreads stale water; (T, M, K;) this is called vaworu AlmaA='i ; (S, Msb;) syn. TuHolubN , (AZ, T, S, M, Msb, K,) and EaromaDN , and galofaqN ; (M;) and the like thereof: (T, M:) and small rubbish, or broken particles of things, (Msb, TA,) or anything, (K,) upon the surface of water, (Msb, K, TA,) which the pastor beats to make the water clear for the bulls or cows. (Msb.) Accord. to some, it has the first of these meanings in the following verse of Anas Ibn-Mudrik El-Khath'amee: A_in~iY waqatoliY sulayokFA vum~a A^aEoqiluhu kaAlv~awori yuDorabu lam~aA EaAfati Albaqaru [ Verily I, with respect to my slaying Suleyk and then paying the price of his blood, am like the green substance upon the surface of stale water, that is beaten when the cows loathe the water ]: but accord. to others, by Alvwr the poet means the bull; for the cows follow him: (M, TA:) the cows are not beaten, because they have milk; but the bull is beaten that they may be frightened and therefore drink. (S.) [See a slightly-different reading, and remarks thereon, in Ham p. 416: and see Freytag's Arab. Prov. ii. 330. The latter hemistich is used as a prov., applied to him who is punished for the offence of another.] ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) Pimples, or small pustules, breaking out in the mouth, in a person who is fevered. (A.) ― -b3- (tropical:) The redness shining, ( naAy^irapN , K,) or spreading and rising, ( vaAy^irapN , M,) in the faint light that is seen above the horizon between sunset and nightfall: (M, K:) or vaworu Al$~afaqi the spreading appearance of the redness above the horizon after sunset. (S, A, Mgh.) You say, saqaTa vaworu Al$~afaqi [ The spreading appearance of the redness above the horizon after sunset sank down, or set ]. (S, A.) definition: [ Elephantiasis;
sourceDefinition: [ Elephantiasis; a species of leprosy; the leprosy that pervaded Europe in the latter part of the Middle Ages; ] a certain disease, (S, K,) arising from the spreading of the black bile throughout the whole person, so that it corrupts the temperament of the members, and the external condition thereof; and sometimes ending in the dissundering, or corrosion, (so accord. to different copies of the K, TA,) of the members, and their falling off, in consequence of ulceration; (K, TA;) so called because it dissunders the flesh, and causes it to fall off; (Msb;) or because the fingers, or toes, become cut off: (TA:) it is a cracking of the skin, and a dissundering, and gradual falling off, of the flesh. (Mgh.)

definition: Having his arm, or hand, cut off, or amputated: (S, Msb, K:) or having lost the endjoints of his fingers: (K:) fem.
sourceDefinition: Having his arm, or hand, cut off, or amputated: (S, Msb, K:) or having lost the endjoints of his fingers: (K:) fem. ja*omaA='u : (Msb:) pl. ja*omaY . (S.) It is said in a trad., mano taEal~ama AlquroA=na vum~a nasiyahu laqiYa A@ll~`ha yawoma AlqiyaAmapi wahuwa A^ajo*amu , (A 'Obeyd, S, *) i. e., [ He who learns the Kur-án and then forgets it shall meet God on the day of resurrection ] having his arm, or hand, cut off: (A 'Obeyd, TA:) or having lost all his limbs, or members: (Kt, TA:) or (assumed tropical:) having his plea cut off; having no tongue with which to speak, nor any plea in his hand: (IAth, TA:) or (assumed tropical:) having his means of access cut off: (TA:) or (assumed tropical:) with his hand devoid of good and of recompense. (IAar, El-Khattábee, TA.) And in another trad., kul~u xuTobapK layosa fiyhaA $ahaAdapN kaA@loyadi Alja*omaA='i [ Every oration from the pulpit in which there is not an acknowledgment of the unity of God and of the mission of Mohammad is like the arm of which the hand is amputated ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Alk~f~u Alja*omaA='u [ The amputated hand; ] (assumed tropical:) a name of the star a of Cetus; (so in the Egyptian Almanacs;) [i. e.] the star that is in the head of Cetus: so called because it is less extended [from the Pleiades] than that called Alkaf~a AlxaDiybu . (Kzw. [See Alkaf~u AlxaDiybu in art. xDb .]) ― -b3- naEolN ja*omaA='u (assumed tropical:) A sandal of which the [ thong called ] qibaAl [ which is between two of the toes ] is cut, or cut off, or severed. (TA.) -A2- See also majo*uwmN .

definition: Camels or sheep or goats pasturing in their place, not returning to their owners (As, S, K) at night: (K:) or [simply] not returning to their owners.

definition: , (S, A, Mgh, &c.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Mgh, &c.,) aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. jalodN , (S, Mgh, Msb,) He hit, or hurt, his skin; (S, K;) like as you say, raA^asahu , and baTanahu : (S:) he beat his skin: (Mgh:) he beat him; namely, a criminal: (Msb:) he struck him with a whip, and with a sword: (TA:) he flogged him (A, K) with a whip, (K,) or with whips: (A:) jaladotu is sometimes written and pronounced jalad~u . (MF on the letter d .) You say, jaladahu AlHad~a , inf. n. as above, He inflicted upon him the flogging ordained by the law. (S, L.) ― -b2- jaladati AlHay~apu The serpent bit: (K:) or, accord. to some, one says of the serpent called A^asowadu , specially, yajolidu bi*anabihi [ it strikes with its tail ]. (TA.) ― -b3- jalada jaAriyatahu , (K,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (TA,) (tropical:) He lay with his young woman, or female slave. (K, TA.) [Hence,] jalada Eumayorapa [(assumed tropical:) i. q. nakaHa Alyada ], a metonymical phrase: jalodu Eumayorapa meaning AlxaDoxaDapu , and AlAisotimonaA='u biAlyadi , also termed Alt~adoliylu , and AlAiEotimaAru : the similar act of a woman is termed AlA_iloTaAfu . (Har p. 572.) ― -b4- jalada bihi AlA^aroDa He smote the ground with him; (TA;) he threw him down prostrate on the ground. (A, TA.) And julida bihi He fell down (K, TA) upon the ground by reason of much sleepiness; as also julida bihi nuwomFA . (TA.) kunotu A^ata$ad~adu fayujoladu biY , in a trad., means [ I used to exert my strength, or energy, but ] sleep would overcome me so that I fell down. (L.) ― -b5- jaladahu EalaY AlA^amori (tropical:) He compelled him against his will to do the thing. (A, K.) ― -b6- yujoladu bikul~i xayorK (or, as related by AHát, yjl* , with * , TA) (tropical:) He is imagined to possess every good quality. (A, K.) But the saying of EshSháfi'ee kaAna mujaAlidN yujoladu means (assumed tropical:) Mujálid used to be pronounced a liar, (K, TA,) or suspected and accused of lying. (TA.) -A2- julidati AlA^aroDu , (S, L, Msb,) the verb being in the pass. form, (Msb,) or jalidat , (A, K,) a verb of the same form as fariHa ; (K;) [or both may be correct, like Duribat and Daribat in the same sense;] and ↓ A^ajoladat ; (K;) [but this last I believe to be a mistake for A^ujolidat , like A^uDoribat ;] The land was, or became, affected or smitten, by hoar-frost, or rime. (S, A, L, Msb, K.) And jld Albaqolu [in the TA jalida ] The herbs, or leguminous plants, were, or became, affected, or smitten, thereby. (L, TA.) And ↓ A^ujoliduwA They (men) were, or became, affected, or smitten, thereby. (L, K.) -A3- jaluda , aor. , inf. n. jalaAdapN and juluwdapN and jaladN (or this last is a simple subst., L) and majoluwdN , (an inf. n. like maHoluwfN and maEoquwlN , (S, or from tajal~ada , M in art. Esr ,) He (a man, S, L) was, or became, hardy, strong, sturdy, (S, * L, K, *) and enduring, or patient. (L.)

definition: He affected hardiness, strength, sturdiness, and endurance, or patience;
sourceDefinition: He affected hardiness, strength, sturdiness, and endurance, or patience; constrained himself to behave with hardiness, &c. (S, * A, * L, K. *) So in the phrase tjl~d lil$~aAmitiyna [ He constrained himself to behave with hardiness, &c., to those who rejoiced at his misfortune ]. (A, TA.) In the phrase tjl~d Eanohu [ He constrained himself to endure with hardiness and patience the loss, or want, of him, or it ], the verb is made trans. by means of En because it implies the meaning of taSab~ara . (L.) ― -b2- Also He feigned, or made a show of, hardiness, strength, sturdiness, and endurance, or patience. (L.)

definition: , (S, Msb, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K, &c.,) the only form of the word mentioned by the generality of the lexicographers; (TA;) occurring at the end of a verse with kesr to the second as well as the first letter, ↓ jilidN , agreeably with a license allowed to a poet in such a case, to give to a quiescent letter in a rhyme the same vowel as that which the preceding letter has; (S;) and ↓ jaladN , (IAar, S, K,) like $ibohN and $abahN , and mivolN and mavalN ; but this is said by ISk to be unknown; (S;) The skin of any animal; (K;) the integument of the body and limbs of an animal: (Az, Msb:) or the exterior of the ba$arapN [or upper skin ] of an animal: (Msb: [but this is a strange explanation:]) pl. juluwdN (S, Msb, K) and (sometimes, Msb) A^ajolaAdN [a pl. of pauc.]. (Msb, K.) ― -b2- [The pl.] A^ajolaAdN signifies also, and ↓ tajaAliydu likewise, The body and limbs (S, A, L) of a man; (S;) the whole person, or body and limbs, of a human being; (L, K;) and his self: (L:) so called because enclosed by the skin: pl. of the former, A^ajaAlidu . (L.) You say, maA A^a$obaha A^ajolaAdahu biA^ajolaAdi A^abiyhi How like are his person and body to the person and body of his father! (L.) And fulaAnN EaZiymu AlA^ajolaAdi and ↓ Alt~ajaAliydi (A, L) Such a one is large and strong (L) in respect of the body and limbs. (A, L.) And rud~uwA AlA^ayomaAna EalaY A^ajolaAdihimo Repeat ye the oaths to the persons, themselves: occurring in a trad.: said on the occasion of a man's entering among others of whom an oath had been demanded. (L.) ― -b3- Aljilodu also signifies (assumed tropical:) The penis. (Fr, L, K: but in the CK, in this sense, it is written Aljalodu .) Agreeably with this explanation, its pl. juluwd is said by Fr to be used in the Kur xli. 20: (L:) or as meaning the pudenda: (L, K:) but ISd holds that this word there means the skins, with which, as in manual operations, acts of disobedience are performed. (L.)

sourceDefinition: : see jilodN . ― -b2- Also The skin of a camel, or other beast, with which another beast is clothed: (L:) the skin of a young camel, which ( being stripped off, S) is put over the body of another young camel, in order that the mother of the skinned young one ( smelling it, S) may conceive an affection for it [ and suckle it ]: (S, K:) or the skin of a young camel, which is stuffed with panic grass ( vumaAm ), (K, TA,) or some other plant, (TA,) and put before a she-camel, in order that she may be induced thereby to affect that which is not her young one [ and so yield her milk ], (K, TA,) or, to affect the young one of another. (L, TA.) -A2- A ewe or she-goat whose young one dies at the time of her bringing it forth; as also ↓ jaladapN : pl. [of the former] jilaAdN and [of the latter] jaladaAtN . (TA.) ― -b2- Also, [as a coll. gen. n.,] Great she-camels, having neither young ones nor milk; n. un. with p : (S:) [see also jalodN :] or great camels, among which are no little ones; (K;) n. un. with p : (TA:) and (app. as a quasipl. n., TA) sheep or goats, and camels, having neither young ones nor milk; (K;) app. meaning having no little ones to which they give such: (Mohammad Ibn-El-Mukarram, TA:) or she-camels having no young ones with them, so that they endure patiently the heat and cold: (Fr, TA:) or she-camels having no milk, and the young ones of which have gone away from them; including what are called banaAtu All~abuwni , and such as are above these in age; and also such as are called maxaASN , and Ei$aArN , and HiyaAlN ; but when they have given birth to their young, they cease to be termed jaladN , and are called Ei$aArN , and liqaAHN : the pl. is A^ajolaAdN and [pl. pl.] A^ajaAliydu . (Az, TA.) -A3- Hard ground; as also ↓ A^ajoladu : (S:) or hard and level ground; as also ↓ jaladapN : (K:) or level but rough ground; (L;) as also ↓ A^ajoladu : (TA:) pl. (of the former, TA) A^ajolaAdN and (of the latter, TA) A^ajaAlidu . (S, TA.) You also say A^aroDN jaladN , with fet-h to the l ; (AHn, TA;) and ↓ jalodapN , with a quiescent l ; (Lth, AHn, TA;) and ArD ↓ jaladapN also; and makaAnN jaladN . (Lth, TA.) -A4- Also, as a subst. or an inf. n., (L, [see jaluda ,]) Hardiness, strength, sturdiness, (S, * A, * L, K, *) and endurance, or patience. (T.)

sourceDefinition: an inf. n. of 1: Ignorance; contr. of EilomN : (S, Msb, * K: *) [and silliness, or foolishness: and wrong conduct: (see 1:)] it is of two kinds; namely, simple, which is the non-existence of knowledge of that which should be known; and compound, which is a decisive belief not agreeable with the fact, or reality: so accord. to Ibn-El-Kemál: or, accord. to Er-Rághib, it is of three kinds; namely, the mind's voidness of knowledge, which is the primary meaning; and the believing a thing to be different from what it is; and the doing a thing in a manner different from that in which it ought to be done: or, accord. to El-Harállee, the proceeding in dubious affairs without knowledge. (TA.) It is said in a prov., kafiY biAl$~ak~i juholFA [ Doubt is sufficient ignorance ]. (Msb.) And it is said in a trad., A_in~a mina AlEilomi jaholFA [ Verily there is, among the kinds of knowledge, what is ignorance ]: this is one's learning what is not requisite, and neglecting what is requisite; or a learned man's affecting, or pretending, a knowledge of that which he does not know. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, K,) aor. yaHojuw , (S, TA,) inf. n. HajowN , (TA,) He thought, or opined: (S, TA:) or he thought, or opined, a thing, and, doing so, claimed it ( Aid~aEaAhu ), not being certain of it: (K:) [or he thought it and asserted it; as appears from a verse here following, cited in the TA as an ex. of the meaning explained as above in the K:] and biZan~ihi ↓ tHj~Y , and tHj~Y alone, he thought, or opined, a thing, not being certain of it. (T, TA.) You say, A^anaA A^aHojuw bihi xayorFA I think, or opine, that there is good in him. (S, TA.) And Aboo-Shembel says, respecting Aboo-'Amr Esh-Sheybánee, qado kunotu A^aHojuw A^abaA EamorKwA^axaAviqapK Hat~aY A^alam~ato binaA yawomFA mulim~aAtu [ I used to think and assert Aboo-'Amr to be a trustworthy person, until, one day, misfortunes befell us ]. (TA.) ― -b2- HajaA Alqawoma ka*aA waka*aA (S, K *) He repaid, requited, compensated, or recompensed, the people, or party, [ with, or for, such and such things, ] syn. jazaAhumo ; [so in my copies of the S, and in the K; but Freytag gives, as the reading found by him in the S, HzAhm , as though meaning he computed them by conjecture to be such and such in number; which is agreeable with what follows;] and he thought them to be so. (S.) -A2- He directed himself, or his course or aim, to, or towards, him, or it: (Az, TA:) and ↓ tHj~Y Al$~aYo'a he directed himself, or his course or aim, to, or towards, the thing. (S, TA.) -A3- Also, (K,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) He kept a secret: (K:) or he concealed it: (AZ, TA:) [and ↓ HaAjiY has a similar meaning; for] you say, laAmuHaAjaApa EinodiY fiY ka*aA , i. e. There is no concealment with me in respect of such a thing; as also lA mukaAfaA^apa . (TA.) ― -b2- laA yaHojuw A_ibilahu , said of a pastor, He does not, or will not, keep and tend, or pasture and defend, his camels. (TA.) One says also of a pastor whose sheep or goats [and camels] are lost by him, and become dispersed, maA yaHojuw ganamahu walaA A_ibilahu [ He does not keep his sheep or goats, nor his camels, from being lost and becoming dispersed ]. (TA.) ― -b3- siq~A='N laA yaHojuw AlmaA='a A skin that will not hold, or retain, water. (TA.) ― -b4- maAHajawotu minohu $ayoy^FA I did not keep, or retain in my memory, of it, aught; as also mA hajawotu . (Ks, TA.) -A4- Also, (K,) inf. n. as above, (TA,) He, or it, prevented, or withheld. (K, TA.) [See HijFA .] -A5- HaAjayotuhu faHajawotuhu : see 3. -A6- HajaA biAlomakaAni , (S, K,) inf. n. as above, (K,) He remained, stayed, dwelt, or abode, in the place, (S, K, TA,) and became fixed [ therein ]; (TA;) as also bihi ↓ tHj~Y . (S, K.) And HajaA , (IAar, K,) inf. n. as above, (IAar,) He stopped, or paused. (IAar, K.) ― -b2- And HajaA bihi , [inf. n. as above, (see Ham p. 523,)] He was, or became, tenacious, or avaricious, of it, namely, a thing; (S, K;) as also bh ↓ tHj~Y . (TA.) And HajiY bihi , (Fr, S, K,) aor. , inf. n. HajFY [or HajFA ], (TK,) He was, or became attached to it, and clave to it; (Fr, S, K;) as also Hajiy^a bh ; and bh ↓ tHj~Y ; (Fr, S;) and tHj~A^bh . (Fr, TA.) ↓ tHj~Y also signifies He kept to the HajaA , or place of bending or turning of a valley. (TA.) And bih`*aA AlmakaAni ↓ taHaj~ayotu I preceded you, or outwent you, to this place, and clave to it before you. (S, TA.) And [hence,] bihimo ↓ tHj~Y is said to mean (assumed tropical:) He was first, or foremost, or quick, to blame them. (TA.) ― -b3- HajiYa , (K, TA,) aor. , (TA,) is also [said to be] syn. with EadaA , (K,) He ran; (TK;) thus bearing two contr. significations: (K:) but this requires consideration. (TA.) ― -b4- [Golius, as on the authority of the KL, assigns to it also the meaning “ Hilaris et lubens fuit: ” but in this sense it is said in the KL to be with ' for its last radical letter: see art. definition: ↓ HaAjayotuhu faHajawotuhu , (T, S, K,) inf.
sourceDefinition: ↓ HaAjayotuhu faHajawotuhu , (T, S, K,) inf. n. of the former muHaAjaApN and HijaA='N , (K,) I contended, or vied, with him in intelligence or skill and knowledge, or in endeavouring to show my superiority in intelligence &c., ( faATanotuhu ,) and I overcame him therein; (K;) from HijFY [or HijFA ] meaning “ intelligence. ” (Har p. 9.) [And hence, I tried him with an enigma or enigmas, and overcame him therein : (see 6:) or] I proposed to him an enigma [&c.]: (T, TA:) [or I contended with him in proposing an enigma or enigmas, &c.]: i. e. daAEayotuhu fagalabotuhu : (S:) so in the handwriting of Aboo-Zekereeyà, and in that of Aboo-Sahl, [and in my two copies of the S,] but in [some of the copies of] the S dEyth . (TA.) And HuwjiYa bihi [ He was tried with it as an enigma to be explained by him; or he had it proposed to him as an enigma ]. (TA.) ― -b2- muHaAjaApN signifies [also] The asking a thing of one much, so as to weary; as also mudaAEaApN . (KL.) ― -b3- And HijaA='N , (K, TA,) [accord. to the CK HajFA , but correctly] like kitaAbN , (TA,) An engaging in conflict, or fight. (K, TA.) ― -b4- See also 1.

sourceDefinition: a subst. signifying muHaAjaApN [i. e. A contention in intelligence &c.; and particularly, in trying with an enigma or enigmas; in proposing an enigma or enigmas; or simply the proposal of an enigma; see 3]; (T, TA;) the subst. denoted by HaAjayotuhu faHajawotuhu ; (K;) [or rather by the verb HaAjayotu , agreeably with the foregoing explanation from the T;] as also ↓ Hujay~aA , (S, K, TA,) with a dammeh, (K, TA,) and with teshdeed of the Y ; (TA; [in some copies of the K erroneously written HujoyuA ;]) and ↓ A^uHojiy~apN : (S:) or ↓ Hujay~FA is the dim. of HajowaY : (T, TA:) and ↓ A^uHojiy~apN signifies a saying of which the meaning differs from the letter, as also ↓ A^uHojuw~apN , (K,) but AHjy~p is preferable, (T, TA,) and kalimapN ↓ muHojiyapN , (K,) like muHosinapN ; (TA; [in the CK, erroneously, muHojiy~apN ;]) [i. e.] ↓ A^uHojiy~apN signifies an enigma; a riddle; (MA, PS, TK;) and so ↓ Hujay~aA ; (PS;) or a question put to one with the view of causing him to make a mistake; (TA;) and is from HijFY [or HijFA ] meaning “ intelligence, ” because muHaAjaApN is like a vying, or contending, in intelligence: (Har p. 9:) the pl. of ↓ A^uHojiy~apN is A^aHaAjiY~u and A^aHaAjK , (MA, and Har ubi suprà,) agreeably with a general rule relating to words of its measure, as A^uvofiy~apN and A^umoniy~apN . (Seer, in Har ubi suprà.) One says, maAkaAna ↓ Hujay~aAka ka*aA waka*aA [ The question of contention with thee in trying thine intelligence by an enigma, or the enigma proposed to thee, is, What is, or was, such a thing, and such a thing? ]: it means a certain game, and a question put with the view of causing one to make a mistake : A 'Obeyd says, It is like their saying, Disclose what is in my hand, and thou shalt have such a thing. (S.) One says also, fiY h`*aA ↓ A^anaA Hujay~aAka , meaning mano yuHaAjiyka [i. e. I am he who contends with thee in intelligence, or in trying with an enigma, &c., respecting this thing ]. (S.) And ↓ bayonahumo A^uHojiy~apN yataHaAjawna bihaA [ Between them is a contention in intelligence, or in proposing enigmas, or between them is an enigma, with which they try one another ]. (S.)

definition: , (S, A, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, K,) aor. , inf. n. Haro$N (S, K) and taHoraA$N , (K,) He hunted, or sought to capture or catch, or captured or caught, the [ lizard called ] Db~ ; syn. SaAdahu ; (S, A, K;) by moving about his hand at its hole, (S, K,) at the entrance thereof, (K,) in order that it might imagine it to be a serpent, and put forth its tail to strike it, whereupon he would seize it; (S, K;) as also ↓ AHtr$hu : (A, K:) or, as also ↓ AHtr$hu , and ↓ tHr~$hu , and bihi ↓ tHr~$ , he traced its hole, and made a noise with his staff, or stick, at it, and inserted the end of this into the hole, and the Db~ , hearing the sound, thought it to be a beast desiring to come in upon it, so it came backwards upon its feet and kinder part, fighting, and striking with its tail, whereupon the man hastened with it, and seized it firmly by its tail, and it was unable to escape from him. (TA.) And hence, He hunted, or sought to capture, or captured, the Db~ in any manner. (Ham p. 61.) Hence also the saying, lahuwa A^axobavu mino Dab~K Hara$otahu [ Verily he is worse than a Db~ which thou hast hunted ]: for sometimes the Db~ scents [its pursuer], and circumvents [him], and cannot be caught. (TA.) And hence the prov., alluding to one's discoursing to a learned man with the desire of instructing him, A^atuEolimuniY biDab~K A^anaA Hara$otuhu [ Dost thou acquaint me with a Db~ which I have captured? ]. (A 'Obeyd, Az.) Hence also the prov., h`*aAA^ajal~u mina AlHaro$i [ This is a greater matter than the hunting, or capturing, of the Db~ ]: (M, A, K:) originating in one of their fables, to the effect that a Db~ said to its young one, “ O my little son, beware thou of AlHaro$ : ” and the young one heard, one day, the fall of a digging-implement upon the mouth of the hole; so he said, “ O my father, is this AlHaro$ ? ” to which his father answered, “ O my little son, this is a greater matter than AlHaro$ : ” (M, K: *) and it became a prov., which is applied to him who fears a thing and falls into that which is more severe. (M.) [Hence also the saying,] Dab~a AlEadaAwapi bayonahumo ↓ AiHotara$a (tropical:) [ He roused the rancour of enmity between them ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Hara$ahu , (S, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. Haro$N (S, K) and taHoraA$N , (K,) signifies also He scratched him with the nails; or wounded him in the outer skin; (S, K;) and so xara$ahu , with x . (S.) ― -b3- Both also signify It (a fly) bit him. (TA in art. xr$ .) ― -b4- And Hara$a AlbaEiyra He scratched, or rubbed, the gaArib [or withers ] of the camel with his staff, or stick, to make him go. (TA.) ― -b5- And He scratched, or rubbed, the camel so as to abrade the upper skin, and make it bleed; whereupon it is smeared with hinaA=' [or tar]; as also xara$ahu . (TA.) -A2- Hara$a bayona Alqawomi ; &c.: see 2, in two places. -A3- Hari$a , aor. , inf. n. Haro$N , He deceived, beguiled, or circumvented; syn. xadaEa : and ↓ AHtr$ signifies the same; or nearly the same; i. e. he endeavoured to deceive, beguile, or circumvent; syn. of the inf. n. xidaAEN . (TA.)

definition: Anything rough, harsh, or coarse;
sourceDefinition: Anything rough, harsh, or coarse; as also ↓ Hari$N , on the authority of AHn, and thought by Az to be a possessive epithet, [meaning having roughness, &c., from Hara$N or Huro$apN ,] because he had not heard any verb belonging to it: (TA:) or the former is applied to a Dab~ , signifying rough; (S, K;) or rough in the skin, (A, TA,) as though notched, or serrated: (TA:) and in like manner, its fem., Haro$aA='u , to a serpent ( Hay~ap ), signifying rough; (K;) or rough in the skin: (S, TA:) and the masc. to a deenár, signifying rough (S, A, K) by reason of its newness; (A, K;) good, rough, recently coined; having upon it the roughness of the stamp: pl. Huru$N (TA) [and Huro$N ]: and to a camel, signifying whose galls, or sores, on his back have healed, or become covered with a skin in healing: (Az, as heard by him from more than one of the Arabs of the desert:) and the fem., above mentioned, is applied to a she-camel, signifying, having the mange, or scab, (K, TA,) and not smeared [ with tar ]; (TA;) she being so called because of the roughness of her skin: (Az, TA:) and to a nuqobap [or scab], signifying having small pustules, (S,) not smeared [ with tar ]. (S, A.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. (S, Msb, K) and , (Mgh, Msb, K,) inf. n. HasorN (S, Msb, K) and HusuwrN , (TA,) He removed it, put it off, took it off, or stripped if off, (Mgh, K, TA,) Eano $aYo'K from a thing which it covered or concealed. (TA.) Husira is said of anything as meaning It was removed, put off, taken off, or stripped off, from a thing which it covered or concealed. (A.) You say, Hasara kum~ahu Eano *iraAEihi He removed his sleeve from his fore arm. (S, A.) And simply Hasara Eano *iraAEihi He uncovered his fore arm. (Msb.) And Hasara EimaAmatahu Eano raA^osihi He removed, or took off, his turban from his head. (A.) And Hasarato diroEahaA , (A, Msb,) aor. , (Msb,) She (a woman) took off her shift (A, Msb) Eano jasadihaA from her body: (A:) and ximaArahaA her head-covering. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence,] Hasarati Alr~iyHu Als~aHaAba (tropical:) [ The wind removed the clouds from the sky]. (A.) And Hasara qinaAEa Alham~i Ean~iY (tropical:) [ He, or it, removed the covering of anxiety from me ]. (A.) ― -b3- Also, (K,) inf. n. HasorN , (TA,) He peeled a branch of a tree. (K, TA.) ― -b4- And He swept a house or chamber. (K, TA.) ― -b5- And Hasaruwhu , aor. , inf. n. HasorN and HusorN , (tropical:) They begged of him and he gave them until nothing remained in his possession. (TA.) -A2- Hasara , (S, A, K,) aor. and , (TA,) inf. n. HasorN (S, TA) and HusuwrN ; (TA;) and ↓ AHsr , (S, K,) inf. n. A_iHosaArN ; and ↓ Hs~r , inf. n. taHosiyrN ; (TA;) He, (a man, S, A,) and it, (a journey, TA,) tired, fatigued, or jaded, (S, A, K,) a beast, (A, TA,) or a camel: (S:) and he drove a camel until he tired, fatigued, or jaded, him. (K.) And Husirati Ald~aAb~apu The beast was fatigued so that it was left to remain where it was. (AHeyth.) ― -b2- And Hasara , aor. , (assumed tropical:) It (the distance to which it looked, and the indistinctness of the object,) fatigued the eye. (TA.) And Husira AlbaSaru mino Tuwli Aln~aZari (tropical:) [ The eye was fatigued by the length of looking: see a similar meaning of Hasara and Hasira , below]. (A.) -A3- See 7, with which Hasara is syn. ― -b2- [Hence,] Hasara , (ISk, A, Mgh, Msb,) aor. , (TA,) (tropical:) It (water) sank and disappeared; or became low; or retired: (ISk, A, Mgh:) it sank and disappeared, or retired, from its place: (Msb:) properly, it became removed from the shore: (Mgh:) and it (the sea, or great river,) sank, or retired, from ( Eano ) El-'Irák, and from the shore, so that the ground which was beneath the water appeared: (TA:) you do not say, in this sense, ↓ AnHsr . (Az. [But this latter is sometimes used, as, for instance, in the Msb art. jzr .]) Hence, in a trad., kulo maA Hasara Eanohu AlbaHoru wadaEo maA TafaA Ealayohi [ Eat thou that from which the sea retires, and leave what floats upon it ]. (Mgh.) -A4- Hasara , aor. , (S, A, K,) inf. n. HusuwrN (S, A) and Hasara ; (TA;) and Hasra , aor. , (A, K,) inf. n. HasarN ; (TA;) and ↓ AstHsr , (S, K,) and ↓ tHs~r ; (S;) He (a camel, S, or a beast, A) became tired, fatigued, or jaded, (S, K, TA,) by travel: (TA:) [or] the last signifies he (a camel) fell down from fatigue. (Ham p. 491.) [Hence,] it is said in a trad., ↓ AudoEuwA A@ll~`ha wa laA tasotaHosiruwA (assumed tropical:) Supplicate ye God, and be not weary: and a similar instance occurs in the Kur xxi. 19. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence also,] Hasara , aor. , (S, K,) or , (Msb,) inf. n. HusuwrN ; (S, Msb, K;) and Hasira , aor. ; (A;) (tropical:) It (the sight) was, or became, dim, dull, or hebetated; (S, Msb, K;) and it failed; (S, K;) [or became fatigued; ] by reason of length of space [overlooked], (S, Msb, K,) and the like; (S, Msb;) or by long looking. (A.) -A5- Hasira Ealayohi , aor. , inf. n. HasarN (S Msb, K) and HasorapN , (S, K,) or the latter is a simple subst., (Msb,) and HasaraAnN , (TA,) He grieved for it, or at it; or regretted it; he felt, or expressed, grief, sorrow, or regret, on account of it; syn. talah~afa ; (Msb, K;) as also ↓ tHs~r : (S, K:) or the former, he grieved for it, or regretted it, ( talah~afa Ealayohi , S, A, or nadima Ealayohi , TA,) namely, a thing that had escaped him, most intensely. (S, A, * TA.) [See HasorapN .]

definition: A man having no migofar [or covering for the head, made of mail, &c.
sourceDefinition: A man having no migofar [or covering for the head, made of mail, &c.,] (S, K,) upon him; (S;) nor a coat of mail; (S, K;) contr. of daAriEN ; (Mgh;) nor a helmet upon his head; (TA;) contr. of muqan~aEN : (Mgh:) or having no jun~ap [or defensive covering, &c.]: (K:) a man having no turban on his head: (TA:) a man having his head uncovered: (A:) pl. Hus~arN , and pl. pl. Hus~aruwna ; the latter a form used by one of the poets; the former pl. applied to foot-soldiers in war, because they uncover their arms and legs, or because they have not upon them coats of mail nor helmets; occurring in this sense in a trad. (TA.) Also, without p , A woman who has taken off her shift from her person: (ISd, Msb, TA:) who has taken off her clothes from her person: who has uncovered her head and her fore arms: who has taken off her head-covering: and, with p , a woman having her face uncovered: pl. Hus~arN and HawaAsiru . (TA.) ― -b2- AibonuwA AlmasaAjida Hus~arFA in a trad. of 'Alee, means Build ye mosques, or oratories, with bare walls, with no $uraf [or acroterial ornaments or crestings ]. (TA.) -A2- See also HasiyrN .

sourceDefinition: One who has no sexual intercourse with women, (S, Mgh, K,) though able to have it, (K,) abstaining from them from a motive of chastity, and for the sake of shunning worldly pleasures: (TA:) or who is prevented from having it, (K, TA,) by impotence: (TA:) or who does not desire them, (IAar, A, Msb, K,) nor approach them: (IAar, K:) applied also to a horse, i. q. Ein~iynN . (IAar, TA in art. Ejz .) In the Kur [iii. 34], applied to John the Baptist. (TA.) ― -b2- Castrated; (K;) having the penis and testicles amputated. (TA.) ― -b3- Very fearful or cautious; who abstains, or refrains, from a thing through fear. (K.) ― -b4- See also HaSirN , in four places. ― -b5- Also A she-camel having a narrow orifice to the teat. (S, K.)
