A possessor, an owner, a lord, or a master, but often better rendered having, possessing, possessed of, or endowed with ], (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K, but omitted in the CK,) used as a prefixed noun, (S, Mgh, Msb, &c.,) is originally *awFA , like EaSFA , the A being changed from w ; (S;) or it is originally *aw~aY ; and if one used it as a proper name, he would say, h`*aA *aw~aYqado jaA='a [ This is Dhawà, he has come ]; (M;) [not *awFA , as in copies of the S; i. e.,] its third radical letter is Y , not, as J says, w ; this Y being afterwards suppressed; (IB;) [so that the word becomes *awN , and then, by reason of its being prefixed to another noun, *uw , like as A^abawN , the original form of A^abN , becomes A^abuw :] it is declined [like A^abuw ] with w and | and Yi ; (Msb;) [i. e.,] the nom. case is *uw , accus. *aA , and gen. *iY : (Mgh:) the fem. is *aAtu ; (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K; in a copy of the M, *Ap , and the CK, *aApN [as though it were not a prefixed noun];) and in the case of a pause, some say *aAto , and others say *aAho : (Lth, T: the latter usage, only, is mentioned in the S:) dual. masc., *awaA , (S, * M,) [accus and gen. *awaYo ;] fem. *awaAtaA , (T, M, Mgh, Msb, K,) for which *aAtaA is allowable in poetry, but *awaAtaA is better, (T,) [accus, and gen. *awaAtaYo :] pl., masc., *awuw , (T, *, S, * M, Msb, K, but omitted in the CK,) [accus, and gen. *awiY ;] fem. *awaAtu , (T, S, * M, Mgh, Msb, K,) accus. and gen. *awaAti ; (S;) and A^uwluw and A^uwlaAt are like *awuw and *awaAt [in signification]. (T. [See art. Alw .]) In this sense it is not used otherwise than as a prefixed noun: when used to characterize an indeterminate noun, prefixed to an indeterminate noun; and when used to characterize a determinate noun, prefixed to [a noun rendered determinate by] the article Al . (S.) [Thus you say rajulN *uw maAlK A man a possessor of wealth; and Alr~ajulu *uw AlmaAli The man the possessor of wealth .] In the phrase gayora *aAti Al$awokapi [ Not those possessed of weapons, &c.], in the Kur [viii. 7], the fem. form is used as meaning the TaAy^ifap [or party]. (T.) SaAra *aA *anobK [ He became one having a sin, or crime, &c., attributable to him, i. e. he had a sin, &c., attributable to him, ] means taHam~ala *anobFA [ he became chargeable with a sin, &c.]. (Msb in art. *nb .) ― -b2- Accord. to the S, it is not prefixed to a pronoun ( muDomar ); nor to a proper name, such as zayod and Eamorw and the like: but there are several instances of its being prefixed, in its pl. form, to a pronoun; among which is the saying of a poet, A_in~amaA yaSoTaniEu AlmaEoruwfu fiY Aln~aAsi *awuwhu [ Only they who are possessors thereof do that which is good among men ]: (TA:) [this usage, however, is perhaps only allowable by poetic license: see another ex. (also here cited in the TA) in the Ham p. 442, and the remarks there appended to it:] and it is also prefixed to proper names, as is shown by the phrase, (TA,) h`*aA *uw zayodK (M, K, TA,) mentioned, as heard from the Arabs, by Ahmad Ibn-Ibráheem, the preceptor of Th, meaning This is Zeyd, (M, TA,) i. e., this is the owner of the name Zeyd; (M, K, TA;) and [perhaps] by the name *uw AlxalaSapi , for AlxlSp is [said by some to be] the name of a certain idol, and *w is a metonymical appellation of its bayot ; and by the proper names *uw ruEayonK and *uw yazana and [accord. to some] *uw jadonK [and the like, of which several are mentioned in the S, as well as in the M &c.]. (IB, TA.) [But see a later portion of this paragraph, where, prefixed to a proper name, it is said to be redundant.] ― -b3- *awuw AlA^aroHaAm , [or, as in the Kur viii. last verse, and xxxiii. 6, A^uwluw AlA^aroHaAmi , pls. of *uw Alr~aHimi ,] in the classical language, means [ The possessors of relationship; i. e.] any relations: and in law, any relations that have no portion [ of the inheritances termed faraAy^iD ] and are not [ such heirs as are designated by the appellation ] EaSabap [q. v.: they are so called because they are relations by the women's side: see raHimN ]. (KT, TA.) ― -b4- If you form a pl. from *uwmaAlK , you say, h`w^ulaA='i *awuwna [ These are possessors of wealth]; because in this case the pl. is not a prefixed noun. (S.) Accord. to Lth, Al*~awuwna signifies The former, or first, [ of persons, ] and the more, or most, distinguished. (T, TA. *) Also, (S, M,) and AlA^a*owaA='u , [which is another pl. of *uw ,] (S,) The kings (S, M) of El-Yemen, of the tribe of Kudá'ah, (S,) whose surnames commenced with *uw , (M,) [i. e.] who were named [or rather surnamed ] (S) *uw yazana (S, M) and *uw jadanK and *uw nuwaAsK (S) and the like. (S, M.) qura$iY~N layosa mino *iY walaA *uw , occurring in a trad., means A Kurashee in respect of lineage, not of the A^a*owaA=' [above mentioned]. (TA.) ― -b5- [ *uw and *aAt and *aA and *iY are also used as prefixed nouns in various expressions here following, in several thereof as meaning Something in possession, or the like; not a possessor: or, in these instances, as is said in explanation of the first of the following phrases, and also of the phrase *aAtu Alyadi (mentioned below) in Har p. 93, that which is contained is made to be as though it were the possessor ( SaAHib ) of that which contains.] ― -b6- maw~ata *aAbaTonihaA [ He killed what was in her belly ]. (Har ubi suprá.) And waDaEati AlmaroA^apu *aA baTonihaA , (T,) or *aAta baTonihaA , (TA,) The woman brought forth [ her child ]. (T, TA.) And navarato *aA baTonihaA She brought forth many children. (T in art. nvr ; and Mgh there and in the present art., in the latter of which it is added that the usual phrase is navarato baTonahaA .) And A^aloqati Ald~ajaAjapu *aA baTonihaA The hen laid her egg, or eggs: or muted. (Mgh.) And A^aloqaY Alr~ajulu *aA baTonihi The man ejected his excrement, or ordure. (T.) And Al*~iy^obu magobuwTN bi*iY baTonihi The wolf is envied [ for what is in his belly, or] for his distention of the belly [ with food ]. (TA.) ― -b7- [In like manner,] *aAtu Alyadi means (tropical:) Wealth; as though it were the possessor of that which contains it: (Har ubi suprá:) [or what is in the possession of the hand: ] or what one possesses, of wealth; because gained by the hand and disposed of by the hand. (Har p. 66.) You say, qal~ato *aAtu yadihi (assumed tropical:) What his hand possessed became little in quantity; (Lth, T;) or the possessions accompanying his hand; (Mgh;) app. meaning his riches. (Lth, T.) ― -b8- *aAtu Alr~iy^api and *aAtu Aljanobi are Two well-known diseases. (TA. [See arts. rA^Y and jnb .]) ― -b9- EaliymN bi*aAti AlS~uduwri , in the Kur iii. 115, means [ Acquainted, or well acquainted, ] with what is in the minds: (Ksh, Bd, Jel: [and the like is indicated in the Mgh:]) or with the true, or real, nature of the notions that are concealed in the minds: (IAmb, T:) or with the hidden things of the minds: or with the minds themselves. (Msb. [If the last meaning be correct, the phrase should be mentioned with others later in this paragraph.]) [And similar to this is the saying,] Earafahu mino *aAti nafosihi He knew it from what he conceived in his mind [without his being informed thereof; i. e. he knew it of himself ]. (Lth, T.) And jaA='a mino *iYnafosihi and mino *aAti nafosihi (M, K) He came [ from a motive in his own mind; of himself; ] of his own accord; or willingly; syn. Tay~iEFA : (M, TA:) in the copies of the K, TaboEFA ; but the former is the right explanation. (TA.) And maA kal~amotu fulaAnFA *aAta $afapK and *aAta famK I spoke not to such a one a word. (AZ, T.) ― -b10- *aAta Alyamiyni and *aAta Al$~imaAli [are adverbial expressions, and] mean In the direction of the right hand and of the left: properly in the direction that has the name of the right hand [and that has the name of the left hand ]. (Bd in xviii. 16.) And A^atayonaA *aA yamiynK means We came on the right hand. (TA.) ― -b11- *aAta mar~apK and *aA SabaAHK [also, and the like,] are adverbial expressions, which may not be used otherwise than as such: (S:) you say, laqiytuhu *aAta mar~apK [ I met him once, or once upon a time ], (S,) and *aAta AlmiraAri many times, (M and K in art. mr ,) or sometimes, (S in that art.,) and *aAta yawomK (Fr, T, S) i. e. mar~apF fiY yawomK [ once upon a day, or one day ], therefore you use the fem. form, (T,) and *aAta layolapK [ one night ], (Fr, T, S,) and *aAta gadaApK [ one morning, or one morning between daybreak and sunrise ], and *aAta AlEi$aA='i [ once in the evening at nightfall ], (S,) meaning, accord. to Th, in the hour, or time, in which is nightfall, (T,) and *aAta Alz~umayoni (Fr, T, S) [ some time ago, or ] three [ or more, to ten, ] seasons ago, ( mu*o valaAvapu A^azomaAnK , T, [by AzmAn being app. meant periods of two, or three, or six, months,]) and *aAta AlEuwayomi (Fr, T, S) [ some years ago, or] three years ago (T,) or three years ago or more, to ten; (Az on the authority of AZ, TA in art. Ewm ;) and *aA SabaAHK [ one morning ], and *aA masaA='K [ one evening ], (T, S,) and *aA SabuwHK [lit, at a time of drinking the morning-draught ], and *aA gabuwqK [lit. at a time of drinking the evening-draught ]; in these four instances without p : and this mode of expression has been heard only in the cases of the times here mentioned: they did not say *aAta $ahorK nor *aAta sanapK : (S:) or one may also well say *aAta SabaAHK , like *aAta yawomK ; for *A and *At both mean the time: and accord. to IAar, one says, A^atayotuhu *aAta AlS~abuwHi and *aAta Algabuwqi , as meaning I came to him in the morning, or in the morning between daybreak and sunrise, and in the evening, or in the evening between sunset and nightfall. (T.) ― -b12- You say also, laqiytuhu *aAta yadayoni , (TA,) or laqiytuhu A^aw~ala *iY yadayoni (M) and *aAti yadayoni , (AZ, M, Msb, [whence it seems to be not improbable that the phrase in the TA is imperfectly transcribed,]) meaning I met him the first thing, (M,) or first of everything. (AZ, Msb, TA.) And A^afoEaluhu A^aw~ala *iY yadayoni and *aAti yadayoni [ I will do it the first thing, or first of everything ]. (M.) And A^am~aA A^aw~ala *aAti yadayoni faA_in~aniY A^aHomadu A@ll~`ha , (AZ, M, Msb,) i. e. [ Whatever be the case, the first thing, or] first of everything, I praise God. (AZ, Msb.) ― -b13- [Respecting the phrase *aAtu Albayoni , which has two contr. meanings, see art. byn . It is inadequately explained in this art. in the T and M and K, as follows.] waA^aSoliHuwA *aAta bayonikumo , (T, M, K, *) in the Kur [viii. 1], accord. to Ahmad Ibn-Yahyà, means [ And do ye rightly dispose, or arrange, or order, ] the case that is between you: (T:) or, accord. to Zj, (M,) that wherein consists your union; ( Haqiyqapa waSolikumo , M, K;) i. e. be ye of one accord, or in unison, respecting that which God and his Apostle have commanded: (M:) or *aAtu Albayoni means the state of circumstances whereby the Muslims become of one accord, or in unison: (K:) this is the meaning in the saying, Aall~`hum~a A^aSoliHo *aAta Albayoni [ O God, do Thou rightly dispose &c.]. (M.) ― -b14- *aAtN is sometimes used as a noun independent in its meaning, (Mgh, Msb,) so as to denote material [or real] things; (Msb;) and is described by the epithets mutamay~izapN [or “ distinct ”] (Mgh, Msb) and qadiymapN [as meaning “ that has existed from eternity ”] (Mgh) and muHodavapN [as meaning “ that has been brought into existence ”]. (Mgh, Msb.) Thus used, (Msb,) it signifies The essence of a thing, meaning that by being which a thing is what it is, or that in being which a thing consists; or the ultimate and radical constituent of a thing: and the essence as meaning the peculiar nature of a thing: syn. HaqiyqapN , (T, IB, Msb, TA,) and maAhiy~apN , (Msb,) and xaAS~apN : (T, IB, TA:) it is also used as meaning a thing's self: (Mgh, * Msb:) [a man's self, or person: (see $axoSN :)] and a thing; a being; anything, whatever it be; every $aYo' being a *aAt , and every *At being a $Y' : (Aboo-Sa'eed, Mgh, Msb:) and particularly a substance, or thing that subsists by itself: [hence Aisomu *aAtK meaning a real substantive; also termed Aisomu EayonK : opposed to Aisomu maEonFY , i. e. an ideal substantive:] and [hence] it signifies also a word that is independent in its meaning; [i. e. *aAtN (alone), though oftener used in the sense assigned above to Aisomu *aAtK , signifies also, absolutely, a substantive; ] opposed to SifapN as signifying a word that is not independent in its meaning. (Kull p. 187.) Its application to God, in the sense of HaqiyqapN and xaAS~apN , is forbidden by most persons: (TA:) [for] *aAtu A@ll~`hi [as meaning The essence of God ], used by the scholastic theologians, is said to be an ignorant expression, because the names of God do not admit the fem. affix p ; so that one does not apply to Him the epithet Eal~aAmapN , though He is the all-surpassing in knowledge. (Msb.) The phrase fiY *aAti A@ll~`hi is like fiY janobi A@ll~`hi [ In, or in respect of, that which is the right, or due, of God; or in, or in respect of, obedience to God, or the means of obtaining nearness to God, or the way of God ]: and like liwajohi A@ll~`hi [ for the sake of God; or to obtain the countenance, or favour, or approbation, or recompense, of God ]: (Msb:) or it means in obedience to God; and in the way of God or his religion: (TA:) [or it may be rendered for the sake of God Himself; and so liwajohi A@ll~`hi : it is said to have been used by the Arabs [of the classical age], as well as by Aboo-Temmám, [who was a Muwelled;] (Mgh, Msb, *) but some deny that it occurs in the old language. (Msb. [See, however, an ex. from a trad. voce A^uxayo$inu .]) [It is said that] the phrase majal~atuhumo *aAtu AlA_il`hi , used by En-Nábighah, (Msb,) i. e. EdhDhubyánee, (TA in art. jl ,) means Their book is the service of God Himself: (Msb:) [but it seems more reasonable to render this phrase agreeably with the primary signification of *At as meaning their book is that of God, in a sense like that in which a house of worship is said to be a house of God; for,] as some relate it, the phrase used by En-Nábighah is maHal~atuhumo *aAtu AlA_il`hi , with HA' , [i. e. their abode is in a peculiar manner that of God, ] meaning, their abode is one of pilgrimage and of sacred sites. (S and TA in art. jl .) ― -b15- *uw is sometimes redundant [in respect of meaning, though governing as a prefixed n.]; and so is its pl. (T, * TA.) Az says, (TA,) I have heard more than one of the Arabs say, kun~aA bimawoDiEi ka*aA maEa *iY EamorKw , i. e. We were in such a place with Amr: (T, TA:) and kaAna maEanaA *uw EamorKw , i. e. 'Amr was with us: and A^atayonaA *aA yamanK , meaning A^atayonaA Alyamana [ We came to El-Yemen ]. (T.) [See an ex. similar to this last, and evidently belonging to the present art., in the latter half of art. *A . And see laA *aA jarama and laA A^ano *aA jarama and laA Eano *aA jarama and laA *aA jara (in which *A is in like manner redundant, as are also A^ano and Eano , the latter of which is a dial. var. of the former of them,) in art. jrm : perhaps belonging to the present art., like A^atayonaA *aAyamanK ; or perhaps to art. *A . See also what is said respecting *uw prefixed to a proper name in an early portion of this paragraph.] ― -b16- It is also used in the sense of Aal~a*iY , (T, S, M, K,) in the dial. of Teiyi, (T, S, TA,) for the purpose of qualifying a determinate noun (S, M, K) by means of a proposition which it connects with that noun: (M, K:) and when thus used, it [generally] retains the same form when it denotes a dual and a pl. (S, M, K) and a fem., (S,) and exhibits no sign of case: (M, K:) you say, A^anaA *uw Earafotu [ I who knew ], and *uw samiEotu [ who heard ]; and h`*ihi AlmaroA^apu *uw qaAlato ka*aA [ This is the woman who said such a thing: (S:) and A^ataAniY *uw qaAla *`lika [ He who said that came to me ]; and A^ataAniY *uw qaAlaA *`lika [ They two who said that came to me ]; and A^ataAni *uw qaAluwA *`lika [ They who said that came to me ]. (M.) But Fr says, I heard an Arab of the desert say, biAlfaDoli *uw faD~alakumo A@ll~`hu bihi waAlkaraAmapi *aAtu A^akoramakumu A@ll~`hu bihaA [ By the excellence wherewith God hath made you to excel, and the honour wherewith God hath honoured you ]; thus they use *aAtu in the place of Aal~atiY , and they make it to be with refa in every case: and they confuse [numbers and genders] in speaking of a dual number and a pl. number [and a fem.]; they sometimes say, [for ex.,] in the case of the dual, h`*aAni *uw taEorifu and haAtaAni *uw taEorifu [ These two whom, or which, thou knowest ]; and a poet says, [namely, Sinán Ibn-El-Fahl, of the tribe of Teiyi, (Ham p. 292,)] faA_in~a AlmaA='a A^abiY wajad~iY wabiy^oriY *uw Hafarotu wa*uw Tawayotu [ For verily the water is the water of my father and my grandfather, and my well which I dug and which I cased; making *w to relate to a fem. noun]: and some, he adds, use the dual and pl. and fem. forms; thus they say, h`*aAna *awaA qaAlaA *aAka [ These two who said that ], and h`w^ulaA='i *awuwA qaAluwA [ These who said ], and h`*ihi *aAtu qaAlato [ This female who said ]; and he cites the saying of a poet, jamaEotuhaA mino A^ayonuqK sawaAbiqo *awaAtu yanohaDona bigayori saAy^iqo [ I collected them from outstripping she-camels, that rise and hasten in their pace without a driver ]; and the prov., A^ataY Ealayohi *uw A^ataY EalaY Aln~aAsi , meaning Al~a*iY A^ataY [i. e. What has come upon men in general has come, or came, upon him ]. (T.) Accord. to the usage most in repute, *uw in this sense is indecl., and has no variation of gender or number; but some decline it, like *w in the sense of SaAHib , except that they make *aAt and *awaAt indecl., with damm for the termination, saying *aAtu and *awaAtu in every case, if they adopt the chaste mode; otherwise, in the accus. and gen. cases, saying *aAti , and in like manner *awaAti (I' Ak pp. 40 and 41.) ― -b17- They said also, laAA^afoEalu *`lika bi*iY tasolamu (M, K) and b*Y tasolamiyna , (M,) and b*Y tasolamaAni , (M, K,) and b*Y tasolamuwna and b*Ytasolamona , (M,) meaning I will not do that by thy, and by your, safety: (M, K:) or by God who, (M,) or by Him who, (K,) maketh thee, and you, to be in safety. (M, K.) [See also art. slm .]

definition: The latter, or kinder, or the last, or kindmost, part of anything.
sourceDefinition: The latter, or kinder, or the last, or kindmost, part of anything. (M, K.) Accord. to MF, this is the proper signification, and the other significations here following are tropical. (TA.) [But in my opinion, the word in each of the next two senses, or at least in the former of them; if not strictly proper, is what is termed HaqiyqapN Eurofiy~apN , i. e. a word so much used in a tropical sense as to be, in that sense, conventionally regarded as proper.] ― -b2- [ A skirt, or lower extremity, of a garment, reaching nearly, or quite, to the ground, or that is dragged upon the ground, when made to hang down: ] the extremity, of a garment, that is next the ground, and so if not touching it [ as well as if touching it ]; an inf. n. used in this sense: (Msb:) or the part of a waist-wrapper ( A_izaAr ), and of a garment [of any kind], that is dragged [ upon the ground ], (M, K,) when it is made to hang down: (M:) or the part, of an A_izaAr , and of a [garment of the kind called] ridaA=' , that is made to hang down, and touches the ground: and the part, of any kind of garment worn by a woman, that the wearer drags upon the ground behind her: (Lth, T:) or the parts, all round, of a woman's garment, that fall upon the ground: and the portion that is made to hang down, of a woman's shift and of her qinaAE [or head-covering]: you do not [properly] say of a man that he has a *ayol [but only when you liken the lower part of his garment to the similar part of a woman's garment]: a man's having a long garment, such as a shirt and a jub~ap , [or his dragging the skirt thereof,] is termed A_irofaAlN : (Khálid Ibn-Jembeh, T:) the pl. of *ayolN (in this sense, T, Msb, as relating to a shirt [&c.], S, and in all its senses, T, M) is A^a*oyaAlN (T, S, M, Msb, K) and A^a*oyulN (El-Hejeree, M, K) [both pls. of pauc.] and *uyuwlN (T, S, M, Msb, K) which is a pl. of mult. (M.) Hence Tuwlu Al*~ayoli is a metonymical expression meaning (tropical:) Richness, or competency; because long A^a*oyaAl generally pertain to the rich and the prodigal and the proud and self-conceited: (Er-Rázee, Har p. 493:) and you say, TaAla *ayolu fulaAnK , meaning (tropical:) The state, or condition, of such a one became good, and his wealth became abundant: and huwa Tawiylu Al*~ayoli , meaning (tropical:) He is rich. (Har p. 319.) ― -b3- Of a horse (T, K) &c., (K,) [i. e.] of a horse and a camel and the like, (M,) The tail: (T, M, K:) or the tail when long: (TA:) or the part, of the tail, that is made to hang down. (M, K.) ― -b4- [(assumed tropical:) Of a cloud, The skirt; or lower, pendent, part: used in this sense in the K voce hayodabN .] ― -b5- *ayolu Alr~iyHi (assumed tropical:) What is dragged along, (T, S, O,) or drawn together, (M,) by the wind, upon the ground, (T, S, O, M,) of dust (T, M, O) and rubbish: (T, O:) or what the wind leaves upon the sand, (M, K,) in the form of a rope, (M,) resembling the track of a *ayol [or skirt ] dragged along: (M, K:) or, as some say, A^a*oyaAluAlr~iyHi means (assumed tropical:) the after-parts of the wind, with which it sweeps what is light to it. (M.) ― -b6- *ayolu jabalK (assumed tropical:) The foot, bottom, base, or lowest part, of a mountain. (A and TA voce jar~N .) ― -b7- A^a*oyaAlu Aln~aAsi (assumed tropical:) The hindmost of the people. (K.) You say, jaA='a A^a*oyaAlN mina Aln~aAsi (assumed tropical:) Some few of the hindmost of the people came. (S, Sgh.) ― -b8- See also 2. -A2- And see *aAy^ilN .

definition: The side, (K,) in a general sense: (TA:) or the side of a well, (S, Msb, K,) and of the sky, (Er-Rághib, TA,) and of anything;
sourceDefinition: The side, (K,) in a general sense: (TA:) or the side of a well, (S, Msb, K,) and of the sky, (Er-Rághib, TA,) and of anything; (S, Msb; *) and ↓ rajaA='N signifies the same: (K:) the side of a well from its top to its bottom; (TA;) and the two sides thereof: which last is also [or properly] the meaning of the dual; which is rajawaAni : (S:) pl. A^arojaA='N . (S, Msb, K.) Hence, in the Kur [lxix. 17], waA@lomalaku EalaY A^arojaAy^ihaA [ The angels being at the sides thereof ]. (S, TA.) They said, rumiYa bihi Alr~ajawaAni , meaning (assumed tropical:) He was cast into places of destruction: (S:) or it is said of one who is held in mean estimation: (M, TA:) AisotihozaA='N in the K is a mistake for Ausotuhiyna bihi , the reading in the M: (TA:) as though the two [opposite] sides of the well were cast at with him. (K.) And one says of him who will not be deceived so as to be turned away from one course to another, laA turomaY bihi Alr~ajawaAni (assumed tropical:) [lit. The two sides of the well will not be cast at with him ]; in allusion to the well's two [opposite] sides' being cast at with the bucket. (Z, TA.)

definition: Redness: (Msb, K:) a certain red dye: (K:) or a certain dye, intensely red: (S:) accord.

sourceDefinition: , (M,) or Ald~iyaAra , (K,) [aor. , accord. to a rule of the K,] inf. n. rasomN , (M,) It (the rain) rased the house or dwelling, or the houses or dwellings, leaving a relic, or relics, thereof cleaving to the ground. (M, K.) In the saying of El-Hotei-ah, A^amino rasomi daArK murobiEN wamuSiyfu liEayonayoka mino maA='i Al$~uw^uwni wakiyfu [ Is it in consequence of autumn-rain's and springrain's rasing of a dwelling so as to leave only a relic thereof cleaving to the ground, that there is to thine eyes a distilling of the water of the tearchannels? ], mrbE and mSyf are in the nom. case because of the inf. n., i.e. rsm . (M, TA. [But in the latter, maSiyfu : and in a copy of the former, marobaEN and maSiyfu , both of which are evidently wrong.]) ― -b2- [ rasama often signifies He marked, or stamped: and he drew, traced, traced out, sketched, sketched out, or planned: and he delineated, or described. ] You say, rasama AlT~aEaAma He stamped, or sealed, the corn; (TA in art. r$m ;) as also ra$amahu . (S, K, TA, all in that art. [See rawosamN .]) And rasamotu AlbinaA='a , aor. and inf. n. as above, I marked out the building. (Msb.) And rasama kitaAbFA walamo yaHo$uhu [ He sketched out a book and did not fill it up ]. (Mz 1st nwE .) And rasamotu AlkitaAba I wrote the book, or letter, or writing. (Msb.) And rasama EalaY ka*aA He wrote upon such a thing; (S, K;) and ra$ama is a dial. var. thereof. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence,] rasama lahu ka*aA , (S, K, TA,) or bika*aA , (Msb,) (tropical:) [ He prescribed to him the doing of such a thing; ] he commanded, ordered, bade, or enjoined, him to do such a thing. (S, * Msb, * K, TA.) (K.) You say, raEadati Als~amaA='u wabaraqato , and, accord. to AO and AA, waA^aboraqat ↓ A^aroEadat , (S, TA,) which latter As disallows in this case as well as in another mentioned below, (S, * TA,) meaning The sky [ thundered and lightened: or] thundered and lightened much before rain. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] raEada , inf. n. raEodN , (tropical:) He threatened, or menaced, with evil; as also ↓ ArEd , inf. n. A_iroEaAdN : (Msb:) or the latter signifies he threatened, or menaced; or he frightened, or terrified: (K:) and raEada wabaraqa he frightened, or terrified, (S, K,) and threatened, or menaced; (S;) as also ↓ A^arEada waA^aboraqa : (AO, AA, S:) and raEadalahu and baraqa lahu he threatened him, or menaced him: (As, TA:) and raEada liY biAlqawoli , aor. , inf. n. raEodN ; and ↓ ArEd ; he threatened me, or he frightened me with speech: (TA:) or, accord. to As, ↓ ArEd and Abrq are not allowable: when one cited against him the verse of El-Kumeyt, A^aroEido waA^aboriqo yaA yaziydu famaA waEiyduka liY biDaAy^iro (tropical:) [ Threaten and menace, O Yezeed, but thy threatening is not harming to me ], he denied ElKumeyt to be an authority. (S, TA.) [See also an ex. in a verse cited voce jal~a .] Hiyna raEada AlA_isolaAmu wabaraqa , occurring in a trad., means When El-Islám came with its threatening and its terrifying. (TA.) ― -b4- See also 8, in two places. ― -b5- And see 4.

sourceDefinition: Thunder; i. e. the sound that is heard from the clouds, (S, K, *) or from the sky: (A:) so say the people of the desert: (Akh, TA:) [thus termed as being supposed to be a trembling, or state of agitation, of the clouds, as is implied in the Ksh and the Expos. of Bd in ii. 18, where it is said to be from AlAirotiEaAd , or as being a cause of trembling:] originally an inf. n., and therefore [it is said that] it has no pl.: (Bd ubi suprà:) [but see what follows, in which ruEuwdN occurs, perhaps as its pl.:] or Alr~aEodu is the name of an angel who drives the clouds [ with his voice ] like as a man drives camels with singing. (I'Ab, Z, K.) ― -b2- [Hence,] jaA='a bi*aAti Alr~aEodi waAlS~aliyli i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ He brought, or brought to pass, that which had thunder and noise; meaning,] (tropical:) war: (S, K, TA:) or calamity: (A, TA:) and bi*awaAti ↓ Alr~awaAEidi (tropical:) calamities: (A:) [for] ↓ *aAtu Alr~awaAEidi [in the CK *awAtu ] signifies calamity. (S, K, TA.) And fiY kitaAbihi ruEuwdN waburuwqN [which may be rendered In his letter are thunders and lightnings; ] meaning, (tropical:) words of threatening. (A.)

sourceDefinition: Cowardly; (S, A, L, K;) that trembles, or quakes, (A, L,) from fear, (A,) or at fighting, by reason of cowardice; (L;) and in like manner riEodiydapN applied to a woman: (A:) or this has the former signification, [but in an intensive sense,] as also ↓ tiroEiydN : pl. [of the first or second] raEaAdiydu . (L.) ― -b2- Also the first, (S, K,) or second, (A, L,) applied to a woman, (S, L, K,) or a girl, (A,) (tropical:) Soft, or tender; (S, A, L, K;) whose flesh quivers by reason of its softness: (L:) pl. as above. (A.) ― -b3- And the first, (assumed tropical:) A soft, or tender, plant. (IAar, TA.) ― -b4- And [(tropical:) Anything quivering or quaking: hence, as a subst., particularly applied to The kind of sweet food called ] faAluw*aj , (A,) or faAluw* . (K.) It was said to an Arab of the desert, “ Dost thou know what is called fAlw* ? ” and he answered, naEamo A^aSofaru riEodiydN [ Yes: it is yellow, quivering ]. (S.) ― -b5- Also, (A,) and ↓ muroEadN , (IAar, A, K,) (tropical:) A hill, or heap, of sand [ shaking, or shaken, and consequently ] pouring down. (IAar, A, K.)

definition: [ That thunders much ].
sourceDefinition: [ That thunders much ]. saHaAbapN raE~aAdapN signifies A cloud that thunders much: (TA:) but Ks says, “ We have not heard them say thus. ” (Lh, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] applied to a man, (S,) (assumed tropical:) Loquacious; (S, K;) and so raE~aAdapN [but in an intensive sense]. (TA.) ― -b3- Also, [as a coll. gen. n., n. un. with p , The torpedo: and the silurus electricus, found in the Nile: generally meaning the latter:] a certain fish; when a man touches it, a numbness affects his hand and arm to the shoulders, and a tremour, as long as the fish remains alive: (S, K: *) so called because he who lays hold upon it, when it is alive, trembles with a kind of trembling wherewith he cannot restrain himself; it is a kind of trembling with a coldness, or chilness, and intense numbness, and formication in the limbs, and heaviness, so that he possesses no power over himself, and cannot lay hold of anything at all with his hand; the numbness rising by degrees to his upper arm and his shoulderblade and the whole of his side, when he touches the fish with the slightest touch in the shortest time. (So says 'Abd-El-Lateef. [See “ Abdollatiphi Hist. Aeg. Comp. ” p. 82; and De Sacy's Translation and Notes.])

(see rafilN )], and in every work. (M, K.) ― -b2- And rafala , (M, K,) or rafala fiY viyaAbihi , (S, TA,) aor. , (S, M,) inf. n. rafolN (Lth, T, M, K) and rufuwlN (T, TA) and rafalaAnN ; (M, K;) and ↓ Arfl ; (S, M, K;) He dragged his skirt, and kicked it with his foot: (Lth, T:) or he made his clothes long, and dragged them, walking with an elegant and a proud and self-conceited gait, with an affected inclining of his body from side to side: (S:) or he dragged his skirt, and walked in the manner described above: or he moved his arm up and down [ in walking ]: (M, K:) and fiY viyaAbihi ↓ trf~l signifies the same as rafala and Arfl : (TA:) or ↓ A_irofaAlN [inf. n. of 4] signifies a man's having a long garment, such as a skirt and a jub~ap : (Khálid Ibn-Jembeh, T in art. *yl :) and one says, fiY mi$oyatihaA xroqFA ↓ tataraf~alu [ She drags her skirt, &c., in her gait, by reason of awkwardness ]. (S.) tarofulu AlmaraAfilaA , a phrase used by Ru-beh, [↓ maraAfilu being app. pl. of marofalN , a regular inf. n. of rafala ,] means She walks with every sort of rafol or rufuwl [i. e. dragging of the skirt, &c.]. (Lth, T accord. to different copies.) And ↓ tarofala , inf. n. tarofalapN , He walked with an inclining of his body from side to side ( tabaxotara ) by reason of pride ( kiborFA ), or by reason of old age ( kibarFA ): (K, accord. to different copies:) the t is augmentative. (TA.) -A2- See also the next paragraph, last sentence, in two places.

sourceDefinition: The making a garment ample, or long towards the ground: the letting it down, or making it to hang down: (TA:) [and so ↓ A_irofaAlN :] you say, viyaAbahu ↓ Arfl , (Sh, T,) or vawobahu , (M,) or rifolahu , (K, TA, in the CK rafilahu ,) He let down, or made to hang down, his garments, or his garment, or his skirt. (Sh, T, M, K.) ― -b2- Hence, (TA,) rf~lhu , (A 'Obeyd, T, S, M,) inf. n. as above, (Sh, T, S, M, K,) (tropical:) He magnified him, or honoured him: (A 'Obeyd, T, S, M, K:) he made him a king, (A 'Obeyd, T, M, K,) and a lord, or chief, (Sh, T, M, K,) and a commander, and a judge: (TA:) [like raf~adahu :] and he rendered him submissive; made him to submit; or brought him under, or into, subjection: (M, K:) thus it has two contr. meanings; (K;) [like tar~afahu ;] for when a man is made judge in an affair, it is as though he were subjected to service therein. (TA.) Dhu-r-Rummeh says, A_i*aA naHonu raf~alonaA A@moraA^F saAda qawomahu waA_ino lamo yakuno mino qaboli *`lika yu*okaru (assumed tropical:) [ When we magnify a man, or make a man a king, &c., he becomes lord, or chief, of his people, though he have been before that not mentioned ]. (T, S, M.) And you say, ruf~ila fulaAnN (assumed tropical:) Such a one was made a lord, or chief, over his people. (Sh, T.) ― -b3- Also (tropical:) He increased, or exceeded, to him that over which he had authority to judge, or to decide. (TA.) ― -b4- And tarofiylN also signifies (tropical:) The leaving a well for its water to collect in it; (S, O, K;) and so ↓ rafolN : (O, K:) you say, rf~l Alr~aky~ap (tropical:) He left the well for its water to collect in it; (Ks, T, M;) as also ↓ rafalahaA , aor. , inf. n. rafolN . (O.)

definition: Awkward (S, M, K) in his manner of wearing his clothes, (S,) or with his clothes [ when walking &c.
sourceDefinition: Awkward (S, M, K) in his manner of wearing his clothes, (S,) or with his clothes [ when walking &c.], and in every work; as also ↓ A^arofalu ; fem. [of the latter] ↓ rafolaA='u . (M, K.) And rafilapN (Lth, T, M, K, TA) and ↓ raAfilapN (Lth, T, TA) A woman who drags her skirt (Lth, T, M, K, TA) well, or beautifully, (M, K, TA,) when she walks, and who walks with an elegant and a proud and self-conceited gait, with an affected inclining of the body from side to side: (Lth, T, TA:) or the former signifies a woman who drags her skirt ( tataraf~alu ), in her gait, by reason of awkwardness: (S, TA:) and ↓ rafolA='u , a woman who does not walk well (ADk, T, S, M, K) in her clothes, (ADk, T, S, M,) dragging her garment, (M,) or dragging her skirt: (K:) and ↓ raAfilN , a man making his clothes long, and dragging them, walking with an elegant and a proud and self-conceited gait, with an affected inclining of his body from side to side; (S;) in which sense rafilapN may be well used as an epithet applied to a woman: (Lth, T:) or ↓ raAfilN (TA) and ↓ tarofiylN , (Seer, M, K, TA,) in which latter the t is augmentative, (TA,) signify a man who drags his skirt, and walks in the manner last described above; or who moves his arm up and down in walking. (Seer, M, K, TA.) ― -b2- Also, i. e. rafilN , Foolish; stupid; or unsound, or deficient, in intellect, or understanding. (S.) ― -b3- And rafilapN , A foul, or an unseemly, or ugly, woman; (M, K;) as also ↓ rifal~apN , (M,) or ↓ rifilapN , with two kesrehs: (K:) and the same epithets are applied likewise in this sense to a man. (M.) -A2- See also rifolN .

Ar. ii. 332:) or a well not made neat; or not constructed [or cased ] with bricks [&c.]: (MA:) pl. rakaAyaA (S, Msb, K) and ↓ rakiY~N , (S, and so in some copies of the K,) or the former is the pl. and ↓ the latter is [properly speaking] a gen. n., [i. e. a coll. gen. n.,] and often occurs as a sing. and as a pl., (Nh, TA,) or the pl. is also rukiY~N : (so in some copies of the K and in the TA:) accord. to ISd, it is from rakaA in the first of the senses assigned to this verb above. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: [pass. part. n. of 1: ― -b2- and hence, as a subst.,] A large watering-trough or tank: (AA, T, S, K:) [in the S and K is added, waAljuromuwzu AlS~agiyru , which may mean either that the small watering- trough is called jrmwz , and such is the case, or that marokuw~N also signifies a small jrmwz , agreeably with what here follows, and with an explanation of this word in the TA voce HawiY~N :] Az, after mentioning AA's explanation given above, says, but what I have heard from the Arabs is, that the mrkw~ is a small watering-trough or tank, which a man makes, or forms, or fashions, in a suitable manner, with his hands, at the head of the well, when he has not, and cannot procure, a vessel in which to give water to a camel or to two camels: and that which is large is not thus called. (TA.) [But see an ex. voce salosN .]

sourceDefinition: , (Mgh,) and AlHijaArapu , (A, Mgh,) [aor. ,] inf. n. ramaDN , (A,) The earth, or ground, (Mgh,) and the stones, (A, Mgh,) became vehemently heated by the sun. (A, Mgh.) ― -b2- ramiDa yawomunaA , (S, A, Msb, K,) aor. as above, (S, Msb,) and so the inf. n., (S, A, Msb,) Our day became intensely hot. (S, A, Msb, K.) ― -b3- ramiDa said of a man, (A, Mgh, TA,) aor. as above, (TA,) and so the inf. n., (Mgh, TA,) He had his fast burnt (A, Mgh, TA) by the ground, or stones, vehemently heated by the sun, (A,) or by the vehemence of the heat: (Mgh, TA:) or he was smitten, or affected, by the heat of the sun: (Ham p. 173:) and ramiDato qadamuhu his foot was burnt by the ground, or stones, vehemently heated by the sun. (S, Msb, K.) In like manner you say, ramiDati AlfiSaAlu The young camels, or young weaned camels, felt the heat of the sun from the ground, or stones, vehemently heated thereby: then is the prayer of the period called AlD~uHaY : (S:) or had their feet burned by the ground, or stones, thus heated: (Mgh, Msb:) or lay down in consequence of the intense heat of the sand, and the burning of their feet. (IAth.) And ramiDati Alganamu The sheep, or goats, from pasturing in intense heat, had their livers ulcerated, (S, K,) and their lungs affected with dropsy: (S:) or had their lungs and livers affected with dropsy, and ulcerated. (L.) And ramiDato Eayonuhu His eye became hot, so that it almost burned: the verb occurs in this sense in a trad., as some relate it, with D [instead of S ]. (TA.) ― -b4- Also, said of a man fasting, His inside became vehemently hot (Fr, K) by reason of intense thirst. (Fr, TA.) ― -b5- And, said of a man, He went upon ground, or stones, vehemently heated by the sun. (TA.) ― -b6- And He returned from the desert to the region of cities, towns, or villages, and of cultivated land. (L, TA.) ― -b7- You say also, ramiDotu mina AlA^amori and ramiDotu lahu and ↓ AirotamaDotu (tropical:) [meaning I was distressed and disquieted by reason of the thing, or affair: or I grieved for it ]: (A:) [for] mino ka*aA ↓ ArtmD signifies (tropical:) he was distressed and disquieted by reason of such a thing: (S, K, TA:) and ↓ ArtmD lifulaAnK (tropical:) he grieved for such a one; i. q. Hazina lahu , accord. to the [S and] L [and CK]: or i. q. Hadiba lahu , [but this I think a mistranscription, for you say Hadiba Ealayohi , not Hadiba lahu ,] accord. to the O and [some copies of the] K. (TA.) -A2- ramaDahu AlHar~u : see 4. ― -b2- s ramaDa Alganama , (K,) aor. , inf. n. ramoDN , (TA,) He pastured the sheep, or goats, upon ground vehemently heated by the sun, (K, TA,) and made them to lie down upon it; (TA;) as also ↓ ArmDhA ; and ↓ rm~DhA , (K, TA,) inf. n. taromiyDN . (TA.) ― -b3- ramaDa Al$~aApa , aor. , (S, M, K,) inf. n. ramoDN , (S, M,) He clave the sheep, or goat, leaving its skin upon it, and threw it upon heated stones, and put hot ashes upon it, in order that it might become thoroughly cooked: (S, K:) or he kindled a fire upon stones, then clave the sheep, or goat, with its skin upon it, then broke its ribs from within, in order that it might lie steadily upon the ground, with the heated stones beneath it, and hot ashes above it, a fire being kindled over it: when it is thoroughly cooked, they skin it and eat it: (M, TA:) you say also ↓ ArmD Al$~aApa : ― -b4- and rumiDa All~aHomu [ The flesh was dressed in the manner above described ]. (TA.) -A3- ramuDa , if used, is the verb whereof ↓ ramaADapN , which is mentioned by Sh and in the K, is the inf. n.; and accord. to the explanation of the latter in the K, signifies It (a large or broad knife or blade) was, or became, sharp. (TA.) -A4- ramaDa Aln~aSola , (S, K,) or AlmuwsaY , (A,) aor. , and , (S, K,) He put the blade between two smooth stones, and then beat it, to make it thin: (ISk, S, K: [but in the text of the K, as given in the TA, the word rendered “ stones ” is omitted:]) or he beat the razor between two stones, in order that it might become thin; as also ↓ ArmD . (A.)

(Sh, * K.) IF says that the m may be original, or it may be a substitute for b . (TA.) ― -b3- rm~D Alganama : see ramaDa . -A2- ram~aDotu AlS~awoma I purposed fasting or the fast [app. during the month of ramaDaAn ]. (Sgh, K.)

definition: The ground, or stones, vehemently heated by the sun, burned me.
sourceDefinition: The ground, or stones, vehemently heated by the sun, burned me. (S.) And ArmDhu AlHar~u The heat burned him; (K, * TA;) as also ↓ ramaDahu , aor. . (TA.) And ArmD AlHar~u Alqawoma (Jm, A, K) The heat distressed the people, or company of men; (Jm, K;) so that it hurt them. (K.) You say also, gaw~iruwA binaA faqado A^aromaDotumuwnaA (Jm, A) Make ye the camels to lie down with us during the vehement midday-heat [ for ye have caused us to be burnt by the heat of the sun, or by the vehemently-heated ground ]. (Jm, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] ArmDhu (tropical:) It (anything, AA) pained him. (AA, K.) And ArmDhu AlA^amoru (tropical:) [ The thing, or affair, pained him ] is a phrase which has originated from the first of the phrases mentioned in this paragraph. (S, TA.) ― -b3- ArmD Alganama : see 1. ― -b4- ArmD Al$~aApa : see 1. -A2- ArmD AlmuwsaY : see 1, last signification.

definition: He drove the gazelles upon the ground, or stones, vehemently heated by the sun, until their hoofs became dissundered, or dislocated, and so they were taken: (A:) or he hunted them during the vehement...
sourceDefinition: He drove the gazelles upon the ground, or stones, vehemently heated by the sun, until their hoofs became dissundered, or dislocated, and so they were taken: (A:) or he hunted them during the vehement midday-heat, (S, K,) pursuing them until, their legs being dislocated by the vehemently-heated ground, he took them. (S, TA.) -A2- Alt~aram~uDu also signifies The heaving of the soul [or stomach ]; or its being agitated by a tendency to vomit; syn. gavayaAnu Aln~afosi . (IAar, K.)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. tarowiyapN : see 4, in two places: ― -b2- and 5. [Hence,] yawomu Alt~arowiyapi [ The day of providing oneself with water; ] the eighth day of Dhu-l-Hijjeh; (T, Msb;) the day before that of 'Arafeh: (M:) so called because they (the pilgrims, T) used to provide themselves ( yatazaw~aduwna , T, M, or ↓ yataraw~awona , Msb, and so in a copy of the T, or ↓ yarotawuwna , S, K) on that day with water (T, S, M, * Msb, K) for the aftertime, (S, Msb, K,) and to rise and go, or when rising to go, to Minè, where is no water, [or, accord. to the Msb, where was little water,] therefore they provided themselves fully with water, or therefore they provided themselves with water from Mekkeh for the alighting and abiding at Minè: (T, accord. to two different copies:) or [it means the day of consideration, or thought; (from another signification of the verb, as will be seen from what follows;) and is so called] because Abraham was considering, or thinking upon, his dream ( wa yatafak~aru fiY ruw^oyaAhu ↓ kaAna yataraw~aY ) [on that day], and on the ninth he knew [that his dream was from God], and on the tenth he desired to act [according to his dream] ( AisotaEomala ). (K. [And in a similar manner it is explained in the Ksh and by Bd in xxxvii. 101. See also 2 in art. rwA^ ]) ― -b3- rw~Y raA^osahu biAld~uhoni , and Alv~ariyda biAld~asami , (T, TA,) He moistened [ his head, app. much, or saturated it, i. e. its hair, with oil, or grease, and the broken, or crumbled, bread with grease, or gravy ]. (TA.) -A2- rw~Ahu Al$~iEora , (T, S, M, Mgh, K,) and AlHadiyva , (M, Mgh, Msb,) inf. n. as above; (S;) and A_iy~aAhu ↓ ArwAhu ; (S, K;) He made him to relate by heart the poetry, (S, M, * Mgh, * K, * TA,) and the tradition, narrative, or story; (M, Mgh, TA;) he made him to bear in his memory, knowing by heart, and to transmit, relate, recite, or rehearse, (Msb, TA,) the poetry, (TA,) and the tradition, narrative, or story; (Msb, TA;) [or he taught him to do so; i. e.] he related to him by heart ( rawaY lahu ) the poetry, (T, TA,) and the tradition, narrative, or story, (TA,) until he retained it in his memory, for the purpose of relating it by heart [ as learned, or heard, or received, ] from him. (T, TA. *) And ruw~iynaA AlHadiyva [ We had the tradition, narrative, or story, related to us by heart; and in like manner, Al$~iEora the poetry ]. (Msb, TA.) -A3- raw~ayotu fiY AlA^amori , (S, K, [though Freytag represents the verb as being in the K without teshdeed, and Golius explains the verb nearly in the same manner with and without teshdeed,]) inf. n. as above, (TA,) He looked into the thing, or affair, or case; inspected it; examined it; considered it; or thought upon it; (S, M, K, TA;) deliberately, or leisurely; without haste; a dial. var. of raw~aA^otu [q. v.]: (M, TA:) [and fiyhi ↓ taraw~ayotu app. signifies the same:] see yataraw~aY in the former half of this paragraph, in an explanation of yawomu Alt~arowiyapi .

definition: [originally rawoyaAnu ] an epithet from rawiYa ;
sourceDefinition: [originally rawoyaAnu ] an epithet from rawiYa ; (T, M, Mgh, Msb, K;) Satisfied with drinking [of water and of milk &c.]; having drunk [thereof] enough to quench, or satisfy, his thirst; contr. of EaTo$aAnu : (S, Mgh: *) fem. ray~aA , (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K,) in which the Y is not changed into w because the word is an epithet; for it is changed into w only in a subst., of the measure faEolaY , of which Y is the final radical, as in taqowaY ; so that if it were a subst., it would be raw~aY ; (S, M;) originally rawoyaA : (M:) as to ray~aA that is thought to be used as the proper name of a woman, it is, thus used, an epithet, like AlHaArivu and AlEab~aAsu , though without the article Al : (S, * M:) the pl. is rwaA='N , (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K,) with kesr and medd., (S,) in measure like kitaAbN , (Msb,) masc. and fem. (Mgh, Msb.) You say qawomN riwaA='N mina AlmaA='i [ A people, or party, satisfied with drinking of water ]. (S.) ― -b2- And nabotN ray~aAnu and $ajarN riwaA='N [ A plant, or herbage, and trees, having plentiful irrigation: or flourishing and fresh, luxuriant, juicy, succulent, or sappy, by reason of plentiful irrigation: see the verb]. (M.) ― -b3- [Hence,] ray~aAnu signifies also (assumed tropical:) Full of fat and flesh. (JM.) And you say wajohN ray~aAnu (tropical:) [ A plump face ]; an expression of dispraise [app. when relating to a man, but not otherwise; for ray~aAnu , or ray~aA , applied to a youth, or to a woman, or a limb of a woman, meaning plump and juicy, is used by way of praise]: opposed to wajohN ZamoA=nu . (A and TA in art. ZmA^ .) And AimoraA^apN ray~aA Almuxaloxali (assumed tropical:) [ A woman full, or plump, in the place of the anklet ]. (JM.) And farasN ray~aAnu AlZ~ahori (assumed tropical:) A horse fat in the portion of flesh and sinew next the back-bone on each side. (T.)

sourceDefinition: [as the act. part. n. of rawaY ] is used in relation to water [as meaning Bringing, or one who brings, water to his family: and drawing, or one who draws, water for others: and a camel carrying, or that carries, water; whence the subst. raAwiyapN , q. v.]. (S, TA.) ― -b2- And [hence] it is used also in relation to poetry (T, S, M) and to traditions or narratives or stories (T, M, Mgh, K) [as meaning A relater, reciter, or rehearser, by heart, of poetry, and of traditions, or narratives or stories, learned, or heard, or received, from another]: and in like manner ↓ raAwiyapN , but in an intensive sense [as meaning a large, or copious, relater or reciter or rehearser, &c.]; (T, S, M, Mgh, K;) i. e. kaviyru Alr~iwaAyapi ; (T, * TA;) as in the phrase rajulN raAwiyapN lil$~iEori [ a man who is a large, or copious, relater &c. of poetry ]: (S:) the pl. of raAwK is ruwaApN . (S, TA.) -A2- Also One who has the superintendence, management, or care, of horses ( mano yaquwmu EalaY Alxayoli [strangely rendered by Freytag, who seems to have read EalaY Aljamali , “ constrictus fune et stans super cameli dorso ”]). (M, K.)

definition: A camel, (A 'Obeyd, T, S, K,) or a mule, or an ass, (S, and so in the K with the exception of “ and ” for “ or, ”) upon which water is drawn: (A 'Obeyd, T, S, K: [see saAniyapN :]) or a camel that carries water;
sourceDefinition: A camel, (A 'Obeyd, T, S, K,) or a mule, or an ass, (S, and so in the K with the exception of “ and ” for “ or, ”) upon which water is drawn: (A 'Obeyd, T, S, K: [see saAniyapN :]) or a camel that carries water; (M, * Mgh, Msb;) and then applied to any beast upon which water is drawn : (Msb:) [but it is disputed whether this be the primary or proper signification, or whether it be secondary or tropical, as will be shown by what follows:] and also a man who draws water (A 'Obeyd, T, TA) for his family: (TA:) the p is affixed [ liln~aqoli , i. e. for the purpose of transferring the word from the category of epithets to that of substantives; or] to give intensiveness to the signification: (Msb:) pl. rawaAyaA [by rule rawaA='K , being originally of the measure fawaAEilu , not faEaAy^ilu ]. (S, M, TA.) Also A mazaAdap [or leathern water-bag ] (A 'Obeyd, T, S, M, Mgh) composed of three skins, (Mgh,) containing water; (M, K;) so called as being the receptacle in which is the water borne by the camel [thus called]; (A 'Obeyd, T;) or the mzAdp is thus termed by the vulgar, but this application of the word is allowable as metaphorical: (S:) or it signifies a pair of such water-bags ( mazaAdataAni [see mazaAdapN in art. zyd ]): (T:) [accord. to ISd,] it is applied to the mzAdp , and then to the camel, because of the nearness of the latter to the former: (M:) or its primary application is to the camel: (S, Mgh:) accord. to some, its application to the camel is proper; and to the mzAdp , tropical: accord. to others, the reverse is the case: (MF, TA:) the pl. is rawaAyaA , as above. (Mgh, TA.) ― -b2- One says of a weak person who is in easy circumstances, maA yarud~u Alr~aAwiyapa , meaning He is unable to turn back the rAwyp [or camel bearing a water-bag or pair of water-bags, ] notwithstanding its being heavily burdened by the water that is upon it. (M.) ― -b3- And the Prophet applied the appellation rawaAyaA AlbilaAdi [ The camels bearing water for the irrigation of the countries, or the water-bags borne by camels for the irrigation of the countries, ] to (assumed tropical:) the clouds, by way of comparison. (TA.) ― -b4- rawaAyaA is also applied as an appellation to (assumed tropical:) The chiefs of a people; (IAar, Th, T;) as pl. of raAwiyapN ; the chief who bears the burden of the bloodwits owed by the tribe being likened to the camel thus termed. (T, M. *) A Temeemee, mentioning a party that had attacked his tribe, said, laqiynaAhumo faqatalonaA Alr~awaAyaA wa A^abaHonaA Alz~awaAyaA meaning [ We encountered them, and ] we slew the chiefs, and gave permission to occupy, or to plunder, the houses, or tents. (T.) ― -b5- rawaAyaA also occurs in a trad., in which it is said, $ar~u Alr~awaAyaA rawaAyaA Alka*ibi , and accord. to some, it is, in this instance, pl. of raAwiyapN (JM, TA) in the first of the senses explained above; so that the meaning is, (assumed tropical:) The worst of those who carry tidings are those who carry false tidings; such persons being likened to the beasts so called, in respect of the fatigue that they undergo: (JM:) or it is pl. of ↓ rawiy~apN ; (JM, TA;) and the meaning is, the worst of thoughts are those that are untrue, not right, nor tending to good: or it is pl. of ↓ riwaAyapN ; and the meaning is, the worst of relations, or recitals, are those that are untrue. (JM.) ― -b6- See also raAwK .

sourceDefinition: , aor. yazur~u , (S, Mgh, Msb,) inf. n. zar~N , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) He buttoned a shirt [&c.]; (S, Mgh, Msb, K; *) as also ↓ zr~r , inf. n. tazoriyrN ; (Mgh; [and so in the present day;]) or the latter verb [relates to several objects, or means he buttoned a shirt &c. with many buttons; for it] has an intensive signification. (Msb.) You say, Auzoruro Ealayoka qamiySaka , and zur~ahu , and zur~ihi , and zur~uhu , Button upon thee thy shirt. (S.) ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) He narrowed his eyes [as when one draws together the edges of a vest in buttoning it]. (K, * [in which, in this instance, as in others, only the inf. n. of the verb zar~a is mentioned,] and TA.) ― -b3- (tropical:) He collected, or drew together, vehemently, or forcibly. (A, Msb, K *) ― -b4- zar~ahaA [referring to the pieces of cloth composing a tent] He made in them what are called A^azoraAr [pl. of zir~N , q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b5- And zar~a , aor. as above, (S, A, TA,) and so the inf. n., (S, K,) (tropical:) He drove away. (S, A, K, TA. [In the TA, the inf. n. is expl. by Al$~ak~u as well as AlT~arodu ; but the former is a mistranscription for Al$~al~u , the reading in the S.]) One says, huwa yazur~u AlkataAy^iba biAls~ayofi (tropical:) He drives away the troops with the sword. (S, A.) ― -b6- (tropical:) He bit another. (S, * A, K. *) ― -b7- (assumed tropical:) He pierced, or thrust, another, (K, TA,) with a spear. (TK.) ― -b8- He plucked out hair. (K, * TA.) ― -b9- He shook goods, or household furniture, or the like, to remove dust &c. (O, K: * only the inf. n. is mentioned in the latter.) -A2- zar~a , (K,) aor. yazir~u , (TA,) He increased in intelligence, (K, TA,) and in probations, or experiences. (TA. [See also zarira , below, in this paragraph.]) -A3- Also, aor. yazir~u , inf. n. zariyrN , It (a spear-head) gleamed, or glistened. (A.) And zar~ato Eayonuhu , aor. tazir~u , (S,) inf. n. zariyrN , (S, K,) His eye gleamed, or glistened. (S, K. *) And EayonaAhu tazr~aAni fiY raA^osihi His eyes gleam, or glisten, in his head. sourceDefinition: , and zw~jhu A_ilayohi , [inf. n. tazowiyjN ,] He coupled, or paired, a thing with a thing; united it to it as its fellow, or like. (TA.) So in the Kur [xliv. 54 and lii. 20], zaw~ajonaAhumo biHuwrK EiynK We will couple them, or pair them, [ with females having eyes like those of gazelles: ] (S, Mgh, K, TA:) the meaning is not the tazowiyj commonly known, [i. e. marriage,] for there will be no [such] tzwyj in Paradise. (MF, TA.) And so in the Kur [lxxxi. 7], waA_i*aA Aln~ufuwsu zuw~ijato And when the souls shall be coupled, or paired, or united with their fellows: (TA:) i. e., with their bodies: (Bd, Jel:) or, each with its register: (Bd:) or with its works: (Bd, TA:) or the souls of the believers with the Huwr , and those of the unbelievers with the devils: (Bd:) or when each sect, or party, shall be united with those whom it has followed. (TA.) And so in the phrase, zaw~ajotu A_ibiliY I coupled, or paired, my camels, one with another: (A:) or zaw~ajotu bayona AlA_ibili I coupled, or paired, every one of the camels with another. (TA.) So too in the Kur [xlii. 49], A^awo yuzaw~ijuhumo *ukoraAnFA waA_inaAvFA Or He maketh them couples, or pairs, males and females: or, accord. to AM, maketh them of different sorts [or sexes ], males and females: for ― -b2- tazowiyjN signifies [also] The making to be of different sorts or species [&c.]. (TA.) ― -b3- zaw~ajotuhu A@moraA^apF , (T, S, A, * Mgh, Msb, K,) thus the Arabs say accord. to Yoo (S, Mgh) and ISK, (Mgh,) making the verb doubly trans. by itself, [without a particle,] meaning I married him, or gave him in marriage, to a woman; (Msb, TA;) as also biA@moraA^apK ; (A, K;) Akh says that this is allowable [app. as being of the dial. of Azd-Shanooäh (see 5)]: (Msb, TA:) [when the verb is trans. by means of bi , it generally has the meaning expl. in the first sentence of this art.:] zaw~ajotu minohu A@moraA^apF is not of the language of the Arabs: (T, Mgh, TA:) [but see a similar phrase in a verse cited in art. definition: primarily signifies A sort of thing of any kind [ that is one of a pair or couple ]: and zawojaAni signifies a pair, or couple, i.
sourceDefinition: primarily signifies A sort of thing of any kind [ that is one of a pair or couple ]: and zawojaAni signifies a pair, or couple, i. e. any two things paired or coupled together, whether they be likes or contraries: zawojN signifying either one of such two things: (Az, TA:) or, accord. to 'Alee Ibn- 'Eesà, a sort of thing [absolutely]: (Mgh:) or a sort of thing having its like, (El-Ghooree, Mgh, Msb,) as in the case of species; (Msb;) or having its contrary, (El-Ghooree, Mgh, Msb,) as the moist and the dry, and the male and the female, and the night and the day, and the bitter and the sweet; (Msb;) though sometimes applied to any sort of thing; and to a single thing: (El-Ghooree, Mgh:) or it is applied to a single thing only when having with it a thing of the same kind; (Mgh, Msb;) zawojaAni signifying a pair, or couple, of such things: (Mgh:) the pl. is A^azowaAji : (TA:) you say zawojaAni mino HamaAmK and zawojaA HamaAmK [ A pair of pigeons ]: (A:) and Ai$otarayotu zawojaY HamaAmK [ I bought a pair of pigeons ], meaning a male and a female: (S:) and zawojaA niEaAlK [ A pair of sandals ]: (S, A:) and in like manner zawojayoni is used in the Kur xi. 42 and xxiii. 28; (S;) meaning a male and a female: (Bd, Jel:) or, accord. to the M, zawojN signifies one of a pair or couple: and also a pair or couple together: (TA:) and in like manner says AO, (Mgh, Msb,) and IKt, and IF: (Msb:) and ISh says that it signifies two; (Mgh;) and so says IDrd: (Msb:) so that you say, humaA zawojN as well as humaA zawojaAni [meaning They two are a pair, or couple ]; (S, K, TA;) like as you say, humaA sawaA='N and humaA siy~aAni : (S, TA:) and EinodiY zawoju niEaAlK , meaning [ I have ] two [ sandals ]; and zawojaAni , meaning four: (Msb:) or zawoju HamaAmK as meaning a male and a female [of pigeons] is a phrase which should not be used; one to which the vulgar are addicted: (TA:) IAmb says, the vulgar are wrong in thinking that zawojN signifies two; for the Arabs used not to employ such a phrase as zawoju HamaAmK , but used to say zawojaAni mina AlHamaAmi , (Mgh, Msb, TA,) meaning a male and a female; (TA;) and zawojaAni mina AlxifaAfi , (Mgh, Msb, TA,) meaning the right and the left [of boots]: (TA:) nor did they apply the term zawojN to one of birds, like as they applied the dual, zawojaAni , to two; but they applied the term farodN to the male, and farodapN to the female: (Mgh, Msb:) Es-Sijistánee, also, says that the term zawojN should not be applied to two, neither of birds nor of other things, for this is a usage of the ignorant; but to every two, zawojaAni : (Msb:) Az says that the grammarians disapprove the saying of ISh that zawojN signifies two of any things, (Mgh, * TA,) and that zawojaAni mino xifaAfK signifies [ Two pairs of boots, or] four [ boots ]; for zawojN with them signifies one [ of a pair or couple ]: a man and his wife [together] are termed zawojaAni : and vamaAniyapa A^azowaAjK in the Kur [vi. 144 and xxxix. 8] means Eight ones [ of pairs or couples ]: the primary meaning of zawojN being that first mentioned in this paragraph; (TA:) in the Kur xxii. 5 and 1. 7 [it seems to be implied that it means pair or couple; but more probably in these instances] it means sort, or species: (Bd, Jel:) it is also expl. by the word lawonN [used in this last sense]: (T, TA;) in the Kur xxxviii. 58, its pl. A^azowaAjN means A^alowaAnN and A^anowaAEN [i. e. sorts, or species ] of punishment: F explains the sing. as meaning lawonN mina Ald~iybaAji wanaHowihi [ a sort, or species, of silk brocade and the like ]; but his restricting the signification by the words mn AldybAj wnHwh is not right, as is shown by a citation, in the T, of a verse of El-Aashà, in which he uses the phrase kul~u zawojK mina Ald~iybaAji [ every sort, or species, of silk brocade ], as an ex. of zwj in the sense of lwn . (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] A woman's husband: and a man's wife: in which latter sense ↓ zawojapN is also used; (S, M, A, Mgh, * Msb, K; *) as in a verse of El-Farezdak cited in art bwl , conj. 10; (S, Mgh;) but it is disallowed by As; (TA;) and the former word is the one of high authority, (Mgh, Msb,) and is that which occurs in the Kur, in ii. 33 and vii. 18, (S, Mgh, Msb, TA,) and in iv. 24, (Mgh, TA,) and in xxxiii. 37: (Mgh:) AHát says that the people of Nejd call a wife ↓ zawojapN , and that the people of the Haram use this word: but ISk says that the people of El-Hijáz call a wife zawojN ; and the rest of the Arabs, ↓ zawojapN : the lawyers use this latter word only, as applied to a wife, for the sake of perspicuity, fearing to confound the male with the female: (Msb:) the pl. of zawojN is A^azowaAjN (Msb, K *) and ziwajapN ; (K;) and the pl. of ↓ zawojapN is zawojaAtN (A, Mgh, Msb) and A^azowaAjN also; (A, Msb;) and A^azaAwiyju occurs [as a pl. pl., i. e. pl. of A^azowaAju ,] in a verse cited by ISk. (TA in art. nA^j .) ― -b3- [Hence also,] A consociate, an associate, or a comrade: (A:) its pl. in this sense is A^azowaAjN , (S, A, K,) occurring in the Kur xxxvii. 22. (S, A.) ― -b4- And A fellow, or like: pl. A^azowaAjN : in this sense, each one of a pair of boots is the zwj of the other; and the husband is the zwj of the wife; and the wife, the zwj of the husband. (TA.) You say, EinodiY mino h`*aA A^azowaAjN I have, of this, fellows, or likes. (TA.) ― -b5- As used by arithmeticians, (Mgh, Msb,) contr. of farodN ; (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) i. e. it signifies An even number; a number that may be divided into two equal numbers; (Msb;) as, for instance, four, and eight, as opposed to three, and seven: (Mgh:) pl. A^azowaAjN . (S, Mgh.) One says zawojN A^awo farodN [ Even or odd? ], like as one says xasFA A^awo zakFA [or rather zakFA A^awo xasFA ] and $afoEN A^awo witorN . (S, Mgh.) ― -b6- Also A [ kind of cloth such as is termed ] namaT [q. v.]: or silk brocade; syn. diybaAjN : (TA:) or a namaT that is thrown over the [ kind of vehicle called ] hawodaj . (S, K, TA.)

for the Arabs used not to employ such a phrase as zawoju HamaAmK , but used to say zawojaAni mina AlHamaAmi , (Mgh, Msb, TA,) meaning a male and a female; (TA;) and zawojaAni mina AlxifaAfi , (Mgh, Msb, TA,) meaning the right and the left [of boots]: (TA:) nor did they apply the term zawojN to one of birds, like as they applied the dual, zawojaAni , to two; but they applied the term farodN to the male, and farodapN to the female: (Mgh, Msb:) Es-Sijistánee, also, says that the term zawojN should not be applied to two, neither of birds nor of other things, for this is a usage of the ignorant; but to every two, zawojaAni : (Msb:) Az says that the grammarians disapprove the saying of ISh that zawojN signifies two of any things, (Mgh, * TA,) and that zawojaAni mino xifaAfK signifies [ Two pairs of boots, or] four [ boots ]; for zawojN with them signifies one [ of a pair or couple ]: a man and his wife [together] are termed zawojaAni : and vamaAniyapa A^azowaAjK in the Kur [vi. 144 and xxxix. 8] means Eight ones [ of pairs or couples ]: the primary meaning of zawojN being that first mentioned in this paragraph; (TA:) in the Kur xxii. 5 and 1. 7 [it seems to be implied that it means pair or couple; but more probably in these instances] it means sort, or species: (Bd, Jel:) it is also expl. by the word lawonN [used in this last sense]: (T, TA;) in the Kur xxxviii. 58, its pl. A^azowaAjN means A^alowaAnN and A^anowaAEN [i. e. sorts, or species ] of punishment: F explains the sing. as meaning lawonN mina Ald~iybaAji wanaHowihi [ a sort, or species, of silk brocade and the like ]; but his restricting the signification by the words mn AldybAj wnHwh is not right, as is shown by a citation, in the T, of a verse of El-Aashà, in which he uses the phrase kul~u zawojK mina Ald~iybaAji [ every sort, or species, of silk brocade ], as an ex. of zwj in the sense of lwn . (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] A woman's husband: and a man's wife: in which latter sense ↓ zawojapN is also used; (S, M, A, Mgh, * Msb, K; *) as in a verse of El-Farezdak cited in art bwl , conj. 10; (S, Mgh;) but it is disallowed by As; (TA;) and the former word is the one of high authority, (Mgh, Msb,) and is that which occurs in the Kur, in ii. 33 and vii. 18, (S, Mgh, Msb, TA,) and in iv. 24, (Mgh, TA,) and in xxxiii. 37: (Mgh:) AHát says that the people of Nejd call a wife ↓ zawojapN , and that the people of the Haram use this word: but ISk says that the people of El-Hijáz call a wife zawojN ; and the rest of the Arabs, ↓ zawojapN : the lawyers use this latter word only, as applied to a wife, for the sake of perspicuity, fearing to confound the male with the female: (Msb:) the pl. of zawojN is A^azowaAjN (Msb, K *) and ziwajapN ; (K;) and the pl. of ↓ zawojapN is zawojaAtN (A, Mgh, Msb) and A^azowaAjN also; (A, Msb;) and A^azaAwiyju occurs [as a pl. pl., i. e. pl. of A^azowaAju ,] in a verse cited by ISk. (TA in art. nA^j .) ― -b3- [Hence also,] A consociate, an associate, or a comrade: (A:) its pl. in this sense is A^azowaAjN , (S, A, K,) occurring in the Kur xxxvii. 22. (S, A.) ― -b4- And A fellow, or like: pl. A^azowaAjN : in this sense, each one of a pair of boots is the zwj of the other; and the husband is the zwj of the wife; and the wife, the zwj of the husband. (TA.) You say, EinodiY mino h`*aA A^azowaAjN I have, of this, fellows, or likes. (TA.) ― -b5- As used by arithmeticians, (Mgh, Msb,) contr. of farodN ; (S, Mgh, Msb, K;) i. e. it signifies An even number; a number that may be divided into two equal numbers; (Msb;) as, for instance, four, and eight, as opposed to three, and seven: (Mgh:) pl. A^azowaAjN . (S, Mgh.) One says zawojN A^awo farodN [ Even or odd? ], like as one says xasFA A^awo zakFA [or rather zakFA A^awo xasFA ] and $afoEN A^awo witorN . (S, Mgh.) ― -b6- Also A [ kind of cloth such as is termed ] namaT [q. v.]: or silk brocade; syn. diybaAjN : (TA:) or a namaT that is thrown over the [ kind of vehicle called ] hawodaj . (S, K, TA.)

definition: Rest: (S, K:) and quiet, stillness, or freedom from motion.
sourceDefinition: Rest: (S, K:) and quiet, stillness, or freedom from motion. (TA.) [See 1, of which it is an inf. n.] See also subaAtN . ― -b2- Als~abotu , (M, K,) or yawomu Als~aboti , (S, Msb,) [ The sabbath, or Saturday; ] one of the days of the week; (M, K;) the seventh of those days: (M:) so called because the creation commenced on the first day of the week and continued to [the end of] Friday, and on the sbt there was no creation, the work having ceased thereon: or, as some say, because the Jews ceased thereon from work, and the management of affairs: (M, TA:) or because the days [of the week] end thereon: (S, TA:) Az says that he errs who asserts it to have been so called because God commanded the Children of Israel to rest thereon, and that God created the heavens and the earth in six days, whereof the last was Friday, then rested, and the work ceased, and therefore He named the seventh day ywm Alsbt : this, he says, is an error, because [he affirms that] sabata as meaning “ he rested ” is not known in the language of the Arabs, but signifies qaTaEa ; and rest cannot be attributed to God, because He knows not fatigue, and rest is only after fatigue and work: (TA:) the pl. [of pauc.] is A^asobutN and [of mult.] subuwtN : (S, M, Msb, K:) it has no dim. (Sb, S in art. Ams .) ― -b3- sabotN also means A week; from the sabot to the sabot [i. e. from the sabbath to the sabbath ]: so in the saying, in a trad., famaA raA^ayonaA Al$~amosa sabotFA [ And we saw not the sun for a week ]: as when one says “ twenty autumns ” meaning “ twenty years: ” or it means in this instance a space of time, whether short or long. (TA.) ― -b4- I. q. burohapN [i. e. A space, or period, or a long space or period, ] (M, K, TA) mina Ald~ahori [ of time ]: (TA:) so in the saying, A^aqamotu sabotFA [ I remained, staid, dwelt, or abode, a space, or a long space, of time ]; as also ↓ sabotapF and ↓ sanobatFA and ↓ sanobatatFA . (M, K.) ― -b5- And i. q. dahorN [meaning Time; or a long time; or a space, or period, of time, whether long or short; &c.]; as also ↓ subaAtN . (S, M, K.) And [hence] ↓ AibonaA subaAtK means (assumed tropical:) The night and the day: (S, M, K:) Ibn Ahmar says, wakun~aA wahumo kaA@bonaYo subaAtK tafar~aqaA siwFY vum~a kaAnaA munojidFA watahaAmiyaA [ And we were, with them, like the night and the day that parted asunder alike, then became one going towards Nejd and one going towards Tihámeh ]: (S, K:) such, they say, is the meaning: (S:) or, as IB says, on the authority of Aboo-Jaafar Mohammad Ibn-Habeeb, AbnA sbAt were two men, one of whom saw the other in a dream, and then one of them awoke in Nejd, and the other in Tihámeh: or they were two brothers, one of whom went to the east to see where the sun rose, and the other to the west to see where it set. (L, TA.) -A2- Also A certain pace (S, M, K) of camels: (S, K:) or a quick pace: (TA:) or i. q. EanaqN [q. v.]: (AA, S:) or a pace exceeding that termed AlEanaqu . (M.) -A3- A swift, or an excellent, horse; (K, TA;) that runs much. (TA.) ― -b2- A boy, or young man, of bad disposition, or illnatured, and bold, or daring. (K) ― -b3- A man cunning, i. e. possessing intelligence, or sagacity, or intelligence mixed with craft and forecast; and excellent in judgment; or very cunning &c.; (K, TA;) silent, or lowering his eyes, looking towards the ground; (TA;) and ↓ subaAtN signifies the same. (K, TA.) ― -b4- A man who sleeps much; (K;) i. e. kaviyru Als~ubaAti . (TA.) See also masobuwtN . -A4- See also what next follows.

(M, K.) ― -b5- And i. q. dahorN [meaning Time; or a long time; or a space, or period, of time, whether long or short; &c.]; as also ↓ subaAtN . (S, M, K.) And [hence] ↓ AibonaA subaAtK means (assumed tropical:) The night and the day: (S, M, K:) Ibn Ahmar says, wakun~aA wahumo kaA@bonaYo subaAtK tafar~aqaA siwFY vum~a kaAnaA munojidFA watahaAmiyaA [ And we were, with them, like the night and the day that parted asunder alike, then became one going towards Nejd and one going towards Tihámeh ]: (S, K:) such, they say, is the meaning: (S:) or, as IB says, on the authority of Aboo-Jaafar Mohammad Ibn-Habeeb, AbnA sbAt were two men, one of whom saw the other in a dream, and then one of them awoke in Nejd, and the other in Tihámeh: or they were two brothers, one of whom went to the east to see where the sun rose, and the other to the west to see where it set. definition: The hides, or skins, of oxen;
sourceDefinition: The hides, or skins, of oxen; (M, K;) whether tanned or not tanned: so some say: (M:) or (so accord. to the M, in the K and TA “ and, ” but the w is omitted in the CK,) any tanned hide; (As, AA, M, K;) said to be so called [because the tanning removes the hair,] from Als~abotu , “ the act of shaving: ” (AA, TA:) or such. as is tanned with qaraZ [q. v.]: (M, K:) or only ox-hides tanned: so says AHn on the authority of As and AZ: (TA:) or ox-hides tanned with qaraZ , (S, Mgh,) whereof are made [ the sandals called ] ↓ niEaAlN siboty~apN : (S) these are hence thus called: (Mgh:) they are sandals having no hair upon them: (M, Msb:) or sandals tanned with qraZ : (AA, TA:) accord. to Az, they are thus called because their hair has been shaven off ( subita , i. e. Huliqa ,) and removed by a wellknown process in tanning, (Mgh, * TA,) so that they are soft; and they are of the sandals of people that lead a life of ease and softness: (Mgh:) IAar says that they are thus called because of their having become soft by the tanning: accord. to this, they should be called ↓ sabotiy~ap ; and so accord. to a saying of EdDáwoodee, that they are called in relation to suwqu Als~aboti [“ the Market of the Sabbath ”]: it is also said that they are called in relation to the ↓ subot , with damm, which is a plant used for tanning therewith; so that they should be called ↓ subotiy~ap , unless the appellation be an instance of a rel. n. deviating from its source of derivation [or unless this plant be also termed sibotN , as it is accord. to a copy of the M]: (TA:) see subotN . It is related of the Prophet, that he saw a man walking among the graves wearing his sandals, and said, yaA SaAHiba Als~ibotayni AixolaEo sibotayoka [meaning (tropical:) O wearer of the pair of sandals of sibot , pull off thy pair of sandals of sibot ]: (S, * TA:) and accord. to the A, they are thus termed tropically: it is like the saying “ Such a one wears wool, and cotton, and silk; ” meaning “ garments made thereof; ” as is said in the Nh: but, as some relate it, what he said was, ↓ yaA SaAHiba Als~ibotiy~ayoni , the last of these words being a rel. n.; and thus it is found in the handwriting of Az, in his book. (TA.)

definition: primarily signifies Rest [like sabotN ]: (S, Msb:) and hence, sleep: (S, K:) or heavy sleep: (Msb:) or sleep that is hardly perceptible ( xafiY~ , M, K, [in some copies of the K, as mentioned by Freytag, xafiyf , i.
sourceDefinition: primarily signifies Rest [like sabotN ]: (S, Msb:) and hence, sleep: (S, K:) or heavy sleep: (Msb:) or sleep that is hardly perceptible ( xafiY~ , M, K, [in some copies of the K, as mentioned by Freytag, xafiyf , i. e. light, ]), like a swoon: (M:) or the commencement of sleep in the head [ and its continuance ] until it reaches the heart: (Th, M, K:) or the sleep of one who is sick; i. e. light sleep: (TA:) and ↓ sabotN signifies the same as subaAtN . (T, TA.) Hence, in the Kur [lxxviii. 9, and in like manner the word is used in xxv. 49], wajaEalonaA nawomakumo subaAtFA ; (S;) i. e. qaToEFA ; as though a man, when he slept, were cut off from [the rest of] mankind: (IAar, TA:) or sbAt is when one is cut off, or ceases, from motion, while the soul still remains in the body; i. e., the text means, And we have made your sleep to be rest unto you: (Zj, TA:) or we have made your sleep to be a cutting off from sensation and motion, for rest to the animal forces, and for causing their weariness to cease: or, to be death: (Bd:) or, to be rest unto your bodies by the interruption of labour, or work. (Jel.) -A2- See also sabotN , latter half, in three places.

sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. saHobN , (Msb, TA,) He dragged it, or drew it along, (S, A, Msb, K,) namely, his *ayol [or skirt], (S,) or a thing, such as a garment &c., (TA,) upon the ground. definition: [termed in the S and K pl.
sourceDefinition: [termed in the S and K pl. of saHaAbapN , as also suHubN and saHaAy^ibu ,] is, accord. to As, [correctly,] a coll. gen. n., used alike as masc. and fem. and sing. and pl.; (MF, TA;) and saHaAbapN is its n. un.; (MF, Msb, * TA;) and suHubN is pl. of saHaAbN or of saHaAbapN ; (L, Msb, * MF, TA;) it may be pl. of either of these; (L, MF, TA;) and saHaAy^ibu is pl. of saHaAbapN absolutely, and of saHaAbN when used as fem.: (MF, TA:) it signifies Clouds [or a collection of clouds ]; (S, K, KL, TA, &c.;) and [ clouds ] from which the rain comes: (TA:) so called because drawn along in the air; (Msb, TA;) or because they draw along one another; or because the winds draw them along; (TA;) or because they draw along their fringes. (TA in art. Hbw .) One says, maTaratohumu Als~aHaAbapu [ The cloud rained upon them ]. (A.) ― -b2- [Hence,] A^aqamotu Einodahu saHaAbapa nahaAriY (tropical:) I remained at his abode the whole of my day: originally said in relation to a cloudy day; and then proverbially used in relation to any day. (A, TA.) And maA zilotu A^afoEaluhu saHaAbapa yawomiY (tropical:) I ceased not to do it the whole of my day. (K, * TA.) ― -b3- maA='u Als~aHaAbi [properly The water of the clouds ] is a term for (assumed tropical:) wine. (TA in art. jfn .) ― -b4- Als~aHaAbu is a name of (assumed tropical:) The Prophet's turban; (Mgh, TA:) it was thus called as being likened to the sHAb of the rain because of its being drawn along in the air. (TA.) ― -b5- Also the name of A sword of Dirar Ibn-El-Khattáb. (K.)

definition: A certain thin food, made of flour;
sourceDefinition: A certain thin food, made of flour; (K;) a kind of food made of flour, thinner than [ the kind of gruel called ] EaSiydap and thicker than [ the soup called ] HasaA=' ; like nafiytap , it is eaten only in a time of straitness, and dearth, and leanness of the cattle; and Kureysh were taunted on account of their eating it; (S, L;) for they ate it much; and were called saxiynap : accord. to Az, it is also called ↓ saxuwnapN : accord. to AHeyth, on the authority of an Arab of the desert, it is flour thrown upon water or upon milk, and cooked, and then eaten [ with dates (see xaziyrN )], or supped; and this is what is called HasaA=' : [it is said in the Mgh to be the same as HasaA=' :] accord. to others, hot food: or food made of flour and clarified butter: or, of flour and dates, thicker than HasaA=' and thinner than EaSiydap . (L.)

definition: A certain plant, (S, Msb, K,) of the kind called buquwl , (Mgh,) well known;
sourceDefinition: A certain plant, (S, Msb, K,) of the kind called buquwl , (Mgh,) well known; (Msb, K;) and applied also to the grain, or seed, thereof: (Mgh:) [ a species of origanum, or majoram: so in the present day; and so says Golius, as on the authority of Ibn-Beytár, “ origani species, sc. consonante voce, satureia, Hisp. axedrea: ” accord. to Forskål, (Flora Aeg. (Ham p. 462.) [In the present day, it is also written with z .]

definition: Palm-branches, (Az, * S, Msb, K,) as long as they have the leaves upon them: when these are removed from them, called jariydN : (Msb:) or the part [or parts ] of palm-branches upon which leaves have...
sourceDefinition: Palm-branches, (Az, * S, Msb, K,) as long as they have the leaves upon them: when these are removed from them, called jariydN : (Msb:) or the part [or parts ] of palm-branches upon which leaves have grown: (S voce EasiybN :) or the leaves of palm-branches, (Mgh, K, TA,) of which are woven [ baskets of the kind called ] zubul (Mgh) or zubolaAn (TA) [pls. of zabiylN ], and [ the similar receptacles called ] jilaAl [pl. of jul~apN ], (TA,) and fans [which are made in the form of small flags], (Mgh, TA,) and the like: (TA:) and sometimes palm-branches themselves are thus called: (Mgh:) accord. to Lth, (Mgh, TA,) such as have become dry [ of palm-branches ] are mostly thus called; the fresh [palm-branch] being called $aTobapN : (Mgh, K, TA:) sing., (S,) or [rather] n. un., (Mgh, Msb,) with p : (S, Mgh, Msb:) which also signifies a palm-tree itself; and its pl. is saEafaAtN . (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence, as being likened to palm-leaves,] The forelock of a horse: so in the saying of Imrael-Keys, waA^arokabu fiY Alr~awoEi xayofaAnapF kasaA wajohahaA saEafN munota$iro [ And I ride, in war, or battle, a brisk, or an agile, leaving mare, whose face a spreading forelock has clad ]: which shows that saEafN [properly] signifies the leaves [of a palm-branch]. (Az, TA.) [Jac. Schultens, as mentioned by Freytag, explains it as meaning A whiteness upon the forehead of a horse: but this explanation is perhaps conjectural, from the verse cited above.] -A2- The paraphernalia ( jahaAz ) of a bride: pl. suEuwfN . (IAar, K.) ― -b2- Anything good, goodly, or excel-lent, and consummate, such as a slave, or any precious thing, or a house that one possesses. (IAar, K.) -A3- A species of fly: mentioned by a poet as smiting a lion. (IB, TA.) -A4- See also 1.
