Ear~N ; (S;) The camels were, or became, mangy, or scabby, or affected with the mange or scab; (S, O, K; *) as also ↓ taEaroEarat ; (O, K; *) and Eur~at : (K: *) or this last verb signifies they (the camels) had purulent pustules, like the [ cutaneous eruption called ] quwabaA=' [q. v.], coming forth dispersedly in their lips (S, O) and their legs, (S,) and discharging a fluid resembling yellow water; in consequence of which the healthy camels are cauterized, in order that the diseased may not communicate to them the malady: (S, O:) or the same verb signifies, (IKtt, K, * TA,) and so the first, and ↓ the second, (K, *) said of young, or unweaned, camels, they had purulent pustules in their necks: (IKtt, K, * TA:) and all the three verbs, said of camels, signify they had a disease which caused their fur to fall off, (K, TA,) so that the skin appeared and shone. (TA.) ― -b2- Ear~a Albadana , said of the mange, or scab, signifies AiEotaraDahu [app. meaning It attacked the body ]. (B, TA.) -A2- Ear~a , aor. , inf. n. Eur~apN , said of a bird, It muted, or dunged. (S, O.) ― -b2- Ear~a , (S, Mgh, TA,) aor. , (S, TA,) inf. n. Ear~N ; (O;) and ↓ Er~r , inf. n. taEoriyrN ; (S, O;) He manured land: he dunged it: (Mgh, TA:) he manured it with human ordure. (TA.) ― -b3- And [hence] Ear~ahu , (Mgh, Msb,) aor. , (Msb,) He defiled, or besmeared, him, or it, (Mgh, Msb,) with Eur~ap , i. e. dung such as is called siroqiyn , (Mgh,) or with a thing. (Msb.) ― -b4- And Ear~ahu bi$ar~K (assumed tropical:) He sullied, or bespattered, him with evil, by charging him therewith; aspersed him; or charged, or upbraided, him with evil: (S, O, K, TA:) from Ear~a signifying “ he dunged ” land; or, accord. to A'Obeyd, it may be from Ear~N signifying “ mange, ” or “ scab: ” and (assumed tropical:) he wronged him, or treated him unjustly or injuriously; and reviled him; and took his property. (TA.) ― -b5- And [in like manner] huwa yaEur~u qawomahu (assumed tropical:) He brings against his people, or party, an abominable, or evil, charge, ( yudoxilu Ealayohimo makoruwhFA ,) aspersing them with it. (S, O.) (assumed tropical:) He disgraces, or dishonours, his people, or party. (TA.) ― -b6- And Ear~ahu , aor. , (assumed tropical:) He applied to him a surname, or nickname, that disgraced him, or dishonoured him: and Eur~a (assumed tropical:) He received, or became called by, such a surname or nickname. (TA.) ― -b7- And Ear~ahu , (S, O, K,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. Ear~N , (K,) (assumed tropical:) He did to him an abominable, or evil, thing: (K:) he displeased him; grieved, or vexed, him; did to him what he disliked, or hated; did evil to him. (S, O, K.) ― -b8- And Ear~ahu also signifies It (a thing that he disliked, or hated, and that distressed him,) befell him; syn. EaraAhu , meaning dahaAhu . (Ksh in xlviii. 25. [In Bd, AgrAh ; app. a mistranscription for EaraAhu .]) ― -b9- Also, (O, Msb, K,) aor. , (O, TA,) inf. n. Ear~N ; (O, K;) and ↓ AEtr~hu , (Msb, K,) and AEtr~ bihi ; (K;) and EaraAhu and AEtrAhu likewise; (Msb, TA; [see art. Erw ;]) He addressed, or applied, himself to obtain favour, or bounty, of him, without asking; (Msb, K;) he came to him, and sought his favour, or bounty; or seeking his favour, or bounty: (O, TA:) or he went round about him, seeking to obtain what he had, whether asking him or not asking him. (TA, as implied in an explanation of muEotar~N .) ― -b10- And Ear~ahu He alighted at his abode as a visiter and guest. (IKtt, TA.) -A3- See also 3.

sourceDefinition: He awoke from his sleep, (S, A, O,) in the night, with a sound, or cry, (S, O,) or speaking, or talking: (A:) he was sleepless, and turned over upon the bed, by night, speaking, or talking, (A, K,) and with a sound, or cry, and, as some say, stretching. definition: The mange, or scab;
sourceDefinition: The mange, or scab; (S, A, Mgh, O, K;) as also ↓ Eur~N (K) and ↓ Eur~apN (IF, Msb, K) and ↓ Ear~apN : (IF, Msb, and so in a copy of the A:) see also EararN : or Ear~N has this signification; but ↓ Eur~N , with damm, signifies purulent pustules in the necks of young, or unweaned, camels: and a certain disease, in consequence of which the fur of the camel falls off, (K, TA,) so that the skin appears and shines; as some say: (TA:) or purulent pustules, like the [ cutaneous eruption called ] quwabaA=' [q. v.], which comes forth in camels, dispersedly, in their lips (S, O) and their legs, (S,) discharging a fluid which resembles yellow water; in consequence of which the healthy camels are cauterized, in order that the diseased may not communicate to them the malady. (S, O.) En-Nábighah says, (addressing En-Noamán Ibn-El-Mundhir, O,) faHam~alotaniY *anoba A@moriy^K watarakotahu yukowaY gayoruhu wahowa raAtiEu ↓ ka*iY AlEur~i [ And thou hast charged me with the crime, or offence, of a man other than myself, and left him like that which has the disease called Eur~ , another than which is cauterized while he is pasturing at pleasure ]: he who says AlEar~ , in relating this verse, errs; for cauterization is not practised as a preservative from the mange, or scab. (IDrd, S, O.) ― -b2- [Hence, app.,] (assumed tropical:) A vice, or fault, or the like. (Har p. 366.) [See also Eur~ap .] ― -b3- And (assumed tropical:) Evil, or mischief. (Har ibid.) One says, laqiytu minohu $ar~FA waEar~FA (assumed tropical:) [ I experienced from him, or it, evil and mischief: the two nouns being synonymous: and the latter of them also an inf. n. of Ear~ahu , q. v.]. (TA: but written without any syll. signs.) [See also an instance of the use of the phrase $ar~N waEar~N voce dafiynN .] ― -b4- See also EaAr~N .

definition: The tree called sarow [which is the common, or evergreen, cypress;
sourceDefinition: The tree called sarow [which is the common, or evergreen, cypress; but the former name is generally applied in the present day to the juniper-tree ]; (S, O, K;) a Pers. word: (K:) it is a kind of great tree, of the trees of the mountains: (O:) some say that it is the [ tree called ] saAsam , and also [ said to be ] called $iyzaY : others, that it is a great kind of mountain-tree, evergreen, called by the Persians sarow : (TA:) AHn says that he had been informed by an Arab of the desert, of the people of the Saráh ( Als~araAp ), who are possessors of the EaroEar , that it is the A^abohal [q. v., a name now applied to the juniper-tree, like EaroEar ; and particularly to the species thereof called the savin ]; and he adds that he knew it in his own country, and afterwards saw it in the province of Kazween, cut for firewood from the mountains thereof, in the borders of Ed-Deylem; whence he knew that his informant was well acquainted with it, for those mountains are places of growth of the Abhl : (O:) he says that it has a fruit like the nabiq [or fruit of the lote-tree called sidor ], first green, then becoming white, then becoming black until it is like Humam [or charcoal, &c. ], and sweet, when it is eaten: (TA:) n. un. with p . (O, TA.)

definition: A place of Ear~ , i.
sourceDefinition: A place of Ear~ , i. e. mange, or scab: this is the primary signification. (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, AlmaEar~apu The region of the sky that is beyond the Milky Way ( Almajar~ap ) in the direction of the North Pole; so called because of the multitude of the stars therein; (O, * TA;) like as the sky is called AljarobaA='u because of its numerous stars; these being compared to scabs on the body of a man: (TA:) and to this and the majar~ap a man alluded, when, being asked respecting the place where he alighted and abode, he informed the inquirer that he alighted and abode between two tribes, (O, TA,) great and numerous; (O;) saying, nazalotu bayona AlmaEar~api waAlmajar~api [ I have alighted between the maEar~ap and the majar~ap ]: (O, TA:) or, as some say, (O,) AlmaEar~apu is the name of a certain star, or asterism, [ which is ] below the majar~ap [or Milky Way, app. meaning when the latter, as viewed from Arabia, is seen stretching across the sky above the North Pole ]. (O, K.) ― -b3- [Hence likewise, app.,] maEar~apN signifies also (assumed tropical:) A cause of reviling, or of being reviled; syn. masab~apN : (TA:) a crime, or sin; syn. A_ivomN ; (S, O, Msb, K;) and jinaAyapN ; (TS, L, TA; in the copies of the K xiyaAnap ; [and thus in the O;] but this is a mistake; TA;) and juromN ; (TA;) as also ↓ Eur~apN : (K:) or a crime, or sin, [ that is noxious ] like the mange, or scab: (L, TA:) a foul, or an abominable, thing: (O, TA:) a cause of grief or vexation: (Mgh, Msb:) annoyance, or hurt; or a thing by which one is annoyed or hurt; syn. A^a*FY ; (Sh, Mgh, K;) or A^a*iy~apN : (O:) displeasing, grieving, or vexing, conduct: (Mgh, Msb:) and i. q. $id~apN [app. as meaning violence, or the like ]. (O: there mentioned between the significations of A_ivomN and A^a*iy~apN .) Also (assumed tropical:) The slaying unexpectedly, (S,) or the fighting, (O, K,) of an army, without the permission of the commander: (S, O, K: [omitted in one of my copies of the S:]) or the alighting of an army among a people, and eating of the produce of their fields without knowledge (Sh, O, TA) of the commander: (O:) or an army's oppressing, or assaulting, those by whom they pass, whether Muslims, or unbelievers with whom terms of peace have been made, and afflicting them in respect of their women under covert and their possessions by conduct not permitted to them. (TA.) ― -b4- And (assumed tropical:) A debt, fine, or mulct, which one is obliged to pay: and a fine for homicide: (K, TA:) thus expl. by Mohammad Ibn-Is-hák Ibn-Yesár: (TA:) or a thing that one dislikes, or hates, relating to fines for homicide; of the measure mafoEalapN from Ear~N signifying “ mange, ” or “ scab. ” (Th, TA.) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) The changing of the face in colour by reason of anger: (O, K, TA:) Az says that it is thus mentioned by Abu-l-'Abbás with teshdeed to the r : but if it be from tamaE~ara wajohuhu , not from AlEar~u , it is without teshdeed. (O, TA.)

Asw :) [and hence, he consoled him; often used in this sense:] or he said to him, A^aHosana A@ll~`hu EazaA='aka , meaning May God grant thee comely patience. (Msb.) definition: He took patience;
sourceDefinition: He took patience; or constrained himself to be patient, or enduring; syn. taSab~ara , (S, Msb, TA,) and tA^as~aY [q. v.]; (TA;) the sign of doing which is the saying, A_in~aA lil~`hi waA_in~aA A_ilayohi raAjiEuwna [Verily to God we belong, and verily unto Him we return]. (Msb.) It is said in a trad., [as some relate it,] mano lamo yataEaz~a biEazaA='i A@ll~`hi falayosa min~aA , expl. by some as meaning Such as does not constrain himself to be patient [ with the patience of God, he is not of us ]. (TA. [See another reading voce taEaz~aza .]) And you say, taEaz~ayotu Eanohu , meaning I constrained myself to endure with patience the loss, or want, of him, or it: [and hence, I consoled myself for the loss, or want, of him, or it: held by some to be] originally taEaz~azotu , meaning I exerted my strength or energy [ to divert myself from him, or it ]; like taZan~ayotu for taZan~anotu . (TA in art. Ez .) You say also tEz~Y bihi , meaning taA^as~uY bh [i. e. He took patience, or constrained himself to be patient, by reflecting upon him, or it; or he took example by him, or became consoled by his example, meaning the example of a person who had suffered in like manner and had been patient]. (S in art. Asw .)

definition: Patience, or endurance;
sourceDefinition: Patience, or endurance; (S, K;) and EizowapN signifies the same, as in the saying huwa Hasanu AlEizowapi [ He is comely in respect of patience or endurance ]: (Ham p. 369:) or patient endurance of the loss of anything: (TA:) or comely patience or endurance; (K, TA;) as also taEozuwapN accord. to the copies of the K, but correctly ↓ taEoziyapN [inf. n. of 2, as though for taEoziyapu Aln~afosi i. e. self-enjoinment, or self-exhortation, to be patient or enduring, as is indicated by what follows]: an Arab of the desert, whose brother had slain a son of his, is cited by the author of the Hamáseh as saying, [on his brother's being brought to him that he might retaliate upon him, (see Ham p. 100,)] A^aquwlu liln~afosi tA^osaA='FA wataEoziyapF A_iHodaY yadaY~a A^aSaAbatoniY walamo turidi [ I say to the soul, i. e. to myself, enjoining patience and enjoining endurance, One of my two hands has smitten me, not desiring, or not meaning, to do so]: (TA:) taA^osaA='N is [syn. with taA^osiyapN , inf. n. of A^as~aY ,] from AlA_isowapu : and Alt~aEoziyapu [signifies as rendered above; or] is derived from AlEazaAzu , i. e. “ the hard ground, ” and means the strengthening of the heart: or it is from Eazawotuhu A_ilaY A^abiyhi ; because the afflicted remembers his ancestors who have gone before him; and he means, I enjoin the soul to endure his loss with patience, becoming consoled by the example of others whose sons have been slain. (Ham ubi suprà.) ― -b2- EazaA='N is also a quasiinf. n.; like EaTaA='N , meaning A_iEoTaA='N , from A^aEoTaY : (TA:) or a subst. [signifying Enjoinment, or exhortation, to be patient: and hence, consolation: and, as often used in the present day, the state, or ceremony, of mourning, when relations and friends come to console the bereaved: ] from Eaz~ayotuhu ; like salaAmN from sal~amN , and kalaAmN from kal~ama . (Msb.) -A2- See also art. Ezw .

definition: is [said by some to be] one of the verbs of appropinquation, implying eager desire, or hope, and fear, and not perfectly inflected, for it is applied in the form of the preterite to that which occurs...
sourceDefinition: is [said by some to be] one of the verbs of appropinquation, implying eager desire, or hope, and fear, and not perfectly inflected, for it is applied in the form of the preterite to that which occurs in the present: one says EasaY zayodN A^ano yaxoruja [meaning, accord. to what has been said above, Zeyd is near to going forth, though generally otherwise expl., as will be shown in what follows], and Easato fulaAnapu A^ano taxoruja [ Such a woman is near to going forth ]; zayodN being the agent of EasaY , and A^ano yaxoruja being its objective complement and meaning Alxuruwja : and one says also, Easayotu A^ano A^afoEala *aAka [as meaning, accord. to what here precedes, I am near to doing that ], and Easiytu , with kesr, agreeably with readings [in the Kur xlvii. 24], fahalo Easiytumo and Easayotumo , with kesr and fet-h; and one says to a woman, Easayoti A^ano tafoEaliY *aAka ; and [to women,] Easayotun~a ; but one does not use the form yafoEalu thereof, nor the form faAEilN ; (S;) both of which [however] are memtioned [as used] by the author of the “ Insáf: ” (I 'Ak p. 88:) [or, accord. to Fei,] EasaY is a preterite verb, [used in the sense of the present,] aplastic, not perfectly inflected, of the verbs of appropinquation, implying hope, and eager desire, and sometimes opinion, and certainty; and it is incomplete [i. e. non-attributive], and complete [i. e. attributive]: the incomplete has for its predicate an aor. mansoob by means of A^ano , as in the saying, EasaY zayodN A^ano yaquwma , meaning qaAraba zayodN AlqiyaAma [ Zeyd is near to standing ], the predicate being an objective complement or having the meaning of an objective complement: or, as some say, the meaning is laEal~a zayodFA A^ano yaquwma , i. e. [virtually, but not literally,] I eagerly desire, or I hope, that Zeyd may be performing the act of standing: [but see Eal~a and laEal~a in art. El , as well as what follows in this paragraph after the explanation of the next ex.:] the complete is such as occurs in the saying, EasaY A^ano yaquwma zayodN [meaning, accord. to what is said above, Zeyd's standing is near to being a fact ]; the agent being literally a phrase composed of a subject and an attribute because A^ano is here what is termed maSodariy~ap [so that A^ano yaquwma zayodN is equivalent to qiyaAmu zayodK ]: (Msb:) ― -b2- [in the MA and PS and TK &c., EasaY is expl. as meaning It may be that; and this, or simply may-be, or may-hap, or perhaps, I regard as the preferable rendering; as being virtually the meaning in all cases: for EasaY zayodN A^ano yaquwma , in which it is used as an incomplete verb, however it may be rendered, virtually means It may be that Zeyd is, or will be, standing; or may-be Zeyd &c.: and EasaY A^ano yaquwma zayodN , in which it is used as a complete verb, virtually means the same, though more properly rendered Zeyd's standing may be a fact: its usages are various, and have occasioned much dispute respecting its grammatical character and its meaning or meanings; as will be shown by what here follows:] ― -b3- it is [said to be] a verb unrestrictedly, or a particle unrestrictedly: (K:) [but this statement seems to have originated from a mistranscription: IHsh says,] it is a verb unrestrictedly: not a particle unrestrictedly, contrary to the opinion of Ibn-Ks-Sarráj and Th; nor when it has an affixed pronoun, as in EasaAka , contrary to an opinion of Sb, ascribed to him by Seer: (Mughnee:) it denotes hope in the case of that which is liked, and fear in the case of that which is disliked; as in the saying in the Kur [ii. 213], waEasaY A^ano takorahuwA $ayoy^FA wahuwa xayorN lakumo waEasaY A^ano tuHib~uwA $ayoy^FA wahuwa $ar~N lakumo [ But it may be that ye dislike a thing when it is good for you, and it may be that ye like a thing when it is evil for you ]: (Mughnee, K: *) ― -b4- it is used in various ways; one of which is the saying, EasaY zayodN A^ano yaquwma [mentioned above], respecting the analysis of which there are different opinions: that of the generality is, that it is like kaAna zayodN yaquwmu [inasmuch as EsY is here an incomplete verb]; but this is deemed dubious, because the predicate [ A^ano yaquwma ] is rendered by an inf. n., and the subject [ zayodN ] is a substance; to which several replies have been made; one being that a prefixed noun is meant to be understood, either before the subject, so that the meaning is, EasaY A^amoru zayodK AlqiyaAmu [ It may be that the case of Zeyd is, or will be, the performing of the act of standing ], or before the predicate, so that the meaning is EasaY zayodN SaAHibu AlqiyaAmi [ It may be that Zeyd is, or will be, the performer of the act of standing ]; and another reply is, that it is of the class of zayodN EadolN and SawomN [meaning EaAdilN and SaAy^imN , for A^ano yaquwma is equivalent to an inf. n., and an inf. n. may be used in the sense of an act. part. n.]; and another is, that A^ano is here redundant, which reply is [ said to be] nought, because An has rendered the aormansoob, and because it seldom falls out [from the phrase, though it should be remarked that laEal~a , which is said in the Mughnee to be like EasaY in meaning, is generally followed by a simple aor. and sometimes by A^ano and an aor.]: another opinion respecting the analysis of the phrase is, that EasaY is a trans. verb, like qaAraba in meaning and in government, [agreeably with the explanations mentioned above from the S and Msb,] or intrans. like qaruba mino with the preposition suppressed; and this is the opinion of Sb and Mbr: the opinion of the generality is, that it is an incomplete verb [like kaAna in the phrase kaAna zayodN yaquwmu , mentioned above], and that A^ano and the verb following it compose a substitute of implication supplying what is wanting in the two preceding portions of the sentence: ― -b5- the second way of using it is, the making it to have A^ano and the verb following this for its object, [as in EasaY A^ano yaquwma zayodN , mentioned above], so that it is a complete verb: ― -b6- the third and fourth and fifth are when it is followed by a simple aor. [being in this case likened to kaAda , (S, K, * TA.)] or an aor. with s prefixed, or a single noun; as in EasaY zayodN yaquwmu [ It may be that Zeyd stands, or will stand ] and EasaY zayodN sayaquwmu [ It may be that Zeyd will stand ] and EasaY zayodN qaAy^imN [ It may be that Zeyd is standing ]; the first whereof is one of which there are few exs., such as the saying, EasaY Alkarobu Al~a*iY A^amosayota fiyhi yakuwnu waraA='ahu farajN qariybu [ It may be that the state of anxiety in which thou hast become (or, as some relate it, A^amosayotu i. e. I hare become, ) is such that after it will be a near removal thereof ]; and the third is one of which there are fewer exs., [and which is said in the S to be not allowable,] such as the saying, A^akovarota fiY AlEa*oli muliH~FA daAy^imaA laA tukovirano A_in~iY Easiytu SaAy^imaA [or, as some relate it, Easayotu , which is more common, i. e. Thou hast been profuse in censuring, persisting constantly: be not thou profuse: verily it may be that I am, or shall be, abstaining ]; and as to the prov., EasaY Alguwayoru A^abow^usFA [expl. in art. bA^s , and of which it is said in the K that the verb therein is used in the manner of kaAna , and in the S that the phrase is extr., that Abw^sA is there put in the place of the predicate, and that there sometimes occurs in provs. what does not occur elsewhere], the right opinion is that yakuwnu is suppressed before Abw^sA ; and [in the latter of the two verses cited above] A^akuwnu is suppressed before SAy^mA ; because thus the primary usage is preserved, and because what is hoped is the person's being an abstainer, not the abstainer him- self; and as to the second of the three modes of using EasaY last mentioned above, with s prefixed to the aor., it is very extr.: ― -b7- the sixth way of using it is the saying EasaAniY and EasaAka and EasaAhu , which is rare: in this case, accord. to Sb, it is used in the manner of laEal~a , as governing the subject in the accus. case, and the predicate in the nom.; the predicate being sometimes expressed, in the nom. case, as in the saying, faqulotu EasaAhaA naAru kaA^osK waEal~ahaA ta$ak~aY faA=tiY naHowahaA faA^aEuwduhaA [ And I said, May-be it is the fire of Ka-s, (for I suppose that kA^s is here a proper name, that of a woman, daughter of El-Kelhabeh El-'Oranee,) and perhaps she has a complaint, ( ta$ak~aY being for taba$ak~aY ,) so I will come towards her, and visit her ]: ― -b8- the seventh way is the saying, EasaY zayodN qaAy^imN , mentioned by Th; which is to be explained on the ground that EsY is here an incomplete verb, and that its subject is the Damiyru Al$~aA^oni [i. e. A_in~ahu is suppressed, the meaning being, It may be that the case is this, Zeyd is standing ], the nominal proposition being the predicate. (Mughnee. [Several other statements in that work, respecting EasaY , I have omitted, as being refuted therein, or as being of little or no importance.]) ― -b9- It also denotes opinion, (Msb,) or doubt, (K, TA,) and certainty: (Msb, K, TA:) the last is meant in the saying of Ibn-Mukbil, Zan~iY bihimo kaEasaY wahumo bitanuwfapK yatanaAzaEuwna jawaAy^iza AlA^amovaAli [ My opinion of them is like an expression of certainty while they, in a desert, or in a desert destitute of water or of herbage and water, &c., are contending in reciting current proverbs instead of attending to the wants of themselves and their camels]. (S, TA.) ― -b10- As uttered by God, it is expressive of an event of necessary occurrence, (S, K,) in the whole of the Kur-án, except the saying, [in lxvi. 5,] EasaY rab~uhu A_ino T~l~aqakun~a A^ano yubodilahu A^azowaAjFA xayorFA minokun~a [ It may be that his Lord, if he divorce you, will give him in exchange wives better than you ]. (S.) ― -b11- halo Easayotumo with what follows it, in the Kur [ii. 247], means [virtually] Are ye near to fleeing? (K:) some read thus; and some, Easiytumo . (TA.) -A2- EasiYa Aln~abaAtu [erroneously written in the CK EasaY ]: see the first sentence in art. Esw .

rawSourceText: is [said by some to be] one of the verbs of appropinquation, implying eager desire, or hope, and fear, and not perfectly inflected, for it is applied in the form of the preterite to that which occurs in the present: one says EasaY zayodN A^ano yaxoruja [meaning, accord. to what has been said above, Zeyd is near to going forth, though generally otherwise expl., as will be shown in what follows], and Easato fulaAnapu A^ano taxoruja [ Such a woman is near to going forth ]; zayodN being the agent of EasaY , and A^ano yaxoruja being its objective complement and meaning Alxuruwja : and one says also, Easayotu A^ano A^afoEala *aAka [as meaning, accord. to what here precedes, I am near to doing that ], and Easiytu , with kesr, agreeably with readings [in the Kur xlvii. 24], fahalo Easiytumo and Easayotumo , with kesr and fet-h; and one says to a woman, Easayoti A^ano tafoEaliY *aAka ; and [to women,] Easayotun~a ; but one does not use the form yafoEalu thereof, nor the form faAEilN ; (S;) both of which [however] are memtioned [as used] by the author of the “ Insáf: ” (I 'Ak p. 88:) [or, accord. to Fei,] EasaY is a preterite verb, [used in the sense of the present,] aplastic, not perfectly inflected, of the verbs of appropinquation, implying hope, and eager desire, and sometimes opinion, and certainty; and it is incomplete [i. e. non-attributive], and complete [i. e. attributive]: the incomplete has for its predicate an aor. mansoob by means of A^ano , as in the saying, EasaY zayodN A^ano yaquwma , meaning qaAraba zayodN AlqiyaAma [ Zeyd is near to standing ], the predicate being an objective complement or having the meaning of an objective complement: or, as some say, the meaning is laEal~a zayodFA A^ano yaquwma , i. e. [virtually, but not literally,] I eagerly desire, or I hope, that Zeyd may be performing the act of standing: [but see Eal~a and laEal~a in art. El , as well as what follows in this paragraph after the explanation of the next ex.:] the complete is such as occurs in the saying, EasaY A^ano yaquwma zayodN [meaning, accord. to what is said above, Zeyd's standing is near to being a fact ]; the agent being literally a phrase composed of a subject and an attribute because A^ano is here what is termed maSodariy~ap [so that A^ano yaquwma zayodN is equivalent to qiyaAmu zayodK ]: (Msb:) ― -b2- [in the MA and PS and TK &c., EasaY is expl. as meaning It may be that; and this, or simply may-be, or may-hap, or perhaps, I regard as the preferable rendering; as being virtually the meaning in all cases: for EasaY zayodN A^ano yaquwma , in which it is used as an incomplete verb, however it may be rendered, virtually means It may be that Zeyd is, or will be, standing; or may-be Zeyd &c.: and EasaY A^ano yaquwma zayodN , in which it is used as a complete verb, virtually means the same, though more properly rendered Zeyd's standing may be a fact: its usages are various, and have occasioned much dispute respecting its grammatical character and its meaning or meanings; as will be shown by what here follows:] ― -b3- it is [said to be] a verb unrestrictedly, or a particle unrestrictedly: (K:) [but this statement seems to have originated from a mistranscription: IHsh says,] it is a verb unrestrictedly: not a particle unrestrictedly, contrary to the opinion of Ibn-Ks-Sarráj and Th; nor when it has an affixed pronoun, as in EasaAka , contrary to an opinion of Sb, ascribed to him by Seer: (Mughnee:) it denotes hope in the case of that which is liked, and fear in the case of that which is disliked; as in the saying in the Kur [ii. 213], waEasaY A^ano takorahuwA $ayoy^FA wahuwa xayorN lakumo waEasaY A^ano tuHib~uwA $ayoy^FA wahuwa $ar~N lakumo [ But it may be that ye dislike a thing when it is good for you, and it may be that ye like a thing when it is evil for you ]: (Mughnee, K: *) ― -b4- it is used in various ways; one of which is the saying, EasaY zayodN A^ano yaquwma [mentioned above], respecting the analysis of which there are different opinions: that of the generality is, that it is like kaAna zayodN yaquwmu [inasmuch as EsY is here an incomplete verb]; but this is deemed dubious, because the predicate [ A^ano yaquwma ] is rendered by an inf. n., and the subject [ zayodN ] is a substance; to which several replies have been made; one being that a prefixed noun is meant to be understood, either before the subject, so that the meaning is, EasaY A^amoru zayodK AlqiyaAmu [ It may be that the case of Zeyd is, or will be, the performing of the act of standing ], or before the predicate, so that the meaning is EasaY zayodN SaAHibu AlqiyaAmi [ It may be that Zeyd is, or will be, the performer of the act of standing ]; and another reply is, that it is of the class of zayodN EadolN and SawomN [meaning EaAdilN and SaAy^imN , for A^ano yaquwma is equivalent to an inf. n., and an inf. n. may be used in the sense of an act. part. n.]; and another is, that A^ano is here redundant, which reply is [ said to be] nought, because An has rendered the aormansoob, and because it seldom falls out [from the phrase, though it should be remarked that laEal~a , which is said in the Mughnee to be like EasaY in meaning, is generally followed by a simple aor. and sometimes by A^ano and an aor.]: another opinion respecting the analysis of the phrase is, that EasaY is a trans. verb, like qaAraba in meaning and in government, [agreeably with the explanations mentioned above from the S and Msb,] or intrans. like qaruba mino with the preposition suppressed; and this is the opinion of Sb and Mbr: the opinion of the generality is, that it is an incomplete verb [like kaAna in the phrase kaAna zayodN yaquwmu , mentioned above], and that A^ano and the verb following it compose a substitute of implication supplying what is wanting in the two preceding portions of the sentence: ― -b5- the second way of using it is, the making it to have A^ano and the verb following this for its object, [as in EasaY A^ano yaquwma zayodN , mentioned above], so that it is a complete verb: ― -b6- the third and fourth and fifth are when it is followed by a simple aor. [being in this case likened to kaAda , (S, K, * TA.)] or an aor. with s prefixed, or a single noun; as in EasaY zayodN yaquwmu [ It may be that Zeyd stands, or will stand ] and EasaY zayodN sayaquwmu [ It may be that Zeyd will stand ] and EasaY zayodN qaAy^imN [ It may be that Zeyd is standing ]; the first whereof is one of which there are few exs., such as the saying, EasaY Alkarobu Al~a*iY A^amosayota fiyhi yakuwnu waraA='ahu farajN qariybu [ It may be that the state of anxiety in which thou hast become (or, as some relate it, A^amosayotu i. e. I hare become, ) is such that after it will be a near removal thereof ]; and the third is one of which there are fewer exs., [and which is said in the S to be not allowable,] such as the saying, A^akovarota fiY AlEa*oli muliH~FA daAy^imaA laA tukovirano A_in~iY Easiytu SaAy^imaA [or, as some relate it, Easayotu , which is more common, i. e. Thou hast been profuse in censuring, persisting constantly: be not thou profuse: verily it may be that I am, or shall be, abstaining ]; and as to the prov., EasaY Alguwayoru A^abow^usFA [expl. in art. bA^s , and of which it is said in the K that the verb therein is used in the manner of kaAna , and in the S that the phrase is extr., that Abw^sA is there put in the place of the predicate, and that there sometimes occurs in provs. what does not occur elsewhere], the right opinion is that yakuwnu is suppressed before Abw^sA ; and [in the latter of the two verses cited above] A^akuwnu is suppressed before SAy^mA ; because thus the primary usage is preserved, and because what is hoped is the person's being an abstainer, not the abstainer him- self; and as to the second of the three modes of using EasaY last mentioned above, with s prefixed to the aor., it is very extr.: ― -b7- the sixth way of using it is the saying EasaAniY and EasaAka and EasaAhu , which is rare: in this case, accord. to Sb, it is used in the manner of laEal~a , as governing the subject in the accus. case, and the predicate in the nom.; the predicate being sometimes expressed, in the nom. case, as in the saying, faqulotu EasaAhaA naAru kaA^osK waEal~ahaA ta$ak~aY faA=tiY naHowahaA faA^aEuwduhaA [ And I said, May-be it is the fire of Ka-s, (for I suppose that kA^s is here a proper name, that of a woman, daughter of El-Kelhabeh El-'Oranee,) and perhaps she has a complaint, ( ta$ak~aY being for taba$ak~aY ,) so I will come towards her, and visit her ]: ― -b8- the seventh way is the saying, EasaY zayodN qaAy^imN , mentioned by Th; which is to be explained on the ground that EsY is here an incomplete verb, and that its subject is the Damiyru Al$~aA^oni [i. e. A_in~ahu is suppressed, the meaning being, It may be that the case is this, Zeyd is standing ], the nominal proposition being the predicate. (Mughnee. [Several other statements in that work, respecting EasaY , I have omitted, as being refuted therein, or as being of little or no importance.]) ― -b9- It also denotes opinion, (Msb,) or doubt, (K, TA,) and certainty: (Msb, K, TA:) the last is meant in the saying of Ibn-Mukbil, Zan~iY bihimo kaEasaY wahumo bitanuwfapK yatanaAzaEuwna jawaAy^iza AlA^amovaAli [ My opinion of them is like an expression of certainty while they, in a desert, or in a desert destitute of water or of herbage and water, &c., are contending in reciting current proverbs instead of attending to the wants of themselves and their camels]. (S, TA.) ― -b10- As uttered by God, it is expressive of an event of necessary occurrence, (S, K,) in the whole of the Kur-án, except the saying, [in lxvi. 5,] EasaY rab~uhu A_ino T~l~aqakun~a A^ano yubodilahu A^azowaAjFA xayorFA minokun~a [ It may be that his Lord, if he divorce you, will give him in exchange wives better than you ]. (S.) ― -b11- halo Easayotumo with what follows it, in the Kur [ii. 247], means [virtually] Are ye near to fleeing? (K:) some read thus; and some, Easiytumo . (TA.) -A2- EasiYa Aln~abaAtu [erroneously written in the CK EasaY ]: see the first sentence in art. Esw .

sourceDefinition: i. q. EuwdN [as meaning A staff, or stick, or rod ]: (K:) originally EaSawN , and accordingly its dual is as below: said to be thus called because the fingers and hand are put together upon it [to grasp it], from the saying EaSawotu Alqawoma “ I collected together the people, or party; ” as related by As from some one or more of the Basrees: (TA:) of the fem. gender: (S, Msb, K:) it is said in a prov., ↓ AlEaSaA mina AlEuSay~api [lit. The staff is from the little staff; the dim. having the affix p because it is the dim. of a fem. n.]; (S;) [or] AlEaSaA in this prov. is the name of a mare of Jedheemeh [mentioned voce Dul~N ], and AlEuSay~ap is that of her dam; meaning that part of the thing, or affair, is from part; (S, K, TA;) and said when one is likened to his father; or meaning that the big thing is in its commencement small: (TA: [see also Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 17:]) it is not allowable to say EaSaA=' ; nor to affix p : (As, TA:) one says, h`*ihi EaSaAYa A^atawak~aA^u EalayohaA [ This is my staff; I support, or stay, myself upon it ]: Fr says that the first incorrect speech heard in El-'Irák was the saying, h`*ihi EaSaAtiY : (S:) the dual is EaSawaAni : (S, Msb:) and the pl. [of mult.] is EuSiY~N , (S, Msb, K,) [originally EuSuwwN ,] of the measure fuEuwlN , (S, Msb,) and EiSiY~N , (S, K,) in which the E is with kesr because of the kesrah following it, and [of pauc.] A^aEoSK (S, Msb, K) and A^aEoSaA='N , (K,) or this last is agreeable with analogy, but has not been transmitted, (ISk, Msb,) and is disallowed by Sb, who says that EuiSiY~N was used in its stead. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence various sayings, here following. ― -b3- ] A^aloqaY EaSaAhu [lit. He threw down his staff; ] meaning (tropical:) he stayed, (S, Msb, K, TA,) and rested, (Msb,) and ceased from journeys, (S,) having reached his place: (K, TA:) a prov.; (S, TA;) applied to him to whom an affair has become suitable and who has therefore kept to it: (TA:) or he made firm his tent-pegs, and pitched his tent, or stayed; (K, TA;) like him who has returned from his journey. (TA.) And rafaEa EaSaAhu [ He took up his staff ] means (assumed tropical:) he ceased from staying [ in a place at which he had alighted; he departed ]. (Har p. 454.) ― -b4- laA tarofaEo EaSaAka Eano A^aholika [ Put not thou away thy staff, or stick, from thy family, or thy wife, ] denotes [the practice of] discipline. (S. [See art. rfE , p. 1122, col. 3.]) ― -b5- humo Eabiydu AlEaSaA [ They are the slaves of the staff ] means (assumed tropical:) they are [ persons ] beaten with the staff. (K, TA.) It is said in the A, Aln~aAsu Eabiydu AlEaSaA [ Mankind are the slaves of the staff ], meaning that they are dreaded by reason of their doing harm [and are therefore to be kept in awe]. (TA.) ― -b6- And maA humo A_il~aA Eabiydu AlEaSaA [ They are none other than the slaves of the staff ] is said of persons regarded as low, base, or vile. (TA.) ― -b7- A_in~ahu lay~inu AlEaSaA [ Verily he is one whose staff is supple ] means (tropical:) he is gentle, a good manager of that whereof he has the charge: (S, K: *) accord. to ISd, alluding to the beating little with the ESA . (TA.) And A_in~ahu DaEiyfu AlEaSaA [ Verily he is one whose staff is weak ], meaning tiroEiy~apN [i. e., (assumed tropical:) one who performs well the act of keeping or tending, or of pasturing or feeding, camels ]: (S:) or one who beats the camels little (K, TA) with the EaSA : and such is commended. (TA.) And Saliybu AlEaSaA and SulobuhaA [ One whose staff is hard ], i. e. (assumed tropical:) one who is ungentle with the camels, beating them with the ESA : and such is discommended. (TA.) See an ex. in a verse of Er-Rá'ee cited voce SulobN . ― -b8- qaraEahu biEaSaA AlmalaAmapi [ He struck him with the staff of censure ] means (assumed tropical:) he exceeded the usual bounds in censuring him. (TA.) ― -b9- See also 1 in art. qrE . ― -b10- fulaAnN yuSal~iY EaSaA fulaAnK [ Such a one straightens the staff of such a one by turning it round over the fire ] means (assumed tropical:) such a one manages, orders, or regulates, the affairs of such a one. (TA.) ― -b11- laA tadoxulo bayona AlEaSaA waliHaAy^ihaA [ Enter not thou between the staff and its peel ] means [(assumed tropical:) intermeddle not thou between two close friends; (see Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 153;) or] enter not thou into that which does not concern thee. (TA.) And qa$arotu lahu AlEaSaA [ I peeled for him the staff ] means (assumed tropical:) I discovered to him what was in my mind. (TA.) ― -b12- $aq~u AlEaSaA [lit. The splitting of the staff ] means (assumed tropical:) the contravening of the collective body [or the community ] of El-Islám [i. e. of the Muslims ]: (K, TA:) and also (assumed tropical:) the disuniting of the collective body of the tribe: (TA:) or $aq~a AlEaSaA means (tropical:) He separated himself from, and he contravened, the collective body [or the community ]: (Msb:) and [it is said that] the primary signification of AlEaSaA is the state of combination and union: (TA:) this is the meaning in the saying, respecting the xawaArij [see xArijiY~N ], qado $aq~uwA EaSaA Almusolimiyna (assumed tropical:) [ They have made a schism in the state of combination and union, or in the communion, of the Muslims ]. (S, TA.) [Hence,] their saying A_iy~aAka waqatola AlEaSaA means (assumed tropical:) Beware thou of slaying or being slain in making a schism in the communion of the Muslims ( fiY $aq~i EaSaA Almusolimiyna ). (TA.) And one says, Aino$aq~ati AlEaSaA (S, TA) [ The staff became split ], meaning, (assumed tropical:) disagreement, or discord, befell. (TA.) And TaArato EaSaA baniY fulaAnK $iqaqFA [lit. The staff of the sons of such a one flew in splinters ], a prov., meaning (assumed tropical:) the sons of such a one became scattered in various directions. (Meyd.) ― -b13- EaSaA AlEabodi [ The stick of the slave ] is the thing with which one stirs the mal~ap [or hot ashes wherein bread is baked ]. (TA.) ― -b14- AlEaSaA signifies also (tropical:) The bone of the shank; (K, TA;) as being likened to the ESA [properly so called]. (TA.) And [the pl.] AlEiSiY~u , (assumed tropical:) The bones that are in the wing. (S.) And [the same, or] AlEuSiY~u , (assumed tropical:) Certain stars, having the form of the EaSaA [or rather of ESY~ ]. (TA. [But what stars these are, I have not been able to determine.]) ― -b15- Also, (i. e. AlEaSaA ,) The tongue. (K.) [Perhaps as being likened to a staff because used in chiding.] ― -b16- And The woman's [ muffler, or headcovering, called ] ximaAr . (K.) ― -b17- EaSaA Alr~aAEiY [ The pastor's rod; and appellation of knot-grass; a species of polygonum, p. aviculare; ] the bTbAT [i. e. baTobaAT , but the former name is the better known]; male, and female, the former of which is the more potent: asserted by Dioscorides to be diuretic, and a remedy for him who suffers suppression of the urine. (Ibn-Seenà, whom we call Avicenna, book ii. p. 229.)

EaTobN and EuTuwbN , (O,) It [i. e. cotton, and wool,] was, or became, soft. (A, O, * K. [See also EuTobN , below.])

sourceDefinition: , (O, K,) inf. n. of ET~b , (TA,) signifies The brewing ( EilaAj ) of beverage, or wine, in order that its odour may become good: (O, K:) so says Aboo-Sa'eed. (O.) The phrase raHiyq muEaT~ab occurs in a poem of Lebeed, as some relate it; but as others relate it, it is muqaT~ab , which means “ mixed: ” (O, TA:) so says Az; and he adds, “ I know not what muEaT~ab is. ” (TA.) -A2- Also, in a grape-vine, The appearing of the knots, or gems, in the places whence grow the bunches of grapes. (K.)

(Msb.) You say, AlA^amora ↓ AEtmd He intended, or purposed, the affair; or aimed at it; &c.; syn. Samadahu ; (A in art. Smd ;) or Samada Samodahu , i. e. qaSada qaSodahu . (M in that art.) And *anobFA ↓ tEm~d He committed a sin, or the like, intentionally. (TA in art. xTA^ .) And ↓ tEm~d SayodFA [ He aimed at an object of the chase ]. (Sgh, in Msb.) And Eamada liraA^osihi biAlEaSaA He aimed at his head with the staff, or stick. (M in art. Smd .) And Eamadahu , [and Eamada A_ilayohi ,] aor. ; and ↓ AEtmdhu ; and ↓ tEm~dhu ; He betook himself to him, or had recourse to him, in a case of need. (A.) ― -b2- And [hence] one says, faEalotuhu EamodFA EalaY EayonK , (S, O, Msb, K,) and Eamoda EayonK , (S, A, O, Msb, K,) I did it seriously, or in earnest, and with certain knowledge, or assurance. (S, A, O, Msb, K. [See also EayonN .]) When a man sees a bodily form and imagines it to be an object of the chase and therefore shoots at it, he cannot use this phrase, for he only aims at what is an object of the chase in his imagination: so says Sgh. (O, K.) And Eamadahu , (K, TA,) aor., in this case, , (TA, [but this, I think, requires confirmation,]) It grieved him, or made him sorrowful. (K, TA.) One says, maA Eamadaka What has grieved thee, or made thee sorrowful? (TA.) -A4- Eamida , (S, O, L, K,) aor. , inf. n. EamadN , (S, O,) said of earth, It became moistened by rain so that when a portion of it was grasped in the hand it became compacted by reason of its moisture: (S, O, L, K:) or it became moistened by rain and compacted, layer upon layer. (L.) And Eamidati AlA^aroDu , inf. n. as above, The land became moistened by the rain's sinking into the earth so that when a portion of it was grasped in the hand it became compacted by reason of its moisture. (AZ.) ― -b2- Also, (inf. n. as above, L,) said of a camel, He had the inner part of his hump broken [or bruised ] by being [ much ] ridden, while the outer part remained whole, or sound: (S, O, L, K:) or he had his hump swollen in consequence of the galling of the saddle and the cloth beneath it, and broken [or bruised ]: whence EamiydN and maEomuwdN as epithets applied to a man. (L.) And Eamidato A^aloyataAhu mina Alr~ukuwbi His buttocks became swollen, and quivered, or throbbed, in consequence of [ long and hard ] riding. (En-Nadr, O, K.) And Eamida , aor. and inf. n. as above, said of a pustule, It became swollen in consequence of its having been squeezed before it had become ripe, and its egg [or white globule ] did not come forth. (L, TA.) ― -b3- Also He suffered pain. (L.) ― -b4- And, (T, O, L, K,) inf. n. as above, (T, L,) He was, or became, angry: (T, O, L, K:) like Eabida (T, L) [and A^amida and A^abida ]. One says, Eamida Ealayohi He was angry with him. (T, L.) ― -b5- [And He wondered. ] One says, A^anaA A^aEomadu minohu I wonder at him, or it: (S, O, L, K:) or, as some say, I am angry at him, or it: and some say that it means I lament at, or complain of, him, or it. (L.) A^aEomadu mino say~idK qatalahu qawomuhu (S, O, L) i. e. Do I wonder at a chief whom his [ own ] people have slain? (L) was said by Aboo-Jahl (S, O, L) when he lay prostrated at Bedr; meaning, hath anything more happened than the slaughter of a chief by his [own] people? this is not a disgrace [to him]: he meant thereby that the destruction that befell him was a light matter to him: (A'Obeyd, L:) the saying is interrogative; (Sh, L;) A^aEomadu being app. contracted from A^aA^aEomadu , by the suppression of one of the two hemzehs. (Az, L.) And A^aEomadu mino kayolK muH~iqa , as related by A'Obeyd, [and thus in the O, in two copies of the S written muHiq~ , and in a third copy omitted,] or muHiqa , without teshdeed, as seen by Az written in an old book, [i. e. Do I wonder at a measure incompletely filled? ] is a saying of the Arabs, expl. in the book above alluded to, and, Az thinks, correctly, as meaning is it anything more than a measure incompletely filled? [and in a similar manner, but not so fully, expl. in two copies of the S and in the O:] or, accord. to IB, is it anything more than the fact of my measure's being incompletely filled? (L:) thus expl. also by ISk: and in a similar manner the saying of Aboo-Jahl. (From a marginal note in one of my copies of the S.) ― -b6- Eamida bihi means He kept, or clave, to it; (Ibn-Buzurj, O, K;) namely, a thing. (O.)

And AEtmdt EalaY AlkitaAbi [and AEtmdt AlkitaAba , and perhaps biAlkitaAbi (see De Sacy's Chrest. Arabe, sec. ed., i. 315),] (tropical:) I relied upon the book, and held to it: a metaphorical phrase, from the first above. (Msb.)

[Hence also the phrase, used by grammarians, yaEotamidu EalaY maA qabolahu (assumed tropical:) It is syntactically dependent upon what is before it; as, for instance, an enunciative upon its inchoative, an epithet upon the subst. which it qualifies, and an objective complement of a verb upon its verb.
AEtmd AlmaTaru EalaY AlA^aroDi , a phrase occurring in the K in art. nkH , app. means The rain rested upon the ground so as to soak into it: see Eamida .]
AEtmd EalaY Als~ayori He went, or journeyed, gently; went a gentle pace. (L in art. hwd .) And AEtmd layolatahu He rode on journeying during his night. (A, O, K.)

definition: Earth moistened by rain so that when a portion of it is grasped in the hand it becomes compacted by reason of its moisture: (S, O, L:) or moistened by rain and compacted, layer upon layer.
sourceDefinition: Earth moistened by rain so that when a portion of it is grasped in the hand it becomes compacted by reason of its moisture: (S, O, L:) or moistened by rain and compacted, layer upon layer. (L.) ― -b2- [Hence] one says, huwa Eamidu Alv~araY Text is missing in original ndant in goodness, beneficence, or bounty. (AZ, Sh, O, K.) ― -b3- EamidN is also applied to a camel, meaning Having the inner part of his hump broken [or bruised ] by his being [ much ] ridden, while the outer part remains whole, or sound: (S, O, L:) or having his hump swollen in consequence of the galling of the saddle and of the cloth beneath it, and broken [or bruised ]: fem. with p : and, with p , a she-camel broken, or subdued, by the weight of her burden. (L.) Lebeed says, describing rain (S, O, L) that caused the valleys to flow, (S,) fabaAta Als~ayolu yarokabu jaAnibayohi mina Albaq~aAri kaAlEamidi Alv~aqaAli [ And the torrent continued during the night, what resembled the heavy, or slow-paced, camel such as is termed Eamid overlying its two sides, from the valley of El-Bakkár ]: As says, he means that a collection of clouds resembling the [camel termed] Eamid overlay the two sides of the torrent; i. e., that clouds encompassed it with rain. (S, O, L.) ― -b4- Also, applied to a pustule, Swollen in consequence of its having been squeezed before it had become ripe, and retaining its egg [or white globule ]. (L.)

definition: A thing by which another thing is stayed, propped, or supported;
sourceDefinition: A thing by which another thing is stayed, propped, or supported; a stay, prop, or support; as also ↓ EimaAdN ; of which latter the pl. [or rather quasi-pl. n.] is ↓ EamadN ; (Msb;) as it is also of EamuwdN : (S, Msb, &c.:) a thing upon which one leans, reclines, or bears; upon which one stays, props, or supports, himself: a thing upon which one relies: (S, * O, * L, * K, TA:) and A^amorK ↓ EimaAdu (S and K voce qiwaAmN ) and ↓ Eamuwduhu and ↓ Eamiyduhu (L) signify the stay, or support, of a thing or an affair; that whereon it rests, or whereby it subsists; its efficient cause of subsistence; that without which it would not subsist: (L, and S * and K * ubi suprà:) and ↓ muEotamadN , applied to a man, is syn. with sanadN [meaning a person upon whom one leans, rests, stays himself, or relies; a man's stay, support, or object of reliance; like EamodapN and ↓ EimaAdN ]: (S and K * in art. snd :) EumodapN is used alike as masc. and fem. and as sing. and dual and pl.: (TA:) one says, A^anota EumodatunaA Thou art he to whom we betake ourselves, or have recourse, in our necessities; (A;) or Eumoda tunaA fiY Al$~adaAy^idi our stay, or support, or object of reliance, (↓ muEotamadunaA ,) in difficulties: (Msb:) and A^anotumo EumodatunaA Ye are they upon whom we stay ourselves, or rely: (TA:) and one says also Hay~ihi ↓ huwa Eamuwdu He is the stay, or support, of his tribe: (A:) and Alqawomi ↓ EimaAdu means the stay, support, or object of reliance, of the people, or party; syn. sanaduhumo . (Ham p. 457.) See also EamuwdN , second quarter. ― -b2- [Hence, as used by grammarians,] (assumed tropical:) An indispensable member of a proposition; as, for instance, the agent; contr. of faDolapN . (I'Ak p. 143.) ― -b3- Also An intention, a purpose, an aim, or a course: so in the phrase Ailozamo Eumodataka [ Keep to thy intention, &c.]. (A.)

definition: a word of well-known meaning, (Msb, K,) The Eamuwd of a bayot , (S, O,) or of a xayomap ;
sourceDefinition: a word of well-known meaning, (Msb, K,) The Eamuwd of a bayot , (S, O,) or of a xayomap ; (Mgh;) [i. e.] a pole of a tent; as also ↓ EimaAdN : and a column, or pillar, of a house or the like: (L:) pl. (of pauc., S, O) A^aEomidapN , and (of mult., S, O) EumudN , and (quasi-pl. n., L) ↓ EamadN . (S, O, L, Msb, K.) [The former is the primary, and more common, meaning: and hence the phrase] A^aholu EamuwdK (Lth, A, Msb) and EumudK or ↓ EamadK , (Msb,) or this last is not said, (L,) and ↓ A^aholu EimaAdK , (Lth, A, Msb, K,) [ The people of the tent-pole or of the tent-poles; ] meaning the people of, or who dwell in, tents: (Lth, A, Msb, K:) or the last means the people of lofty tents, (K,) or of lofty structures. (TA.) tarawonahaA ↓ xalaqa A@ls~am`waAti bigayori EamadK , in the Kur [xxxi. 9 (and see also xiii. 2)], (O, L,) accord. to Ibn-'Arafeh, (O,) or Fr, (L,) means either He created the heavens without Eamad [or pillars ] as ye see them; and with the sight ye need not information: or He created the heavens with pillars ( Eamad ) that ye see not; [i. e., with invisible pillars; ] (O, * L;) the pillars that are not seen being his power; or, accord. to Lth, Mount Káf, which surrounds the world [or earth]; the sky being like a cupola, whereof the extremities rest on that mountain, which is of green chrysolite, whence, it is said, results the greenness of the sky. (L.) And ↓ EamadK and EumudK in the Kur [civ., last verse], accord. to different readings, are pls. [or rather the former is a quasipl. n.] of EamuwdN ; (Fr, L;) or of ↓ EimaAdN ; and mean [ pillars ] of fire. (Zj, L.) ― -b2- Also Any tent ( xibaA=' ) supported on poles: or any tent extending to a considerable length along the ground, supported on many poles. (L.) ― -b3- See also EumodapN , in two places. ― -b4- [Hence,] A lord, master, or chief, (S, O, K,) of a people, or party; (S, O;) as also ↓ EamiydN ; (S, A, O, K;) both signify a lord, master, or chief, upon whom persons stay themselves, or rely, in their affairs, or to whom they betake themselves, or have recourse; and the pl. of the latter is EumadaA='u . (TA.) And (accord. to IAar, O, L, TA) The ray^iys [or chief, or commander ], (so in the L, and in the copy of the K followed in the TA,) or rasiyl [app. meaning, if correct, the scout, or emissary, or perhaps the advanced guard ], (so in the O, and in the CK, and in my MS. copy of the K,) of an army; (O, L, K;) also called the zuwayor [which corroborates the former explanation, being syn. with ray^iys ]; (L, TA; [in the O written zawiyr ;]) as also ↓ EimaAdN and ↓ EumodapN and ↓ EumodaAnN . (O, L, K.) ― -b5- Also, [from the same word in the first of the senses expl. above,] A staff, or stick. (L.) ― -b6- And A weapon made of iron, with which one beats, or strikes; (Mgh;) a rod of iron; (L;) [ a kind of mace; app. a rod of iron with a ball of the same metal at the head: I have heard this appellation applied to the kind of weapon which I have mentioned in an explanation of TawaAriqu , pl. of TaAriqapN , q. v.; and it is vulgarly said, in Egypt, to have been used by the fidaAwiy~ap , the sect called in our histories of the Crusades “ the Assassins: ”] pl. [of pauc.] A^aEomidapN . (Mgh.) ― -b7- [And A bar of iron, or of any metal. ― -b8- And A perpendicular. ] ― -b9- And A slender and lofty mountain: so in the saying, AlEuqaAbu tabiyDu fiY raA^osi EamuwdK [ The eagle lays her eggs in the top of a slender and lofty mountain ]. (A.) ― -b10- Eamuwdu Albiy^ori [ Each of ] the two upright supports ( qaAy^imataAni [or qaAmataAni ]) upon which is [ placed the horizontal cross-piece of wood whereto is suspended ] the great pulley ( maHaAlap ) of the well: (O, K:) [both together being termed the EamuwdaAni :] a poet says, A_i*aA A@sotaqal~ato rajafa AlEamuwdaAno [ When it (the bucket, Ald~alowu ,) rises, the two upright supports of the piece of wood to which hangs the great pulley tremble ]. (O.) ― -b11- Eamuwdu AlZ~aliym [ Each of ] the two legs of the male ostrich: (K:) his two legs are called his EamuwdaAni . (O, L, TA.) ― -b12- Eamuwdu AlS~aliybi [ The upright timber of the cross ] is an appellation applied by the vulgar to the star [e] upon the tail of the constellation Delphinus. (Kzw.) ― -b13- Eamuwdu AlmiyzaAni The $aAhiyn , (K voce $Ahyn ,) i. e. the beam of the balance; the same as the minojam , except that it (the Eamuwd ) is generally of the qab~aAn , or steelyard. sourceDefinition: , aor. yaEowiY , inf. n. EuwaA='N (S, K, TA) and EaY~N and Eaw~apN (K, TA) and EawoyapN , with fet-h and then sukoon, thus in the M, but in the copies of the K Eawiy~apN , (TA,) said of a dog, (S, CK, TA,) and of a wolf, and of a jackal, (S, TA,) He cried, or cried loudly: (S:) [meaning he howled: ] he twisted his muzzle, then uttered a cry: or he prolonged his cry, not doing so with clearness: and ↓ AEtwY signifies the same: (K, TA:) [in the Ham p. 693, the former is expl. as signifying nabaHa and SaAHa ; but] it is said that Eaw~apN signifies a prolonged crying; and is not the same as naboHN [which means “ a barking ”]. (TA.) It is said in a prov. lawo laka A^aEowiY maA Eawayotu [ If to thee I were howling, I had not howled ]; (TA;) or lawo laka Eawayotu lamo A^aEowiho , in which the h may be the h of pausation, or it may be put by metonymy for the inf. n. so that the meaning is lamo A^aEowi AlEuwaA='a : (Meyd:) it originated from the fact that a man used, [and still uses, as I have had occasion to do,] when becoming benighted, in the desert, to howl, in order that the dogs, if any person by whose presence he might be cheered were near him, might hear, and reply to him, and he might be guided by their howling: so this man howled, and the wolf came to him, whereupon he said thus: it relates to the seeker of succour from him who will not succour him. (Meyd, * TA.) And it is said in a trad., kaA^an~iY A^asomaEu EuwaA='a A^aholi Aln~aAri i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ As though I heard ] the crying or loud crying [or howling ] of the people of the fire [of Hell]: (TA:) [for] EawaYa is used metaphorically as meaning he suffered distress, and complained; from the EuwaA=' of the dog: (Har p. 634:) as IAth says, it is more especially used in relation to the wolf and the dog. (TA.) And one says of him who is esteemed, or found to be, weak, maA yaEowiY wamaA yanobaHu (assumed tropical:) [ He does not howl nor does he bark ]. (Ham p. 693.) ― -b2- And EawaY A_ilaY Alfitonapi means (assumed tropical:) He called (K, TA) people, or a party, (TA,) [ to conflict and faction, or the like; ] EawaY being used in this sense by way of likening the person who does so to a dog, or in contempt of him. (Ham p. 693.) [See also 10.] ― -b3- EuwaA='N signifies also The grumbling cry ( rugaA=' ) of a weak young camel: used in this sense by a poet. (TA.) ― -b4- EuwaA='u AlmugotaAbi ; and the phrase EawaY Eani Alr~ajuli ; see in the next paragraph. -A2- EawaY , (S, K, TA,) inf. n. EaY~N , (S, TA,) He bent a thing; as also ↓ AEtwY ; and likewise a bow; as also ↓ Ew~Y , (K, TA,) inf. n. taEowiyapN : (TA:) and (TA) he twisted hair, and a rope; (S, TA;) as also ↓ Ew~Y , inf. n. taEowiyapN . (S.) One says also EawaY AlEimaAmapa Eay~apF He twisted the turban with a single twisting. (TA.) And Eawayotu raA^osa Aln~aAqapi I turned the head of the she-camel by means of the nose-rein. (S, TA.) And Alqawomu Suduwra rikaAbhimo ↓ Ew~Y and EawawohaA The party inclined the breasts of their camels that they were riding. (TA.) And EawaY Alburapa He bent, or inclined, the nose-ring of the she-camel. (K, * TA.) And Aln~aAqapu taEowiY buratahaA fiY sayorihaA The she-camel twists her nose-ring with her xiTaAm [or halter ] in her going. (S, TA.) And EawaAhu Eani Al$~aYo'i He turned him from the thing. (TA.) And one says of the man who possesses prudence, or discretion, and precaution, or good judgment, and who is hardy, strong, or sturdy, mA ynhY wlA yEwY [i. e. maA yunohaY walaA yuEowaY He is not forbidden nor is he turned ]. (TA.) ― -b2- And EawaY signifies also He (a man) attained to the age of thirty years, so that his arm, or hand, became strong, and he twisted vehemently the arm, or hand, of another. (ISd, K.)

definition: (S, K) and AlEaw~aA (K) The dog (S, K) that howls ( yaEowiY ) much.
sourceDefinition: (S, K) and AlEaw~aA (K) The dog (S, K) that howls ( yaEowiY ) much. (S.) Hence the saying, Ealayohi AlEafaA^'u waAlkalobu AlEaw~aA='u [ Upon him be the dust, and the howling dog ]: a form of imprecation. (TA.) ― -b2- And the latter signifies also The wolf. (TA.) ― -b3- Also, both, (S, K, TA,) but the latter is the more common, and its A is to denote the fem. gender, like that of HubolaY [in which it is written Y ], the word being fem., (TA,) (tropical:) One of the Mansions of the Moon, (S, K, TA,) namely, the Thirteenth; (Kzw in his Descr. of the Mansions of the Moon;) consisting of five stars, (S, K,) said to be the haunch of the Lion [of which the Arabs, or some of them, extended the figure (as they did also that of the Scorpion) far beyond the limits that we assign to it: see *iraAEN ]: (S:) or four stars [g, d, e and h, of Virgo ], (K, and Kzw ubi suprà,) behind AlS~arofap [q. v.], (Kzw ibid.,) resembling an alif (K, Kzw) with the lower part turned back, in the Koofee handwriting [in which it is nearly like the Roman L (see zaAwiyapN , in art. zwY )]; (Kzw ibid;) also called Euroquwbu AlA^asadi ; (TA, as from the S, in my copies of which I do not find this;) they regard it as dogs following the Lion; and some say that it is the haunches of the Lion; (Kzw ubi suprà;) accord. to the A, it is thus called because it rises [a mistake for sets, aurorally, (see manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl ,)] in the tail, or latter part, of the cold, as though it were howling ( kaA^an~ahu yaEowiY ) after it, driving it away, wherefore they call it TaAruwdapu Albarodi : (TA:) or it is an appellation applied by the Arabs to the star that is on the edge of the left shoulder of Virgo, which is the Thirteenth Mansion of the Moon: or, accord. to some, the stars that are upon her belly and beneath her armpit; as though they were dogs howling ( taEowiY ) behind the Lion; so called because of the vehemence of the cold; for when they rise or set [aurorally], they bring cold. sourceDefinition: , (Lth, O, K, TA,) inf. n. EayojN (Lth, O, TA *) and EuyuwjN (Lth, O, TA) and EuwuwjN [app. Euw^uwjN ], (TA,) I do not regard it; do not care for it. (Lth, O, TA.) One says, maA EaAja biqawolihi , inf. n. EayojN and EayojuwjapN , He did not regard his saying: or he did not believe it. (ISd, TA.) And maA A^aEiyju mino kalaAmihi bi$aYo'K I care not for anything of his speech, or of what he says: (Fr, ISk, S, O:) and the Benoo-Asad say, maA A^aEuwju bikalaAmihi [expl. in art. Ewj ]; taking it from Eujotu Aln~aAqapa . (ISk, S.) ― -b2- maA Eijotu bihi I was not pleased, well pleased, content, or satisfied, with it; or did not approve it. (IAar, S, O, K.) ― -b3- maA Eijotu bixabari fulaAnK I was not satisfied in my mind by the information of such a one, and did not deem it certain. (L.) ― -b4- maA Eijotu biAlmaA='i I did not satisfy my thirst with the water: (S, O, K, TA:) said by one who has drunk salt water: (S, O, TA:) or I did not profit by it: and sometimes the verb is used in this sense in an affirmative phrase. (TA.) And maA Eijotu biAld~awaA='i I did not profit by the medicine. (S, O, K.) And EAj , aor. yaEiyju , [thus used affirmatively,] He profited by speech, &c. (B.) -A2- gadara , aor. , (T, O, K,) inf. n. gadorN , (T, O,) He drank the water of the gadiyr [q. v.]: (T, O, K:) and, accord. to the K, gadira , he drank the water of the sky; but this is a sheer mistake, occasioned by a misunderstanding of a saying in the T; here following: (TA:) Az says that gadara meaning as expl. above should accord. to analogy be gadira , like kariEa meaning “ he drank the karaE , ” i. e. the water of the sky: (O, TA:) moreover, a distinction is strangely made in the K between the water of the gadiyr and the water of the sky. (S.) -A6- gadirati Alganamu , (K,) inf. n. gadarN , (TA,) The sheep, or goats, became satiated in the place of pasture in the first of the growth thereof. (K.) -A7- gadirati AlA^aroDu The land abounded with gadar [q. v.]. (K.)

sourceDefinition: ; pl. guduwrN : see gudorapN , in three places. ― -b2- [Hence,] one says, A^aloqati Aln~aAqapu gadarahaA The she-camel cast forth what her womb had left remaining in it of blood and foul matter [ after her bringing forth ]. (TA.) And A^aloqati Al$~aApu guduwrahaA The ewe, or she-goat, cast forth the water and blood and other remains in her womb after bringing forth. (TA.) ― -b3- And fiY Aln~ahori gadarN In the river, or rivulet, is slime remaining when the water has sunk into the earth. (TA.) -A2- gadarN signifies also A place such as is termed Zalif [app. as meaning hard, and that does not show a footmark, or rugged and hard ], abounding with stones: (S, O, TA:) or a place abounding with stones, difficult to traverse: (TA:) or any difficult place, through which the beast can hardly, or in nowise, pass: (K:) or soft ground, in which are [ trenches, or channels, such as are termed ] laxaAqiyq : (TA:) or burrows, (Lh, S, K, TA,) and banks, or ridges, worn and undermined by water, (Lh, TA,) and uneven laxaAqiyq in the ground: (Lh, S, K, TA: [and the like is also said in the TA on the authority of As:]) and stones (K, TA) with trees; thus accord. to AZ and IKtt: (TA:) and anything that conceals one, and obstructs his sight: pl. A^agodaArN . (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] one says, maA A^avobata gadarahu , meaning maA A^avobatahu fiY Algadari [ How firm is he in traversing the rugged and hard and stony place! &c.]: this is said of the horse: and also (assumed tropical:) of the man when his tongue is firm in the place of slipping and of contention or litigation: (S, TA:) or, accord. to Lh, it means (assumed tropical:) how firm, or valid, is his argument, or plea, and how seldom does harm in consequence of slipping and stumbling befall him! or, accord. to Ks, how firm is what remains of his intellect or understanding! but ISd says that this explanation did not please him. (TA.) And farasN vabotu Algadari A horse firm, or steady, in the place of slipping. (Ibn-Buzurj, TA.) And rajulN vabotu Algadari (tropical:) A man firm, or steadfast, in fight, or conflict, (S, K, TA,) or in altercation or disputation, or in speech, (S accord. to different copies,) or and in altercation or disputation, (K, TA,) and in speech; (TA;) and also in everything that he commences. (K, TA.) And accord. to Ibn-Buzurj one says, A_in~ahu lavabotu Algadari , meaning (assumed tropical:) Verily he is strong in talking or discoursing, with men, and in contending, or disputing, with them. (L.) [See also vabotN .]

definition: A pool of water left by a torrent: (A 'Obeyd, S, M, K:) of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure mufaAEilN , from gaAdarhu , or mufoEalN , from A^agodarahu ;
sourceDefinition: A pool of water left by a torrent: (A 'Obeyd, S, M, K:) of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure mufaAEilN , from gaAdarhu , or mufoEalN , from A^agodarahu ; or, as some say, of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure faAEilN ; (S;) because it is unfaithful to those who come to it to water, failing when much wanted: (S, * TA:) but it is a subst.; [not an epithet; or an epithet in which the quality of a subst. predominates, and only used as a subst.:] you do not say h`*aA maA='N gadiyrN : (Lh:) or a place in which rain-water stagnates, whether small or large, not remaining until the summer: (Lth:) or a river: (Msb:) [but this is extr.:] pl. [of pauc. A^agodirapN , (occurring in a verse cited voce A_il~aA , &c.,) and of mult.] gudoraAnN (S, Msb, K, TA) and gudurN (S, Nh, L, TA,) which last is sometimes contracted into gudorN : (TA:) in the K, the last pl. is said to be of the measure of SuradN ; [i. e. ↓ gudarN ;] but this is inconsistent with what is said in other lexicons, as shown above: and it is also said in the K that gudarN signifies the same as gadiyrN , in the sense first given above; but it appears that this is a pl. of gudorapN ; and that, in the K, we should read, for waAlgadiyru, kaAlgadiyri , and place this before, instead of after, its explanation. (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (tropical:) A piece of herbage; (TA;) as also ↓ gadiyrapN : pl. gudoraAnN : (K, TA;) this is the only pl. (TA.) ― -b3- Hence also, (TA,) (tropical:) A sword; (K, TA;) like as it is called luj~N . (TA.) ― -b4- And ↓ gadiyrapN also signifies A she-camel left by the pastor (S, K) behind the other camels; and in like manner, a sheep, or goat. (S.)

definition: and ↓ gudarN [respecting which see below] (S, K) and ↓ gaduwrN and ↓ gad~aArN and ↓ gid~iyrN (K) are epithets applied to a man [and signifying, the first, Perfidious, unfaithful, faithless, or treacherous;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ gudarN [respecting which see below] (S, K) and ↓ gaduwrN and ↓ gad~aArN and ↓ gid~iyrN (K) are epithets applied to a man [and signifying, the first, Perfidious, unfaithful, faithless, or treacherous; or acting perfidiously, &c.; and the rest, very perfidious, &c.]: (S, K:) and ↓ gaduwrN and ↓ gad~aArN and ↓ gad~aArapN are epithets applied to a woman [and signifying as above]: (K:) but ↓ gudar is mostly used in calling to a man and reviling him: (S:) you say to a man, yaA gu*aru [ O very perfidious man]; (S, K;) and in like manner, ↓ yaA magodaru , and ↓ yA magodiru , and ↓ yaA A@bona magodarK , and ↓ yA Abn magodirK , all determinate; (K, TA;) and to a woman, ↓ yA gadaAri , like qaTaAmi : (K:) [accord. to some, ↓ gudar is only used in this manner, and is therefore without tenween; for] it is said that rajulN gudaru is not allowable, because gudaru is determinate: but Sh says rajulN gudarN , writing it, says Az, with tenween, contr. to what Lth says; and this is correct; a word of the measure fuEal being imperfectly decl. [only] when it is a determinate subst., like Eumaru and zufaru : and IAth says that gudaru is altered from its original form, which is gaAdirN , for the sake of intensiveness: (TA:) in the pl. [sense] you say yaAla gudara , (S,) or yaA lagudara , [for yaA A=la gudara , (see the letter l , and see A=lN , in art. Awl ,)] like yaA lafujara . (TA.) It is said in a trad., ↓ yaA gudaru ↓ A^alasotu A^asoEaY fiY gadoratika [app. meaning, O thou very perfidious: am I not striving, or labouring, in respect of thine act of perfidy, to rectify it? ]. (S: but in one copy, gudoratika .) And in another trad., relating to El-Hodeybiyeh, wahalo ↓ yaA gudaru A_il~aA biA@loA^amosi ↓ gasalota gadorataka [ O thou very perfidious: and didst thou wash away thine act of perfidy save yesterday? ]: said by 'Orweh Ibn-Mes'ood to El-Mugheereh. (TA.) And in another trad., ↓ Aijoliso gudaru [ Sit thou, O very perfidious ]; for yaA gudaru : said by 'Áïsheh to El-Kásim. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] ↓ sinuwna gad~aArapN (tropical:) Years in which is much rain and little herbage; from [the inf. n.] Algadoru ; i. e. that excite people's eager desire for abundance of herbage, by the rain, and then fail to fulfil their promise. (TA.) ― -b3- [And ↓ gadirN is app. syn. with gaAdirN ; for] gadirapN occurs in a trad. applied to land ( A^aroD ), as though meaning (assumed tropical:) Not producing herbage bountifully; or giving growth to herbage, and then soon becoming blighted, or blasted; wherefore it is likened to the gaAdir , who acts unfaithfully. (TA.) -A2- See also gudorapN , last sentence.

sourceDefinition: an inf. n. of gaDiba [q. v.]. (S, Msb, K.) AlgaDabu is The contr. of Alr~iDaY : (K, TA:) it is variously defined: some say that it is a state of excitement of the blood of the heart for the purpose of revenge: some say that pain on account of anything reparable is gaDab ; and for anything irreparable, A^asaf : some say that it [is a passion which ] includes all that is evil; wherefore the Prophet, to a man who asked of him a precept, said, laA tagoDabo : and some say that AlgaDab is [ a passion ] accompanied by an eagerness to obtain revenge; and Algam~ is accompanied by despair of obtaining it: (TA: [see also gayoZN :]) there is a gaDab that is commended, and a gaDab that is discommended; the former being that which is for the sake of religion and truth, or right; and the latter being that which is in a wrong case: and the gaDab of God is his disapproving of the conduct of him who disobeys Him, and whom He will therefore punish. (Ibn- 'Arafeh, TA.)

(O, K.) -A2- gamita He became like one intoxicated, by grease [ in his stomach ]: (Sh, O:) or he suffered from the heaviness of food upon his heart [or stomach ] so that he became like one intoxicated. (K.)

definition: , (S, A, K,) or gamazahu biyadihi , (Msb,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, K,) or gamazahu biyadihi , (Msb,) aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. gamozN , (TA,) He felt him, (namely, a ram,) to know if he were fat: (S, A, Msb, K:) and gamazahaA he put his hand upon her (a camel's) back, to see how fat she was. (TA.) ― -b2- Hence, (Msb,) gamazahu biyadihi , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. gamozN , (A, K,) He pressed, or squeezed, it, [ with his hand, ] namely, a limb, (A, K, TA,) and a man's back. (TA.) So in a trad. of 'Omar: daxala Ealayohi waEinodahu gulayomN yagomizu Zahorahu [ He went in to him, and with him was a little boy pressing, or squeezing, or kneading, his back ]. (TA.) And in a trad. respecting the ablution termed Algusol , it is said, AigomiziY quruwnaki , meaning Press thou, or squeeze thou, the locks of thy hair, in washing. (TA.) You also say, gamaza Alv~iqaAfu AlqanaApa The straightening-instrument pinched and pressed the spear. (A, * Mgh, TA. *) A poet (namely Ziyád El-Aajam, TA) says, wakunotu A_i*aA gamazotu qanaApa qawomK kasarotu kuEuwbahaA A^awo tasotaqiymaA [ And I used, when I pinched and pressed the spear of a people, to break its knots, or internodal portions, unless it became straight ]. (S, TA. It is a prov., respecting which see remarks in art. Aw .) -A2- gamaza , (A, Msb,) and gamazahu , (S, Mgh, K,) aor. , (Mgh, Msb, K,) inf. n. gamozN , (Msb, TA,) (tropical:) He made a sign, (A, Msb,) and he made a sign to him, (Mgh, K, *) with the eye, (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) or eyebrow, (A, Mgh, Msb, K,) or eyelid [by winking]. (K.) So in the saying, in a trad., gamazaniY EaliY~N A^ano qulo naEamo (tropical:) '4 lee made a sign to me with the eye, or eyebrow, meaning, Say thou Yes. (Mgh.) The people of the West say, gamazahu fulaAnN bifulaAnK , meaning, (tropical:) Such a one blinked towards such a one, to instigate him against him, or in order that he should have recourse to him for protection or the like, or seek aid of him. (Mgh.) ― -b2- Hence, Algamozu biAln~aAsi : (S:) you say, gamaza biAlr~ajuli , aor. , (K,) inf. n. gamozN , (TA,) (tropical:) He calumniated, or slandered, the man. (K.) [See also 4.] ― -b3- You say also, gumizato $ahaAdatahu [(assumed tropical:) His testimony was suspected (see magomuwzN ), or impugned ]. (TA in art. zwr .) -A3- gamazati Ald~aAb~apu , (K,) or gamaza fiY ma$oyihi , (Msb,) or mino rijolihi , (S,) aor. , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. gamozN , (S, Msb,) (assumed tropical:) The beast limped, or it halted, with its hind leg; had a slight lameness thereof: (K, * TA:) or he had what resembled Earaj [or natural lameness ] in his gait: (Msb:) or, as IKtt says, gamazati Ald~aAb~apu birijolihaA the beast gave an indication of a limping, or halting, or slight lameness, in its hind leg: whence it appears that this signification may be tropical. (TA.) -A4- gamaza said of a disease, or of a vice, or fault, of a man, It appeared. (AA, K.) -A5- See also 4.

definition: She (a camel) had fat, (O, K,) or a little fat, (ISd, IKtt, TA,) in her hump.
sourceDefinition: She (a camel) had fat, (O, K,) or a little fat, (ISd, IKtt, TA,) in her hump. (ISd, IKtt, O, K.) Hence the epithet ↓ gamuwzN , applied to her. (TA.) -A2- Agmz fiY fulaAnK (tropical:) He blamed, or found fault with, such a one; attributed or imputed to him, or charged him with, or accused him of, a vice, or fault; (S, IKtt, K, TA;) deemed him weak; (TA;) lessened his rank, or dignity: (S, IKtt, K, * TA:) he found in him that for which he should be deemed weak: (A, TA:) and ↓ Agtmzhu he impugned his character; blamed him; censured him; or spoke against him. (K.) You say, fulaAnN ↓ faEalotu $ayoy^FA fA@gotamazahu (tropical:) I did a thing, and such a one impugned my character, or found in it that by which my character was impugned. (S, TA.) And samiEa min~iY kalimapF fiY Eaqolihi ↓ faA@gotamazahaA (tropical:) He heard from me a saying, and deemed it weak: (A, TA:) and in like manner, A^agomaza fiyhaA found in it that for which it was to be deemed weak. (TA.) -A3- A^agomazaniY AlHar~u (tropical:) The heat remitted, or abated, to me, so that I became emboldened to encounter it, and went upon the road: (AA, ISk, S, IKtt, K, * TA:) Az says ↓ gamazaniY AlHar~u , on the authority of AA: (TA:) and AA mentioned AgmrnY AlHr~ in this sense, but afterwards doubted, and said, I think that it is with zAY . (TA in art. gmr .) ― -b2- And A^agomaza (assumed tropical:) He (a man) became gentle, so that others were emboldened against him. (IKtt, TA.) -A4- And A^agomaza [for which A^agomazah is erroneously put in the CK] He acquired cattle such as are termed gamaz [q. v.]: (O, K, TA:) like A^aqomaza . (O.)

definition: (tropical:) A thing for which one's character is to be impugned;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) A thing for which one's character is to be impugned; for which one is to be blamed, censured, or spoken against; a vice, or fault; (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K;) as also ↓ gamiyzN (TA) and ↓ magomazN (S, A, Mgh, K) or ↓ magomazapN : (Msb:) and weakness in work, and impotence of mind, (TA,) and ignorance: (T, TA:) the pl. of ↓ magomazN is magaAmizu , (TA,) syn. with maEaAyibu . (S.) You say, layosa fiyhi gamiyzapN , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) and ↓ gamiyzN , (TA,) and ↓ magomazN , (A, Mgh, K,) or ↓ magomazapN , (Msb,) (tropical:) There is not in him anything for which his character is to be impugned; or for which he is to be blamed; &c.: (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K:) or there is not in it anything for which it is to be coveted: (K:) or ↓ maA fiyhi magomazN has both of the above-mentioned significations. (A.) And fiY jam~apN ↓ fulaAnapa magaAmizu (tropical:) In such a woman are many vices, or faults. (A.) [See magomazN , below.]

definition: [should by rule be magomizN : its primary signification is A place of feeling, to know if an animal be fat: hence, a place of pressing or squeezing a limb &c.
sourceDefinition: [should by rule be magomizN : its primary signification is A place of feeling, to know if an animal be fat: hence, a place of pressing or squeezing a limb &c.: and a place of pinching and pressing a spear, to straighten it]. ― -b2- nukotapN laAmagomaza liqanaAtihaA walaA maqoraEa liSafaAtihaA (tropical:) [lit.
