definition: , (S, M, Msb,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, Msb,) aor. , (M, Msb,) inf. n. naqo$N . (S, M, A, Msb, K,) He variegated a thing; or decorated or embellished it; syn. namonama ; as also ↓ Antq$ : (M:) [ he charactered in any manner a coin &c.:] and he engraved, agreeably with modern usage: he coloured a thing with two colours, (K,) or with colours; (A, K;) and ↓ nq~$ , (S,) inf. n. tanoqiy$u , (S, K,) signifies the same. (S, K.) ― -b2- naqa$a fY xaAtamihi ka*aA , and EalaY faS~i xaAtamihi , (A,) inf. n. as above, (K,) [ He engraved upon his signet-ring such a thing, and upon the stone of his signet-ring: and naqa$a also signifies he marked with a cutting or a pointed instrument: he sculptured a thing in any manner.] ― -b3- naqa$a Alr~aHaA (tropical:) He pecked the mill-stone with a minoqaAr ; syn. naqarahaA . (A, TA.) ― -b4- naqa$a , inf. n. as above, also signifies He, or it, scratched, lacerated, or wounded in the outer skin. (TA.) They said, kaA^an~a wajohahu nuqi$a biqataAdapK [ As though his face were scratched, or lacerated, by a tragacanth-bush ]; syn. xudi$a : relating to hatefulness, and austerity or moroseness of countenance, (M, TA,) and anger. (M.) ― -b5- naqo$u AlEi*oqi signifies The striking the raceme of dates with thorns, in order that the dates may ripen: (S, K:) or and their consequently ripening. (AA.) And one says, nuqi$a AlEi*oqu , meaning, The raceme of dates had specks apparent in it, in consequence of ripening. (S.) ― -b6- And [hence, perhaps,] naqo$N is used as (tropical:) syn. with jimaAEN (S, A, Sgh, K,) accord. to AA, (S,) or IAar; (Sgh;) naqa$a signifying (tropical:) Inivit puellam. (T, K.) [This signification is mentioned in the A among those which are proper; but in the TA it is said, to be tropical.] -A2- Also naqa$a , (S, M, A, Msb,) aor. as above, (M, TA,) and so the inf. n., (S, M, Msb, K,) He extracted, or drew, or pulled, out, or forth, a thorn (S, M, A, Msb, K) from his foot, (S, M,) with the minoqa$ or minoqaA$ ; (Msb, K; *) as also ↓ Antq$ : (S, M, A, K:) thought by A 'Obeyd to be from AlmunaAqa$apu ; but others say the reverse: (TA:) and in like manner, bones from a wound in the head: (S, K:) and he plucked out (S, A,) hair, (A,) with the minoqaA$ ; (S, A;) as also ↓ Antq$ . (A.) A certain poet says, (namely, Yezeed Ibn-Maksam [?] EthThakafee, O in art. $wk ,) laA tanoqu$an~a birijoli gayorika $awokapF fataqiY birijolika rijola mano qado $aAkahaA [ Do not thou by any means extract from the foot of another a thorn, and so preserve, by (risking) thy foot, the foot of him who has pierced himself therewith ]: the [former] b is put in the place of Eano : he says, do not thou extract from the foot of another a thorn and put it in thy foot: (TA:) or mano $aAkahaA means who has entered among the thorns. (S and O, in art. $wk .) And it is said in a trad. of Aboo-Hureyreh, Eavara falaA A@notaEa$a wa$iyka falaA A@notaqa$a [ May he stumble, and not rise again; and may he be pierced with a thorn, and not extract the thorn ]: (M, TA: *) the words meaning an imprecation. (TA.) See also 8, below. ― -b2- [Hence,] naqa$a , aor. as above, (TA,) and so the inf. n., (K,) He cleared the nightly resting-place of sheep or goats from thorns and the like, (K,) or from what might hurt them, of stones and thorns and the like. (TA.) ― -b3- Hence also, naqa$a Eani Al$~aYo'i , (TK,) inf. n. as above, (IDrd, K,) He explored the thing to the utmost. (IDrd, K, TK.) ― -b4- [Hence also,] maA naqa$a minohu $ayoy^FA (assumed tropical:) He did not obtain from him anything: but the word commonly known is nata$a . (M, TA.) See also 8.

definition: , (Msb,) or nAq$hu AlHisaAba , (S, * M, A,) and fiY AlHisaAbi , (A,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (Msb,) or nAq$hu AlHisaAba , (S, * M, A,) and fiY AlHisaAbi , (A,) inf. n. munaAqa$apN (S, M, Msb, K) and niqaA$N , (M, TA,) He did the utmost with him, or went to the utmost length with him, in reckoning, (S, M, Msb, K,) so as to omit nothing therein: (A 'Obeyd:) A 'Obeyd thinks that naqo$N signifying the “ extracting ” a thorn from the foot is from this; but others say the reverse; that the primary signification of munaAqa$apN is the extracting a thorn from the body with difficulty; and that it then became [conventionally regarded as] a proper term in the sense of doing the utmost, or going to the utmost length, in reckoning; as observed by MF. (TA.) It is said in a trad., mano nuwqi$a AlHisaAba Eud~iba , (S,) or halaka , (M,) He with whom the utmost is done in reckoning (S, M,) is punished, (S,) or perishes. (M.) See also 4. ― -b2- [Hence,] nAq$ AlkalaAma (assumed tropical:) He picked out the faults of the language; syn. naqadahu . (TA, art. nqd .)

definition: , aor. , (A, TA,) inf. n. hamos (AHeyth, L, TA) and hamiysN and humuwsN , (L, TA,) He spoke inaudibly: (AHeyth, TA:) or in a low, faint, gentle, or soft, manner, (AHeyth, TA,) so as to be hardly...
sourceDefinition: , aor. , (A, TA,) inf. n. hamos (AHeyth, L, TA) and hamiysN and humuwsN , (L, TA,) He spoke inaudibly: (AHeyth, TA:) or in a low, faint, gentle, or soft, manner, (AHeyth, TA,) so as to be hardly intelligible. (TA.) It is said in a trad. fajaEala baEoDunaA yahomisu A_ilaY baEoDK And some of us began to speak to others in a low, faint, gentle, or soft, manner, so as to be hardly intelligible. (TA.) And in another trad., kaAna *aA A_iSal~aY AlEaSora hamasa bi$aYo'K laA nafohamuhu He used, when he performed the afternoon-prayer, to utter something in a low, faint, gentle, or soft manner, we not understanding it. (TA.) You say also, hamasa A_ilaY~a biHadiyvihi [ He uttered his discourse to me inaudibly: or in a low, faint, gentle, or soft, manner. ] (A.) And Al$~ayoTaAnu yahomisu biwasowasatihi Sadora AlA_inosaAni [ The devil speaks inaudibly in his suggesting vain or unprofitable things into the bosom of man ]. (A.) And hamasa Al$~ayoTaAnu fiY AlS~adori The devil suggested vain, or unprofitable things in the bosom; syn. wasowasa . (TA.) See also hamosN below. ― -b2- Also, aor. and inf. n. as above, He made the faintest, or slightest, sound in treading. So in the saying, A_ihomiso waSaho and hamosFA waSaho Make thou the faintest, or slightest, sound in treading, and be thou silent: addressed by a thief to his companion. (TA.) And hence the saying of the Rájiz, fahun~a yamo$iyna bihi hamiysaA And they walk with him making the faintest, or slightest, sound in treading. (S.) hamiysN also signifies The walking softly; with a soft-sounding tread: (TA:) [and so hamosN ; as in the saying,] samiEotu hamosa AlA^axofaAfi waAlA^aqodaAmi [ I heard the soft-sounding treading of the feet of camels and of the feet of men ]. (A.) See also hamosN below. -A2- hamasa AlS~awota , aor. , inf. n. hamosN , He made the sound, or voice to be low, faint, gentle, or soft. (Msb.) And hamasa AlkalaAma , [aor. and] inf. n. as above, [ He spoke in a low, faint, gentle, or soft manner; like hamasa alone; lit.,] he made speech, or the speech to be low, faint, gentle, or soft. (A, TA.) -A3- hamasa AlT~aEaAma , (TK), [aor. and] inf. n. as above, (AZ, K,) He chewed the food with the mouth closed: (AZ, K, TA:) or without opening the mouth. (TA.) You say, huwa yaokulu hamosFA He eats without opening his mouth. (A.) Hence, a toothless old woman's eating is termed hamosN . (AHeyth.) hamasahu also signifies [simply] He chewed it. (TA.)

definition: A low, faint, gentle, or soft, sound.
sourceDefinition: A low, faint, gentle, or soft, sound. (S, A, Msb, K.) So it has been explained as occurring in the words of the Kur, [xx. 107,] falaA tasomaEu A_il~aA hamosFA [ So that thou shalt not hear aught save ] a low, faint, gentle, or soft, sound, arising from the shifting of the feet from place to place towards the scene of congregation [for the general judgment]: or, as Az thinks, the meaning here is, the sound of the patting, or pattering, of the feet ( xafoqa AlA^aqodaAmi ) upon the ground. (TA.) ― -b2- The faint, or gentle, sound of the voice in the mouth, of such kind as has no mixture of the voice of the chest, nor loudness of utterance. (Lth, K.) See also mahomuwsN . ― -b3- And Anything low, faint, gentle, or soft, ( kul~u xafiY~K , K, TA,) of speech and the like: (TA:) [see again, mahomuwsN :] or the faintest, or slightest, sound of the feet; (S, K;) i. e., of their tread upon the ground: (TA:) so [accord. to J] in the instance in the Kur, [xx. 107,] mentioned above: (S:) and [in like manner] ↓ hamiysN signifies the sound of the shifting from place to place of the feet of camels. (K.) See also 1.

sourceDefinition: A certain bird, (S, Mgh, K,) of the pigeon-kind, (AHát, Mgh, Msb,) or resembling the pigeon, (TA,) also called saAqu Hur~K , (S, Msb, K,) which is the male of the qamaAriY~ [or kind of collared turtle-doves of which a single female is called qumoriy~apN (see qumoriY~N )], (Msb,) of the birds of the desert, (TA,) the flesh of which is lighter than that of the [ common ] pigeon: (K:) fem. with p : (K:) pl. waraA$iynu (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and wiro$aAnN , (S, Msb, K,) like as kiruwaAnN is a pl. of karawaAnN , contr. to rule. (S.) It is said in a proverb, biEil~api Alwara$aAni taA^okulu ruTaba Almu$aAni [ With the pretext of the warashán, thou eatest the fresh ripe dates of the excellent kind called m$An ]: (S, A, K:) said to him who pretends one thing and means another: (A, K:) originating from the fact that some people employed a slave belonging to them to guard the fresh ripe dates of their palm-trees, and he used to eat them, and, when reproved for his evil conduct, laid the blame upon the warashán; wherefore this was said to him. (Sgh.)

definition: Light, and whiteness, (S,) of anything: (TA:) the whiteness of daybreak, or dawn: and of the moon;

(TA.) ― -b2- SuwmuwA mina AlwaDaHi A_ilaY AlwaDaHi Fast ye from new moon to new moon. (IAth, from a trad.) ― -b3- waDaHN (tropical:) Leprosy; syn. baraSN . (S, K.) It is sometimes used in this sense, metonymically. (S.) ― -b4- waDaHN A mark in a horse differing in colour from the generality of his coat. You say biAlfarasi waDaHN In the horse is such a mark. (S.) ― -b5- waDaHN A blaze, or white mark on a horse's forehead or face. (K.) ― -b6- What is termed taHojiylN in the legs of a horse. (L, K.) And also applied to other varieties of colour. (L.) ― -b7- frasN *uw A^awoDaAHK A horse having a blaze and what is termed tHjyl . (A.) ― -b8- waDaHN Whiteness of the hair, or hoariness; or white, or hoary, hair. (K.) ― -b9- (tropical:) Milk: (L, K:) thought by ISd to be so called because of its whiteness: or milk that has not been mixed with water: (L:) or that is just drawn. (TA, art. zhr .) Aboo-Dhueyb says, Eaq~awoA bisahomK falamo ya$oEuro bihi A^aHadN vum~a A@sotafaw^uwA waqaAluwAHab~a*aA AlwaDaHu [ They shot an arrow towards the sky, and no one knew of it: then they returned, and said, An excellent thing is milk ]: meaning, we would rather have milk than the blood of him who has killed our companion: they preferred that camels should be given them in compensation. (TA.) ― -b11- waDaHN The middle, or main part and middle, of a road; the part of a road along which one travels. (S, K.) ― -b12- waDaHN A woman's ornament ( HaloYN ) of silver: (A 'Obeyd, K:) or, of stones; (El-Meshárik;) i. e. of silverstones: (Towsheeh:) so called because of its whiteness: (TA:) pl. A^awoDaAHN : (K:) or A^awoDaAHN signifies a kind of woman's ornament ( HaloYN ) made of whole [ silver coins such as are called ] daraAhim : (S:) and (according to some, TA,) waDaHN signifies an anklet; syn. xaloxaAlN (K) ― -b13- waDaHN (K) or waDaHN AlT~ariyfapi , (L, but the latter word is there written; Tryqp ,) Small portions, or parts, of herbage; (L, K;) what he has become white thereof: (AHn:) pl. A^awoDaAHN : (L:) or A^awoDaAHN mino kalaA_K signifies somewhat of herbage that has become white: (As:) Az says, I have mostly heard the term waDaHN , with respect to herbage, applied to the naSiY~ and Sil~iyaAn SayofiY~ which is not a year old and has not become black: and on another occasion he says, that it is the remains of the HaliY~ and Sil~iyaAn only. (L.) ― -b14- waDaHN Whiteness predominating over other colours in sheep or goats, overspreading generally the whole body: pl. A^awoDaAHN : (L:) or, in the breast and back and face: (T:) you say also ↓ lahu tawoDyHN . (L.) ― -b15- mino A^ayona badaA waDaHuka : see 1. ― -b16- waDaHu Alqadami Whiteness of the hollow of the sole of the foot. (L.)

definition: and ↓ waD~aAHN [but the latter has an intensive signification] Apparent, or plainly apparent;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ waD~aAHN [but the latter has an intensive signification] Apparent, or plainly apparent; overt; conspicuous; manifest; notorious; plain; obvious; or evident; (L, K;) clear, or unobscured; exposed to view; displayed; laid open; disclosed, or uncovered. (So accord. to the explanation of the verb in the Msb.) ― -b2- Perspicuous language. (The Lexicons passim.) ― -b3- Also the ↓ latter, A man of white, or fair, and beautiful, complexion: (S, L, K:) of beautiful and smiling countenance. (L.) ― -b4- See mutawaD~iHN . ― -b5- Also the ↓ latter, (tropical:) Leprous. Hence Jedheemeh El-Abrash was called AlwaD~aAHu . (S.) ― -b6- ↓ AlwaD~aAHu The day. (L, K.) The night is called Ald~ahomaAnu . (L.) ― -b7- ↓ bikoru AlwaD~aAHi The prayer of morning, or daybreak. The prayer of nightfall is called vinoYu dahomaAna . (L, K [but in the CK and a MS. copy of the K, for dahomaAna , we find duhomaAna ].) ― -b8- ↓ EaZomu waD~aAHK , (L, K,) and EuZayomu waD~aAHK , (L,) A certain game ( of the children of the Arabs of the desert, L,) in which children take a white bone and throw it in the darkness of night, and then disperse themselves in search of it: (L, K:) he who finds it wins. (L.) [See more in art. EZm .] ― -b9- ↓ huwa minoka A^adonaY waADiHapK He is plainly apparent to thee, as though he had become white. (Th.) ― -b10- rajulN waADHu AlHasabi , and ↓ waD~aAHuhu , (tropical:) A man as though he were conspicuous, clean, or pure, and white, with respect to rank or quality, nobility, reputation, or the like. (L.) ― -b11- In like manner one says, ↓ lahu Aln~asabu AlwaD~aAHu (tropical:) He is of conspicuous and pure race, or lineage. (TA.) ― -b12- waADiHN (assumed tropical:) An illustrious man. (EsSaadee.) ― -b13- [And so] min Aln~aAsi waA^awobaA$N ↓ A^awoDaAHN [ Illustrious people, and mixed people of the baser sort; ] companies of people of various tribes. No sing. of AwDAH in this sense has been heard. (L.) ― -b14- AlwuD~axu [pl. of waADiHN ] The stars called AlkawaAkibu Alxun~asu [namely, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury, ] when in conjunction with the bright stars of the Mansions of the Moon. (L.)

definition: , (aor. yahabu , K; said to be originally yawohibu ; which is changed into yahibu because of the kesr; and then, into yahabu because of the medial guttural letter; Msb, voce wasiEa ;) inf. n. wahobN...
sourceDefinition: , (aor. yahabu , K; said to be originally yawohibu ; which is changed into yahibu because of the kesr; and then, into yahabu because of the medial guttural letter; Msb, voce wasiEa ;) inf. n. wahobN and wahabN and hibapN (S, K) and mawohibN and mawohibapN , (Msb,) or the last two are substs., (S, K, &c.) He gave him a thing; properly, as a free gift, disinterestedly, and not for any compensation. (Msb, TA.) You should not say wahabakahu [ he gave it to thee ], (K, &c.,) making the verb doubly trans.: (TA:) or [this is allowable, as it is said that] AA has related this on the authority of an Arab of the desert: so in the K: but in the L, it is said that Seer has related this, from 'Amr, (meaning Sb,) from an Arab of the desert. (TA.) En-Nawawee allows the expression wahabutu ka*aA minohu , meaning, I gave such a thing to him, &c.; ( mn being redundant, as in biEotu ka*aA minohu “ I sold such a thing to him; ”) as occurring in several trads. (MF.) ― -b2- See 3. ― -b3- wahabaniYA@ll~`hu fidaAka May God make me [or give me as ] thy ransom! (IAar, K.) wuhibotu fidaAka May I be made [or given as ] thy ransom! Ibn-Umm-Kásim says, that whb is one of the verbs which signify He caused to be, or to become: and he cites the above phrase from IAar; and adds, that the verb is only used in the pret. tense. definition: He prepared, or made ready, the thing for him.
sourceDefinition: He prepared, or made ready, the thing for him. (K.) ― -b2- A^awohabotuka AlT~aEaAma waAl$~araAba I prepared, or made ready, for thee the food and beverage, and abundance of them. (Tahdheeb el-Af'ál.) But see this verb in an intrans. sense. ― -b3- A^awohaba AlT~aEaAmu (tropical:) The food, or corn, or the like, became abundant and ample, so that some of it was given away. (A.) -A2- A^awohabotu liA^amori ka*aA (tropical:) I became capable of such a thing and able to do it. (A.) ― -b2- A^awohaba laka Al$~aYo'u The thing was, or became, within thy power, or reach, so that thou mightest take it. (K. *) Related on the authority of IAar alone, who says, They did not say A^awohabotuhu laka . (TA.) ― -b3- A^awohaba lahu Al$~aYo'u The thing was lasting to him. (A'Obeyd, AZ, S, K.) J cites the following verse: EaZiymu AlqafaA rixowu AlxawaASiri A^awohabato lahu EajowapN masomuwnapN waxamiyru [ Large in the back of the neck, soft (or loose or flabby ) in the flanks: dates of the best that ElMedeeneh produces, prepared with clarified butter, and leaven, are lasting ( provisions ) to him ]. But 'Alee Ibn-Hamzeh says, that this is a mistake, and that the right reading is A^urohinato , meaning “ are prepared, and continued. ” So in a marginal note in a copy of the S. (TA.) [So too in the margin of one of my MS. copies of the S.]

definition: A thought, or an idea, occurring in the mind: (Mgh, Msb, * K: *) pl.
sourceDefinition: A thought, or an idea, occurring in the mind: (Mgh, Msb, * K: *) pl. A^awohaAmN : (Msb:) or of the two extremes [or different opinions or ideas ] between which one wavers, that which is outweighed [ in probability ]. (K.) An [ indecisive ] opinion or idea outweighed in probability [ or formed from evidence outweighed in probability; a presumption; a surmise; a fancy; a supposition ]: opposed to Zan~N , q. v. (Kull, p. 376.) ― -b2- Also Doubt, or suspicion: but for this I have found no authority; though it is well known, and plainly indicated in the Msb, in art. xyl ; voce xay~ala , q. v. in this Lex. ― -b3- Also The object of a thought, or of an idea, occurring in the mind. (Mgh.) And The mind itself, or intellect; syn. EaqolN . (MF, TA.) In modern Arabic it signifies An imagination, a fancy, a chimera, and a conjecture.
